The Planning Commission informed that tentative allocation of the Department would be Rs.5400.00 
crores. Subsequently, in the meeting held in the Planning Commission to discuss the proposal for 
Annual Plan 2003-2004, it was emphasised that additional funds of Rs.194.00 crores would be required 
on account of increased coverage for Polio rounds in the affected States and two additional rounds of 
Sub-National Immunisation Days (SNIDs). An additional allocation of Rs.120.00 crores based on the 
requirement as per the 1991 population was also accepted for opening additional Sub-Centres.  Thus, an 
allocation of Rs.5714.00 crores was agreed and recommended. However, later the approved outlay as 
communicated by the Planning Commission was Rs.4930.00 crores only. 
Further, the Department informed that the reduced allocation would result in major cut in the Grant-in-
aid to the States for the maintenance of infrastructural units (particularly the Sub-Centres) and payment 
of the arrears. Some of the other adversely affected schemes are RCH Programme; Measures under 
National Population Policy; Maternity Benefit Scheme; Supply of Contraceptives and USAID assisted 
SIFPSA Project. 
            While the Committee appreciates the constraints of budgetary exercise of matching the 
known resources of revenue  with the requirements of outflow of funds, it expresses its concern 
over   huge cut in the allocation.    We are already seized of the effects of over population.  Family  
Planning as well as Welfare  are  therefore, unavoidable vital component of the Planning in our 
country.    Abdication of responsibility by way of non allocation is fraught with disastrous 
consequences.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission should review 
the allocation and provide additional funds at the earliest so that continuity of welfare 
programmes and Schemes is ensured so that it does not affect the pace of steps being taken to 
right-size the population of the country. 
III        RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES 
            The Rural Family Welfare Centres (RFWCs)  were set up at all block level PHCs 
sanctioned upto 1.4.1980 to provide Family Planning and MCH services in rural areas. The 
scheme of Rural Family Welfare Centres (RFWCs) has been merged into the Primary Health 
Care System of the States.   As per information available from States/UTs, all the 1,37,311 Sub-
Centres are functional in the country. Government of India funds all these Centres with effect 
from 1.4.2002.  97,757 Sub-Centres were funded by Department of Family Welfare till March 
2002, and the remaining Sub-Centres i.e. 39,554 Sub-Centres were funded by State Governments. 
The Department was targeting to establish 8669 Sub-Centres during the Tenth Five -Year Plan.  
All these 8669 Sub-Centres (which include 461 for the desert areas of Rajasthan) would be  set up 
during 2003-2004. 
The Department has also informed that a facility survey was conducted in 12 Districts/ Sub-Divisions of 
the States in the year 1999 to assess the availability of health care facilities and its utilization at Primary 
Health Centres (PHCs)/Community Health Centres (CHCs)/First Referral Units (FRUs)/District 
Hospitals and in all, 221 districts were covered under this.  The survey assessed the availability and 
utilization of facilities at these primary health care institutions.  The survey in the remaining 372 
districts covering Primary Health Centres/Sub-Centres including Indian System of Medicine & 
Homeopathy facilities on sample basis started in 2002. The results of these surveys are expected to be 
available shortly.    
While the Committee keenly awaits the outcome of survey referred to above in respect of 
PHCs /CHCs/FRU/ District Hospitals etc., it can assess the plight of these units based on the 
grossly inadequate and poor health care system that prevails in Metros and other big towns of the 
country.    The Committee, however, recommends that steps should continue to be taken to 
strengthen these units to provide maximum health care facilities as also in terms of man power.

            The scheme was launched in 1950 to provide Family welfare services in urban areas.Under

V         REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH (RCH) PROGRAMME 
            The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) programme that is being implemented by the 
Government of India is expected to provide quality services and achieve multiple objectives. There has 
been a positive paradigm shift from the method-mix target based approach to client centered, demand 
driven quality services. The main objective of the Scheme is to strengthen reproductive and child health 
care services in the country with the aim of reducing maternal and infant mortality and creating a greater 
awareness about the rights of the population in health care. Four major initiatives were taken by 
Department of Family Welfare to address critical problems of high infant and maternal mortality and 
relatively low contraceptive prevalence which are: (i) Provision of capital investment in form of non-
recurring grant for construction, repair and refurbishing health infrastructure.; (ii) Provision of financial 
assistance to higher medical and para medical personnel on contract basis; (iii) Supply of drugs, 
vaccines and equipment of delivering RCH including immunization services; (iv) Community based 
initiatives such as cash assistance for providing transport to pregnant women to referral centers, 
community incentives for involving the PRIs, training and provision of training to Trained Birth 
Attendants(TBAs) in conducting safe deliveries, conducting of outreach camps in underserved areas etc; 
and  (v) Computerization and improved data management for Family Welfare. 
The allocation in BE 2002-2003 was Rs. 800.53 crores but in RE it was reduced to Rs. 445.54 crores . 
The allocation in BE 2003-2004 has been increased to Rs. 712.41 crores for this Scheme.

VI        REPRODUCTIVE TRACT INFECTION/SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS 
Reproductive Tract Infection/Sexually Transmitted Infections are very common among the women in 
the reproductive age (15-44 years).   In order to overcome the problem, RTI/STI clinics were being 
setup in the First Referral Units (FRUs) in a phased manner.   429 RTI /STI clinics in the FRUs have 
been identified by the states for management of RTI/STI cases exclusively. 
Since it is linked to HIV / AIDS, the planning and implementation of services for RTI/STI has been 
done in close collaboration with National AIDs Control Organisation (NACO). 307 Laboratory 
technicians have been appointed in 25 States/UTs for this purpose and based on the proposals  received 
from States funds to the tune of   Rs. 450.14 lakhs have been released to them.   Training arrangements 
in RTI/STI were being set up under the RCH Programme organized through the National Institute of 
Health and Family Welfare.  
            The Committee notes with concern that only 307 Laboratory  Technicians have been 
appointed  for 429 identified clinics.   The Committee  observes that it is  not  sufficient to redress 
the problem.   It  therefore, recommends that the appointment of Technicians for rest of the clinics 
be expedited.

Haryana, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and West Bengal.

XII      LOGISTIC IMPROVEMENT 
To reduce wastage in the supply of contraceptives and vaccines due to poor management of stores, a 
scheme to strengthen the logistics system for receiving, storing and distributing drugs, vaccines and 
contraceptives for Family Welfare Programme in the States has been initiated. Under the scheme States 
are being asked to draw state specific plans for managing the stores along with distribution network till 
the Sub-centre to ensure availability of right material at the right time. For this purpose organizational 
systems and infrastructure for procurement, storage and distribution is required to be strengthened. On 
the basis of experience of system developed in Tamil Nadu, studies were underway to have in place a 
practical logistic system in the State of Karnataka, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa. 
The budget allocation under ‘Logistic Improvement’ in BE 2002-2003 from Rs 9.00 crores was reduced 
drastically at RE stage to Rs. 2.00 crores.   A notional amount of Rs. 0.90 crores has been put in the BE 
2003-2004 for this purpose.   The Department has informed that State Governments as well as M/s. 
Hindustan Latex Ltd has undertaken number of studies.  Some of the study reports, which have been 
received were being examined and would be discussed further with the State Governments.  Since, it 
would take time to examine these proposals, provision has been reduced in the last year as well as for 
the year 2003-2004. It is, however, proposed to address the issues related to logistics in a more 
comprehensive manner under the RCH-II Project. 
The Committee expresses its displeasure that the Scheme was finalized and budget allocated 
without making details of the procedure to be followed to run the Scheme. The Department should 
fix a timeframe to study the reports and implement the modified Scheme. Since, the Department is 
proposing a lot for RCH II Project, it should be ensured that all the steps are taken in a manner to 
make the project practically viable to achieve the target.

The Department has informed  that the implementation of the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques.

from the States and UTs show that more than 19,600 bodies have been registered, 373 cases have been

campaigns are also being conducted by States and UTs.

XV       NEW INITIATIVES- NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY, 2000 
The National Population Policy, 2000 (NPP, 2000) affirms the commitment of Government of India 
towards voluntary and informed choice and consent of citizens while availing of reproductive healthcare 
services. And continuation of the target free approach in administering family planning services. The 
NPP 2000 provides a policy framework for advancing goals and prioritizing strategies during the next 
decade, to meet the reproductive and child health needs of the people of India, and to achieve net 
replacement levels (TFR) by 2010. It is based upon the need to simultaneously address issues of child 
survival, maternal health, and contraception, while increasing outreach and coverage of a comprehensive 
package of reproductive and child health services by Government, industry and the voluntary non-

         The immediate objective of the NPP 2000 is to address the unmet needs for contraception, health 
care infrastructure, and health personnel, and to provide integrated service delivery for basic 
reproductive and child health care. The medium-term objective is to bring the TFR to replacement levels 
by 2010, through vigorous implementation of inter-sectoral operational strategies. The long-term 
objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirements of 
sustainable economic growth, social development and environmental protection.

A&N Islands, Chandigarh and Mizoram have already achieved replacement levels of fertility. The 11 
States and Union Territories of Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Punjab, 
Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Lakshwadeep, Daman and Diu and Sikkim have Total 
Fertility Rate of more than 2.1 but less than 3.0. There are at least 11 States and Union Territories that

during the period 1996-2016. Demographic outcomes in these States would determine the timing and 
size of population at which India achieves population stabilization.

country.    Abdication of responsibility by way of non allocation is fraught with disastrous 
consequences.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission should review

I           INTRODUCTION 
The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy was set up by the Government of 
India as an independent Department in March, 1995 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  
The main objective of the Department is to provide focused attention for the proper development and 
propagation of ISM&H, namely, Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy and 
to fully utilise the potentials of these systems. 
The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM& H) is headed by a Secretary 
to the Government of India who is assisted by a Joint Secretary and four Directors/Deputy Secretaries, 4 
Advisers and several Deputy Advisors of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani &. Homoeopathy. Senior level posts 
such as Director (Ayurveda & Siddha), Adviser (Ayurveda), Adviser (Unani) & Adviser (Homoeopathy) 
have been created for providing expert advice on policy formulation and execution, complex technical 
and pharmacopoeial matters. There are 3 subordinate offices and 15  autonomous bodies under this 
Department and more than 4000 personnel are working in these institutions/ organizations/subordinate 
offices. A manufacturing company is also working under the Department. A Medicinal plants Board is 
functioning under the Department to co-ordinate activities relating to conservation, cultivation, 
marketing, export and drawing policies and strategies for the development of medicinal plants sector. A 
Medicinal Plants Cell (MPC) is working under the Department for implementing the Central Scheme for 
development and cultivation of Medicinal Plants and developing agro-techniques. A  nucleus Patent Cell 
is working under the Department for dealing with developing Traditional Knowledge Digital Library
(TKDL) and matters relating to Intellectual Property Rights as also coordination with Government of 
India Ministries/Departments concerned with IPR.

did not pass on the funds to the implementing agencies and thereby causing delay in utilization of funds

2.5       The Committee feels that non submission of utilization certificates by the States is a perennial 
problem which is derailing several developmental activities in the States.  The Committee is happy to 
note that Ministry of Finance has formulated  guidelines on furnishing of utilisation certificates by the

states to submit utilization certificates and vigorously  implement the Finance Ministry’s Guideline. 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department for the 10th Plan.  However, the Committee, 
feels that unless the causes for low utilization of funds as identified in the 9th  Plan are  addressed, the 
objectives of the 10th Plan may not be fully realized.  As far as non submission of utilization certificates 
by the ‘Implementing Agencies’ is concerned, the Committee feels that there could be possibilities of 
diversion, misutilisation or in some cases misappropriation of Government funds. The Committee,

V         AYURVEDA 
5.1       Ayurveda (Ayu +Veda) means the "Science of Life". The documentation of Ayurveda is referred 
to in Vedas (5000 BC). The origin of Ayurveda or the Indian Science of life is linked with the origin of 
Universe and developed out of the various Vedic hymns describing fundamentals/philosophies about the 
world and life, diseases and medicines. Around 1000 B.C, the knowledge of Ayurveda was 
comprehensively documented in Charak Samhita and Sushruta Samhita. According to Ayurveda, health 
is considered a pre-requisite for achieving the goals of life, dharma, artha, kama &. moksha (salvation). 
Ayurveda takes an integrated view of the physical ,mental and spiritual and social aspects of human 
beings, each impinging on the other. The philosophy of Ayurveda is based on the theory of 
Panchmahabhutas (five element theory) of which all the objects and living bodies are composed of. The 
combination of these five elements are represented in the form of Tridosha eg., Vata (Ether+ Air), Pitta 
(Fire) and Kaph (Water + Earth). These three 'Doshas' are physiological entities in living beings. These 
are also known as three humours. The mental, spiritual and physical attributes are described as Satva, 
Rajas and Tamas. The doctrine of Ayurveda aims to keep these structural and functional entities in a 
functional state of equilibrium which signifies good health (Swastha). Any imbalance due to internal or 
external factors causes disease and restoring the equilibrium through various techniques, procedures, 
regimen, diet and medicine constitute the treatment. Ayurveda considers the human being as a 
microcosm (Yatha pinde tatha brahmande), a replica of macrocosm (Universe). The treatment in 
Ayurveda system is individualized. Treatment in Ayurveda has two components; (a) Preventive; and (b) 
Curative: Preventive aspect of Ayurveda is called Svasth-Vritt and includes personal hygiene, regular 
daily routine, appropriate social behaviour and Rasayana Sevana, i.e, use of  rejuvenative materials/food 
and rasayans drugs. The curative treatment consists of three major categories of procedures (i)Aushadhi 
(drugs); (ii) Anna (diets) and (iii) Vihara(exercises and general mode of life) 
The Plan allocation for Ayurveda in 2003-2004 is Rs.14.46 crores. The Committee has been informed 
that amongst the European Countries only Hungry  has recognized the system of Ayurveda. Countries 
like, Russia, Italy, Spain, Belgium, U.K. and U.S.A. though have shown keen interest for the system, are 
yet to recognize it.  These Countries, though are positive about recognizing the system of Ayurveda but 
want assurance about the quality and safety of drugs.  The Department has further informed that for 
ensuring quality control it has recently introduced good manufacturing practices and land down certain 
norms and standards for manufacture of Ayurvedic Medicine. 
   The Committee feels that the European Countries, USA and other developed and prosperous countries 
have tremendous potential to become an extremely lucrative market for the Ayurvedic drugs of our 
country and can generate a lot of foreign exchange for the Country. However, in order to achieve this, as 
rightly pointed out by the Department, the confidence of such countries w.r.t. the safety and quality of 
such drugs has to be won. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should 
keep a tight vigil of the quality and safety of the Ayurveda drugs manufactured and used in India or 
exported out of India so that more and more countries recognize our traditional system of medicine.

The Committee observes that people opt for traditional medicine because they are affordable and less 
harmful. However, the experts have voiced concerns about the safety and quality, licensing of providers 
and standards of training in connection with traditional medicines. 
            The World Health Organization has come out with a traditional medicine strategy for 2002-2005 
which focuses on these issues. According to WHO, 70 per cent of Indian population use traditional 
medicine for their primary health needs.  
            A group of experts recently met in Delhi to chalk out an adequate strategy for integration of 
traditional medicine with the health care system in India. According to these experts, a set of standards 
for regulating traditional medicine and setting up of a body to provide to medical claims is necessary. 
            The Committee feels the safety and efficiency of traditional medicine has been established 
through centuries of use. However, in order to make it acceptable to the outside world it may be 
necessary to validate its scientific basis. Here, the Committee is of the view that we need not tinker with 
our system for this purpose. Chernobyl incident convinced Russians about the efficacy of our system of 
medicine when the victims’ burns were miraculously healed. Likewise there are many simple plants and 
products like neem and turmeric, the efficacy of which tempted some countries abroad to have these 
products patented for commercial exploitation. The Committee therefore reiterates that the system need 
not be tinkered with to convince the outside world.  
            The attention of the Committee has been drawn to the fact that there are many traditional 
medicine practitioners who have claimed a cure for some disease or the other. In most cases they end up 
making rounds of Government agencies or try to sell their formula to pharmaceuticals but to little avail 
e.g. the person who claimed to have developed a herbal contraceptive in the 
 1980, passed away by the time Government decided to follow it up. The Committee observes the need 
to avoid such situations. The Government machinery should be suitably geared up and be responsive in 
such situations. 
VI        HOMOEOPATHY 
6.1       Homoeopathy is a specialized method of drug therapy of curing natural diseases by 
administration of drugs which has been experimentally proved to possess the power of producing similar 
artificial symptoms on healthy human beings . In Homoeopathy, medicines are prepared from natural 
sources Vegetable, Mineral, Animal, etc. There is no toxic or poisonous effect in these medicines since 
it is not the chemical or physical properties that are acting on the human system. Homoeopathy has its 
own areas of strength in therapeutics. Its curative capability extends to allergic manifestations, auto-
immune disorders and viral infections. Many Surgical, Gynaecological & Obstetrical conditions, 
ailments, affecting eyes, nose, ear, teeth, skin, sexual organs etc. are amenable to the homoeopathic 
treatment. Behaviour disorders, neurological problems, metabolic diseases are successfully handled by 
the physicians of this system. Homoeopathy has effective answer to addiction to drugs, tobacco and 
alcohol and is highly efficacious in ridding of addicts and their craving for these noxious substances)  
  Plan allocation for Homoeopathy was Rs. 10.21 crores in BE 2002-2003. However it has been reduced 
to Rs. 9.17 crores in BE 2003-2004. The Secretary while deposing before the Committee informed that 
presently there are 80 colleges of homoeopathy in the Country and out of which 17 colleges are 
imparting PG education.  However, there is no separate university for Homoeopathy. 
6.3       The Committee feels that in the absence of a separate university, the Homoeopathy education is 
perhaps not getting the attention it deserves. The Committee further feels that the quality of imparting 
Homoeopathy education can be vastly improved if an exclusive Homoeopathy university is established 
to regulate and monitor the functioning of the medical colleges throughout the Country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should consider establishing a separate Homoeopathy 
University and the allocation under the head `Homoeopathy should be increased accordingly. 
            At the same time there have been illiterate persons who acquired marvelous proficiency in 
developing this system of medicine.  The Committee, therefore, feels that there should be room for 
persons with average qualification to study and develop their skills in the field of Homoeopathy.  Part 
time colleges should also be encouraged to help people come forward to acquire knowledge and 
expertise in this system of medicine.

VII       YOGA AND NATUROPATHY 
7.1       Yoga is primarily a way of life propounded by Patanjali in a systematic form. It consists of eight 
components, namely, restraint, observance of austerity, physical postures, breathing exercise, restraining 
of sense  organs, contemplation, meditation and samadhi. These steps in the practice of Yoga have 
potential for improvement of social and personal behaviour, improvement of physical health by 
encouraging better  circulation of oxygenated blood in the body, restraining the sense organs and thereby 
inducing tranquility and a serenity of mind. The practice of Yoga prevents psychosomatic 
disorders/diseases and improves individual resistance and ability to endure stressful situations. 
Meditation, one of the eight  components, if regularly practiced, has the capacity to reduce wholesome 
bodily responses to a bare minimum so that the mind can be directed to perform more fruitful functions. 
7.2       The Plan allocation for Yoga and Naturopathy for the year 2003-2004 is Rs. 5.10 crores.  The 
Committee has been informed that there are 6 colleges in the country which are imparting training in 
yoga and naturopathy and there is also a Central Council for Yoga and Naturopathy which provides 
money for research and running of various schemes.  The Secretary while deposing before the 
Committee informed that the Department of ISMH is planning to pass an Act in the Parliament so as to 
empower the Council to grant recognition to the council so that Naturopathy and Yoga are regulated like 
other disciplines. 
            The Committee observes that the pros and cons should be considered before taking a decision to 
introduce legislation  in this regard.   
VIII          QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS 
8.1       A Drug Control Cell (ISM &. H) is working in the Department to deal with the matters 
pertaining to licensing and regulation of drugs and control of misbranded/adulterated and spurious 
manufacturing of Ayurvedic, Unani and Siddha Drugs and other matters related thereto. Besides, 
Information, Education & Communication Cell and Facilitation Centre have also been set up in the 
Department. 
8.2       Quality Control of ISM&H drugs is one of the priority areas of the Department.  The Secretary 
informed the Committee that the state Drug Licensing Authority has been designated as the ‘Licensing 
Authority’ and are mandated to take  all measures to ensure quality control.  However, the machinery 
and infrastructure required for testing of drugs is very poor in most of the States.  The Secretary has 
further informed that during the 10th Five Year Plan, the Department of ISM&H would be providing 
some assistance to the State Government to strengthen the machinery. 
            The Committee is happy to note that despite all odds, the Department has been able to provide 
assistance to the State Governments.  However, the Committee feels that mere strengthening  of 
machinery would not serve any useful purpose unless the State Drug Control Authorities vigorously 
monitor the quality of drugs produced.  Otherwise the machines will remain idle.   At the same time, as 
pointed out in the foregoing paragraph,  the Committee is of the view that the machinery should be 
responsive, devoid of corruption and preserve the system and should not unnecessarily promote too 
much of commercialization by diluting the principles.    
8.3       It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that innumerable advertisements claiming that 
by using Ayurveda drugs a person height can be increased or weight can be reduced or a drug claiming 
to be an Indian version of viagra appear in the magazines and newspapers which are exploiting common 
people and taking them for a ride.  Committee's attention was drawn to advertisements by a doctor  from 
Rishikesh who claims to treat and cure epilepsy.  In reply to a query whether the claims made have been 
verified, the Department replied that 
‘The Department is aware of advertisements appearing in Newspaper about treatment of Epilepsy by Dr 
Gupta of Rishikesh (Uttranchal).  However, the clinical data have not been made available to the 
Department for evaluation of the claim.  In normal course, persons claiming to have developed treatment 
of any particular disease should approach the Government with full data in regard to efficacy of drugs 
and clinical evaluation for verification by the Department’. 
            In this context the Committee would like to quote Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 3715 
dated the 24.4. 2000 and the reply of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on the same subject as

matter for taking such action as is called for in the situation after examining the claims made by the 
doctor in this regard.     
9.         After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of  Indian System of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy and assessing the progress of various programmes and projects administered by it, the 
Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 196.47 crores as sought by the Department 
of Health for the year 2003-2004, under Demand No. 47 may be approved.  
            It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that a high level Committee known as 
"TIKKU Committee" which was constituted in 1989 recommended to constitute a cadre for ISM&H for 
the physicians to safeguard their career progression.   The Central Pay Commission has also 
recommended three time bound promotion up to the level of Chief Medical Officer (Non-Functional 
Selection Grade) after completion of 14 years of Group A service.  
This was the same recommendation for the CHS doctors also.  A decision has already been taken to 
grant time bound promotion to the allopathic doctors working in CGHS. However, the same has not 
been extended to ISM&H doctors so far nor there is any serious effort to do so quickly, in spite of about 
7 years of its recommendation by the Central Pay Commission and after about 14 years of the 
recommendation of the TIKKU Committee which has put the ISM&H Physicians at a great 
disadvantage in terms of promotion compared to their  counterpart in Allopathy.   
The Committee feels that the matter is unduly delayed.  Unless the Phsicians are granted  proper 
promotional avenues they shall continue to be demoralized in Government service.  As almost 90% of 
the Physicians working in CGHS and ministry have completed 14 years of Group A service the 
Committee recommends that the Department should  either  constitute the cadre on a time bound manner 
or approach the concerned Departments and Pay implementation cell to grant them 100% time bound 
promotion of Chief Medical Officer to the eligible ISM&H Physicians by seeking a one time relaxation 
in the cadre formation.

II          STRATEGIES  FOR  TENTH  FIVE  YEAR  PLAN 
2.5       The Committee feels that non submission of utilization certificates by the States is a perennial 
problem which is derailing several developmental activities in the States.  The Committee is happy to 
note that Ministry of Finance has formulated  guidelines on furnishing of utilisation certificates by the 
States. The Committee recommends that the Department should constantly keep on hammering the 
states to submit utilization certificates and vigorously  implement the Finance Ministry’s Guideline. 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department for the 10th Plan.  However, the Committee, 
feels that unless the causes for low utilization of funds as identified in the 9th  Plan are  addressed, the 
objectives of the 10th Plan may not be fully realized.  As far as non submission of utilization certificates 
by the ‘Implementing Agencies’ is concerned, the Committee feels that there could be possibilities of 
diversion, misutilisation or in some cases misappropriation of Government funds. The Committee, 
therefore,  recommends that the Department should make an investigation as to how the 1st Instalment 
of money has been utilized and fix responsibility in cases where  funds  have been  found to be 
misappropriated .  The Committee is dismayed at the fact that most of the civic work required for the 
development of the country gets trapped into labyrinths  of laws and by laws.  More laws means more 
beauracratization and more red tape and thereby causing unnecessary postponement of or delay in 
implementing various developmental schemes.  The Committee, therefore, feels that it is high time for 
the  Government including its various Department and Ministries to put their head together, simplify the 
rules and procedures and also consider giving publicity to the schemes and programmes aimed at the 
welfare of the people.  
(Para 2.5) 
III        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
    The Committee is constrained to observe that in all the abovementioned 11 schemes, the allocation 
was reduced at  RE stage. The Committee feels that prior to submitting its demands before Parliament, 
the Department should conclude all necessary consultations with the Planning Commission and Ministry 
of Finance and obtain their clearance so that its budgetary allocation, once approved by  Parliament,  is 
not reduced subsequently. (Para 3.2) 
IV.       PRACTICE OF INDIAN SYSTEMS OF MEDICINE AND HOMOEOPATHY IN PRIMARY 
HEALTH CENTRES 
4.3       While the Committee appreciates the  steps taken by the State of Himachal Pradesh and feels that 
such steps should not only solve the problem of non-availability of allopathic doctors in PHCs but 
would also popularize Indian System of Medicine and make career prospects in this field more attractive 
even though this may not be legally advisable step.  The Committee, recommends that the Department 
should persuade the States to follow the example of Himachal Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.  The 
Department should also do away with legal hudles, if any, in this regard. (Para 4.3) 
V         AYURVEDA 
5.5      The Committee feels that the European Countries, USA and other developed and prosperous 
countries have tremendous potential to become an extremely lucrative market for the Ayurvedic drugs of 
our country and can generate a lot of foreign exchange for the Country. However, in order to achieve 
this, as rightly pointed out by the Department, the confidence of such countries w.r.t. the safety and 
quality of such drugs has to be won. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the 
Department should keep a tight vigil of the quality and safety of the Ayurveda drugs manufactured and 
used in India or exported out of India so that more and more countries recognize our traditional system 
of medicine. 
The Committee observes that people opt for traditional medicine because they are affordable and less 
harmful. However, the experts have voiced concerns about the safety and quality, licensing of providers 
and standards of training in connection with traditional medicines. 
            The World Health Organization has come out with a traditional medicine strategy for 2002-2005

which focuses on these issues. According to WHO, 70 per cent of Indian population use traditional 
medicine for their primary health needs.  
            A group of experts recently met in Delhi to chalk out an adequate strategy for integration of 
traditional medicine with the health care system in India. According to these experts, a set of standards 
for regulating traditional medicine and setting up of a body to provide to medical claims is necessary. 
            The Committee feels the safety and efficiency of traditional medicine has been established 
through centuries of use. However, in order to make it acceptable to the outside world it may be 
necessary to validate its scientific basis. Here, the Committee is of the view that we need not tinker with 
our system for this purpose. Chernobyl incident convinced Russians about the efficacy of our system of 
medicine when the victims’ burns were miraculously healed. Likewise there are many simple plants and 
products like neem and turmeric, the efficacy of which tempted some countries abroad to have these 
products patented for commercial exploitation. The Committee therefore reiterates that the system need 
not be tinkered with to convince the outside world.  
            The attention of the Committee has been drawn to the fact that there are many traditional 
medicine practitioners who have claimed a cure for some disease or the other. In most cases they end up 
making rounds of Government agencies or try to sell their formula to pharmaceuticals but to little avail 
e.g. the person who claimed to have developed a herbal contraceptive in the 
 1980, passed away by the time Government decided to follow it up. The Committee observes the need 
to avoid such situations. The Government machinery should be suitably geared up and be responsive in 
such situations. (Para 5.5) 
VI        HOMOEOPATHY 
6.3       The Committee feels that in the absence of a separate university, the Homoeopathy education is 
perhaps not getting the attention it deserves. The Committee further feels that the quality of imparting 
Homoeopathy education can be vastly improved if an exclusive Homoeopathy university is established 
to regulate and monitor the functioning of the medical colleges throughout the Country. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department should consider establishing a separate Homoeopathy 
University and the allocation under the head `Homoeopathy should be increased accordingly. 
            At the same time there have been illiterate persons who acquired marvelous proficiency in 
developing this system of medicine.  The Committee, therefore, feels that there should be room for 
persons with average qualification to study and develop their skills in the field of Homoeopathy.  Part 
time colleges should also be encouraged to help people come forward to acquire knowledge and 
expertise in this system of medicine. (Para 6.3) 
VII       YOGA AND NATUROPATHY 
            The Committee observes that the pros and cons should be considered before taking a decision to 
introduce legislation  in this regard. (Para 7.2)  
VIII          QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS 
8.3       The Committee is happy to note that despite all odds, the Department has been able to provide 
assistance to the State Governments.  However, the Committee feels that mere strengthening  of 
machinery would not serve any useful purpose unless the State Drug Control Authorities vigorously 
monitor the quality of drugs produced.  Otherwise the machines will remain idle.   At the same time, as 
pointed out in the foregoing paragraph,  the Committee is of the view that the machinery should be 
responsive, devoid of corruption and preserve the system and should not unnecessarily promote too 
much of commercialization by diluting the principles.  (Para 8.2)

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
            Elementary education is the foundation upon which a modern society imbued with scientific 
temper and progressive outlook is built. In its strive to become a modern nation with healthy social 
indicators, the Parliament through 86th Amendment Act, 2002 has bestowed constitutional mandate in 
the form of Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education to every child of 6-14 years of age. 
             It is an established fact that basic education improves the level of human well- being. Unless we 
achieve the universalisation of elementary education we will be far away from the ideal goal of human
well-being. In fact, social justice and equity, the two basic necessities to our march into modernity, are
by themselves a strong argument for providing basic education for all. 
            The existing state of affairs in prim ary education clearly reveals that Universalisation of primary
education by 2010 is an uphill task, yet attainable. It needs cons iderable and trem endous efforts with
right insight and dedication to ac hieve the desired goal. Though th e Government has made primary
education compulsory under the Constitution and it is hoped that it will soon come up with the
accompanying legislation, the Govern ment should also take into account  the inter related aspects which
may hinder the progress viz., growing population, child- labour, feasibility and relevance of primary 
education to the unprivileged, the community involvement as it envisaged under the programme and last
but not least the proper implementation of the programme.

2.1         As per census 1951, literacy rate was only 18.33%.  The overall national literacy rate in 2001 is 
at 65.38% as against 52.21% in 1991 recording an increase of 13.17 percentage points, which is the
highest in any decade.  Growth of female literacy was recorded more than male literacy.  Female literacy 
increased by 14.87 percentage points i.e. from 39.29% to 54.16%  as compared to ma le literacy growth
by 11.72 percentage points i.e. 64.1% to 75.85%.  The differential in male-fem ale literacy rates has 
decreased from 24.84 percentage points in 1991 to 21.70 percentage points in 2001. [But it is still to
reach the level of Census year of 1971.]  However,  female literacy rate in Bihar, Jharkhand, J&K, 
Arunachal Pradesh, UP, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Raja sthan is less than 50% as per census 2001.  Fo r 
the first time,  there is a decline in absolute number of illiterates by 31.9 million.  During 1991-2001, the 
population in 7+ age group increased by 171.6 mi llion while 203.6 million additional persons became
literate.  All the States and Union Territories have not only shown increase in literacy rates during 1991-
2001 but have achieved male li teracy rates over 60%. As pe r the Department, the rate of  growth  o f 
literacy is higher in rural areas than in urba n areas. Between 1991 and 2001, rural literacy rates
increased by 14.52% while ur ban literacy rates went  up by 6.98%,  thereby narrowing the urban-rural 
gap from 28.39% in 1991 to 20.85% in 2001.  
2.2       Similarly, as  per NSSO 55 th  round (1999-2000), 53% of SCs ar e literate as compared to 
37.41% in the 1991 Census.  49% of STs are literate as compared to 29.60% in the 1991 Census.  This 
has shown a somewhat positive trend.  However, gender difference in Elementary Education, urban rural
gap and low literacy among SCs/STs and among educational mi norities still remain a cause of  concern 
for the Committee.  Effective monitoring and implementation is, therefore, needed. 
III        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 3.1       The Ninth Plan allocation for Elem entary Education has been Rs. 16,369.59 crores.  Howeve r 
approved allocation was Rs.11,963.41 crores.  Expenditure during Ninth Plan was Rs. 14,523.29 crores.  
It will, thus be seen th at there was a drastic cu t in the approved allocati on vis-à-vis the original 
allocation for the Ninth Plan.  However, the expenditure exceeded the approved allocation. Similarly, for 
Adult Education, Ninth Plan allo cation was Rs. 650.97 crore and expendi ture during the Plan was Rs.
521.20 crores.  If the expenditure on Adult Education is  taken into consideration, it appears that full 
utilization of the Ninth Pl an allocation would not  be possible.  There is li kely to be some saving unde r 
this head.  
3.2       The Tenth Plan requirement based on Wo rking Group Report for Elementary Education is Rs. 
59,684.31 crore but the approved outlay for the Tenth Plan is Rs. 28,750.00 crore which is 48 % of the
recommended allocation  of the Working Group. However, total budget provision for 2003-2004 fo r 
Elementary Education is Rs. 4900.00 crore against th e Department's projection of Rs 7096.15 crore. As
regards Adult Education, Tenth Plan requireme nt based on Working Gr oup Report is Rs.  6339.50 
crores but the approved outlay for the Tenth Plan  is Rs. 1250.00 crore which is approximately 20 % o f
the recommended allocation of th e Working Group.  However, B udget provision for 2003-2004 is Rs.  
233.00 crores only. 
 3.3       The Committee notes that there is c onsiderable gap between the  projections made by the 
Working Group and the final allocati ons.  The Committee observes that in order to achieve the plan 
targets in respect of Elementary Education as also Adult Education it is nece ssary to provide adequate
Budgetary Support for the purpose. Alternatively, th e Working Group Report may be reexamined to see
whether the projections with  regard to fund requirements can be brought to realistic levels.   In any case 
budgetary support has to be provided without comp romising with the goals set forth in regard to
Universalisation of Elementary Education for 2003-2004.   
 3.4     The Committee deprecates the tendency reflected over the years for various schemes unde r
Elementary Education under where budge t projected at BE stage is qui te high but it is considerably
reduced at the RE stage.  However, what is more distressing is that even this reduced allocation is not 
fully utilised.

 4.1      In pursuance of the NPE, 1986, the Scheme of  Operation Blackboard (OB) was launched in 
1987-88 with the aim of improving the human and physical resources available in the primary schools of
the country. 
4.2       The Scheme provided for at least two classrooms in each primary school with facilities o f
separate toilets for boys and girl s apart from provision of  additional teacher to single teacher primary
school and of teaching learning   equipment (TLE) ; including blackboards, maps, charts, and small 
library, toys and some equipment for work experience. 
4.3       During the Eighth Five- Year Plan th e scheme was revised in 1993-94 and was expanded to 
provide a third classroom and a third teacher to primary sc hools where enrolment exceeded 100
students. It was also extended to cover upper pr imary schools to provide financial assistance fo r
procurement of TLE and payment of salaries to additional teachers.  
4.4       The Committee has been informed that provision for construction of  school building was made 
under programmes of rural employment like Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) and Employment Assurance
Scheme (EAS).      
4.5       Under the Scheme of OB financial assi stance for procurement of Teaching Learning Equipment

far.  About 1.49 lakhs posts of additional teachers for single teacher primary schools, 0.83 lakhs posts of 
third teachers in primary schools where enrolment exceeds 100 and 0.77 lakhs of additional teachers for
upper primary schools have been sanctioned.  1.85 la khs classrooms have also  been constructed unde r
the scheme by State/UTs. 
4.6       The OB scheme has been subsumed un der the SSA with effect from  1April 2002. The Budget

V      SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA) 
5.1       Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is an ambitious proj ect to redeem the constitutional pledge of giving free
and compulsory education to every ch ild of 6-14 years. It is an attemp t to pursue unive rsal elementary 
education in a mission mode. 
5.2       The programme covers th e entire country and addresses the needs of 192 million children in 11 
lakh habitations. Nearly 8.5 lakh existing primary  and upper primary sc hools and 33 lakh existing
teachers would be covered under the scheme.  The programme seek s to open new schools in habitation  
which do not have schooling faciliti es and strengthen existing school infrastructre through provision o f
additional grant and school improvement grant. Existing schools with inadequate teacher strength would
be provided additional teachers under the programme. The capacity of existing teacher would be built by
extensive training, provision of gr ant for developing teaching-learni ng material and development of  
academic support structure. The SS A has a special focus on girls and children of  weaker sections. A
number of initiatives, including the provision of free textbooks, ta rget these children under the
programme. The SSA also seeks to provide computer educat ion in rural areas to  bridge the digital
divide. 
5.3       The SSA aims to involve the communit y in this effort towards UEE. The local village 
community is responsible for the following specific activities under the programme: 
•                   Preparation of need- based habitation level plans based on 
detailed                                                                     household survey. 
•                         Implementation of  the approved habitation plan, including civil construction 
•              Monitoring of the functioning of school to ensure regular quality teaching. 
The involvement of the community is ensured through the participation of the Village Education 
Committee(VEC), Panchayati Raj institutions and women’s groups in the above tasks. 
5.4       The goals of the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan are: 
•                         All children in the 6-14 age group in school/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003; 
•                         All children in the 6-14 age group complete five years of primary education by 2007; 
•                         All children in the 6-14 age group complete eight years of schooling by 2010; 
•                         Focus on elementary education of satisfactory quality with emphasis on education for life;

elementary school teachers in the country. The Scheme  envisages setting up of District Institutes o f

Colleges of Teacher Education (C TEs)/Institute of Adva nced Study in Education (IASEs) to organize

service to secondary schools. 
6.2       The Scheme also envisages strengthening of  SCERTs; orientation of sc hool teachers in the use
of Operation Blackboard (OB) materials and implementation of MLL strategy with focus on teaching of
languages, mathematics and environmental studies.

VIII   MAHILA SAMAKHYA 
8.1       The Mahila Samakhya Programme was launc hed in 1989 with Dutch assi stance to tr anslate the 
goals enshrined in the National Po licy on Education (NPE), 1986 a nd the Programme of Action (POA),
1992 into a concrete programme for the education and empowerme nt of women in rural areas,
particularly women from socially and economically marginalized groups.  
8.2       The underlying theme of th e programme is to use education as an agent of basic change in the 
status of women and empower them to achieve equality. Mahila Samakhya has adopted an innovative
approach which emphasises the process rather than mere  fulfilment of targets. It seeks to bring about a
change in women's perception about themselves and the perception of society with regard to women's
traditional role. Under this program me, education is understood as a pr ocess of learning to question,
critically analysing issues a nd problems and seeking solutions. The Mahila Samakhya endeavours to
create an environment for women to learn at their own pace, set their own priorities and seek knowledge
and information to make informed choices. This involves enabling women (especially from socially and
economically disadvantaged and marginalised groups) to address and deal with  problems of isolation
and lack of self-confidence, oppressi ve social customs and struggle for survival, all of which inhibit 
their learning. It is in this process that women become empowered. 
8.3       The Mahila Samakhya programme has generated a demand for literacy and education for women 
and girls. It has thereby strengthe ned women's abilities to effectiv ely participate in village-level 
educational processes. The Mahi la Samakhya provide specialised inputs for vocational and skill
development as well as for the educat ional needs of girls in general a nd adolescent girls in particular. It
endeavours to develop gender- sensitive pedagogical and learning material. 
8.4       The Ninth Plan outlay for the Mahila Samakhya Scheme was Rs. 35.00 crore, out of which a
sum of Rs. 31.41 crore was spent. The Tenth Plan outlay for the scheme is Rs. 100 crore. The Scheme is
poised for expansion in the Tenth Plan period (2002-03 to 2007 -08).  
8.5       Currently, the Mahila Samakhya programme is operating in 60 districts covering more than 9000
villages in 10  States of Ut tar Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Bihar, Madhya
Pradesh, Assam, Jharkhand and Uttaranchal. The effe ctiveness of the Mahila Samakhya strategy has
resulted in its being adopted by other basic education pr oject like DPEP.  Se veral evaluation studies
have shown that the Ma hila Samakhya programme has been highly successful in design and
implementation. It has  helped generate a demand for literacy, increased women’s recognition and 
visibility both within the family and the commun ity, given women the strength and ability to demand
accountability from Government deli very systems, increased women’s participation in Panchayati Raj 
bodies, created an awareness of the need to struggle for a gender just society. 
8.6       The Committee notes that Pl an allocation for the current financial year 2002-03 was proposed at

 IX     DISTRICT PRIMARY EDUCATION PROGRAMME                            
9.1       The DPEP is a centrally sponsored scheme  providing special thrust to  achieve Universalisation
of Primary Education (UPE). The programme takes a holistic view of  primary education development
and seeks to operationalise the strategy of UPE through district-s pecific planning with emphasis on 
decentralised management, participatory processes, empowerment and capacity building at all levels. 
9.2       The programme is structured to provide additional inputs over and above the provisions made by 
the state governments for elementa ry education. The programme fill s in the existing gaps in the
development of primary education and seeks to revitalise the existi ng system. The DPEP is contextual
and has a marked gender focus. The programme components include construction of classrooms and
new schools, opening of non-formal/alternative schooling centres, appointment of new teachers, setting 
up Block Resource Centres/ Cluste r Resource Centres, teacher training, deve lopment of teaching
learning material, research-based inte rventions, special interventions for education of  girls,  SCs/STs, 
etc. The components of integrated  education to children with disa bility and a distance education
component for improving teacher training have also been incorporated in the programme. 
9.3       The programme mainly aims at providing access to primary education for all children, reducing
primary drop out rates to less than 10 per cent, incr easing large achievement of primary school students
by at least 25 per cent, and reducing the gap among gender and social groups to less than 5 per cent. 
9.4       The district which is the Unit of progr amme implementation is sel ected on the basis of the
following criteria, viz., educationally backward districts with female literacy below the national average
and districts where Total Literacy Campaigns (TLCs) have been successful, leading to enhanced demand
for elementary education.  
9.5       The DPEP is an externally aided projec t. 85 per cent of the pr oject cost is met by the
Government of India and the rema ining 15 per cent is shared by th e concerned State government. The
Government of India share is resourced through extern al assistance. At present, external assistance o f
about Rs. 6938 crore, comprising Rs. 5137 crore as cr edit from IDA and Rs. 1801 crore as grant from
the European Commission (EC), Depa rtment for International Devel opment of UK  (DFID), UNICEF 
and Government of the Netherlands has been tied up for the DPEP.  
9.6       During Ninth Plan there has been 93 per cent utilization of funds. In 26 districts of Madhya 
Pradesh and Chhattisgarh the project closed on 31.12.2002. In 118 districts of DPEP phase- I & II, the 
project will close on 30.6.2003. Thereafter  the project will continue in 129 districts of 9 States namely:
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gu jarat, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Ben gal, Ra jasthan, Jharkhand and

X         ADULT EDUCATION 
10.1     Literacy as a qualitative at tribute of the population is one of the most impor tant indicators of the 
socio-economic and political devel opment of a society. It is a ma jor component of human resource
development (HRD) and is thus basi c to any programme of social and economic progr ess. It is a basic
step towards adult education, which is a process of lifelong learning and an entry point into the world o f
communication and information.    
10.2     The stride of the nation towards literacy and adult educati on is being made mainly under the 
aegis of National Literacy Mission (NLM).  New life and vigour has been infused into the NLM to meet 
the new challenges. On 30 Nove mber 1999, the governme nt approved the exte nsion of the Mission,
stressing on life-long learning and decentralisation, a dopting integrated liter acy campaign approach, 
devolution of authority to State a nd district-level institutions. The parameters and norms of financial
assistance of schemes under the NL M have been enhanced. The main features of the revised schemes
are as follows: 
-           An integrated approach to literacy was adopted to amalgamate a ll the features of the earlie r 
literacy and post-literacy phases.  
-           Zilla Saksharta Samitis (District Lite racy Societies) to continue  to oversee and run literacy 
programmes. They have been given freedom to synergise their strengths with those of local youth clubs,
Mahila Mandals, voluntary agencies, panchayati raj institutions , small scale industries, cooperative
societies, etc. 
-           Scheme of continuing education enco mpassing removal of residual illiteracy, individual interest
programmes, skill development, rural libraries, etc., is given due priority.  
-           The role of NGOs has been expande d to impart vocati onal/skill development programmes and 
also to run continuing education centres in addition to their pres ent activities -imparting training, 
material development, innovative and impact studies etc.

-           Devolution of financial and administ rative powers to State Lite racy Mission Authorities fo r
sanctioning of projects. 
-           The Scheme of Rural Functional Lite racy Projects is subsumed unde r the Scheme of Literacy 
Campaigns and Operation Restoration. . 
10.3     It is hoped that the revised mission would continue to consolidate the gains of previous years and
accelerate the growth of literacy movement. 
10.4     After experimenting with successive and alternative models of adult literacy, the NLM adopte d
the Total Literacy Campaign (TLC) approach as its pr incipal strategy for eradication of illiteracy. TLCs  
which provide basic literacy skills to the non-literate population pr imarily in the age group 15-35 years, 
have been launched in almost all the district s of the country. The TLC has certain positive
characteristics: area-specific, tim e-bound, participative,  delivery th rough voluntarism, cost-effective 
and outcome oriented. The campaigns are implemented through Zilla Saksharata Samitis as independent
and autonomous bodies, having due representation of all  sections of society. 
10.5     On conclusion of a TLC, Post Literacy Programme is there to enable the neo-literates to learn the 
application of literacy skill as problem solving tool, so that  learning becomes relevant to living.
Similarly, the Government of In dia had approved a new scheme of Conti nuing Education for Neo
literates in December, 1995.  Main thrust under it was given to setting up of continuing education centre 
which functions as a focal point for providing lear ning opportunities such as  library, reading room,
learning centre, training centre, info rmation centre, cultural  centre, sports centre etc. Besides that, the
Scheme of Jan Shikshan Sansth an or Institute of people's E ducation till now known as Shrami k
Vidyapeeth was launched as a multi-faceted adul t education programme ai med at improving the 
vocational skill and qualit y of life of workers and their fa mily members. Support was provided to
NGOs /VAs for carrying out activiti es such as running total and post literacy and continuing education
programmes, undertaking resource development activities through es tablishment of State Resource
Centres, organizing vocational an d technical education programme for neo literates, promoting
innovation, experimentation and act ion research, conducting evaluation and impact studies and
organising symposia and conference publication of  relevant books and pe riodicals and production o f
Mass media support aids. 
10.6     Out of 600 districts in the country, 587 have since been covere d under adult education
programmes; 174 under TLCs, 212 under post-Liter acy programme and 201 under the Continuing
Education Programme. About 96.69 mi llion persons have been ma de literate as on 31 March,2002.

Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively. 
10.7     The Committee, while appreciating the progress made towards literacy, also expresses its serious
concern over the functioning of various schemes of A dult Education.  At the end of Ninth Plan, NLM

the way of  attainment of 70 per ce nt literacy by the end of Ninth Pl an.   The Committee hopes that the

components/projects of Adult Education Programme.

PREFACE 
  
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do 
hereby present this Hundred thirty-ninth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand 
No.57) of the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource 
Development for the year 2003-2004. 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the 
Department of Secondary and Higher Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development and also 
heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting 
held on 25th March, 2003. 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on  
22nd April, 2003. 
  
  
REPORT 
I           INTRODUCTION 
Education is a nectar and has been considered a liberating force.    An educated society treads the path of 
rationality, breaks the shackles of ignorance and rigidity and takes the nation to a new high in the comity 
of nations. 
The system of education in India has broadly been divided in two categories: elementary education and 
secondary and higher education.  It has been observed over the years that new initiatives are being taken 
to strengthen school education. Programmes like National Open School (renamed National Institute of 
Open Schooling) are being strengthened to reach out more and more children in distant areas, National 
Council of Educational Research and Training is playing an active role in providing resource support in 
the areas of education research and training at school level.  The Navodaya Vidyalayas have been set up 
with the objective of providing a progressive and forward looking school system in the rural areas. 
Secondary Education  is of  crucial importance to our students  who spend formative years of their life 
here.    The secondary stage of Education   gains more importance as hardly 19% students reach the 
university level of education.   While changes have been made from time to time by the Government, 
fact remains that this stage of education does not lead students anywhere.   In fact, on the other hand, the 
subjects like English, Hindi and mathematics (i.e. modern mathematics) which has been introduced in 
the recent years etc.  are beyond one’s comprehension and on an average parents are not able to support 
their children financially.   These reasons alone have compelled students more so from the vulnerable 
sections of the society to drop out at secondary level only.    There is thus a need to involve the school 
more effectively to prevent drop-outs and reorient the education at this level, may be in the form of 
making it more vocational and need based so that in case of students who are not able to enter the 
university stage, at least the secondary education helps them to stand in the world on their own account. 
More so, vocationalisation of education is the need of the hour as the country faces a paradox of more 
and more number of children at entry level and corresponding flow of students at exit level of secondary

and university stages with meagre opportunities in the development of one’s career, or, for that matter, 
employment.   
The Special Subject Group appointed by the Prime Minister's Office in its Report on Policy Framework 
for Reforms in Education of  April 2000 has estimated that as per the enrolment figures of 1997-98 two-
third of the eligible population  remains out of the school system and only 270 lakhs are attending 
schools at the secondary level.    
The challenge before the nation is how best to tap the potential of this upcoming workforce and 
gainfully employ them in projects of national importance and provide them a need based system of 
education and keep them away from the world of crime and ignorance and help them become a useful  
citizen of the society. 
II          BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 2.1        During the Tenth Plan, the approved outlay for Secondary & Higher Education is Rs. 13,825.00 
crore. The Planning Commission, while making the annual plan allocations for the year 2001-2002 had 
assured to give due priority to the Education Sector as soon as the funds were available through 
disinvestment. However, instead of additional funds being provided to the Department, the BE 
allocation was reduced at RE stage. Similarly, the projected outlay for 2002-2003 was Rs. 4223.37 
crore, whereas approved Plan allocation was only Rs. 2125.00 crores but this too came down  to Rs. 
1942.33 crore at RE stage. During 2003-2004 the Plan outlay (BE) has been fixed at the level of 
previous year's BE level i.e., at Rs. 2125.00 crore.  Non-Plan allocation for 2003-2004 is Rs. 2832.40 
crore.   
2.2       The Committee was informed that as state funding of the education sector has been inadequate 
and the desired six per cent of the national income could not be set apart for education, the Department 
has decided to constitute the `Bharat Shiksha Kosh' for mobilizing extra-budgetary resources by 
receiving donations/contributions/endowments from individuals and corporates, central and state 
Governments, NRIs and People of Indian Origin (PIO) in order to fill in the gap between actual 
requirement and the available budgetary support.     
2.3       In absence of any authoritative figures the Committee has taken the total outlay (plan and non 
plan) of Rs. 4749 crores and maximum number of students who registered themselves for 2002 
examinations i.e. 530401.    The  total outlay per head comes to Rs. 9345 half of which is non-plan 
expenditure.     The Plan  expenditure per student is thus Rs. 4500/- approximately which includes 
expenditure  on creation of infrastructure, peripheral  or administrative expenditure.   The net available 
per student is thus a pittance.    The Committee, therefore, observes that there is a need to provide more 
funds in this section as this is an investment to secure the future of our young generation.   Government 
must provide at least six percent of the national income to this sector which is much starved of funds.  
2.4     At the same time in many of the schemes/projects, the Committee, has observed  that substantial 
funds are lying with State Governments/NGOs and Utilization Certificates are not forthcoming from 
them for years together.  The Committee does not know whether these funds have been utilized at all.   
The Department must give a serious thought to this aspect and take necessary remedial measures for 
optimum utilisation of funds.

organisation to assist and advise the state Governments on matters related to school education.   It 
provides academic and technical support for qualitative improvement of school education.  Programmes 
and activities related to improvement of courses of studies, textual materials, support and ancillary 
materials for enrichment of instructions were undertaken to improve the content and process of 
secondary education and vocationalisation of education.  
3.2       The Committee notes with satisfaction that non-utilisation of funds has declined  from 22.68 per 
cent in 1999-2000 to about zero per cent by 2002-2003.   In fact, the NCERT has asked for more funds 
than Rs.15.05 crore which was allocated to it at RE stage for the financial year 2002-2003.   The 
Committee recommends that the requirement of extra funds by NCERT must be looked into with a view

to help the organisation in its pursuits.              
3.3       The Committee notes that NCERT undertakes programmes and activities in relation to 
improvement of courses in vocational education. The developmental programmes/activities in progress 
include norms and standards for accreditation of institutions and programmes of vocational education, 
database for vocational education, software on question bank, competency-based curriculum on agro-
forestry, curriculum for NVQ in the area of transport  service, curriculum and modules in specific areas

the education.   At the same time there is a need to introduce some ‘Earn and Learn’ kind of schemes to 
inculcate the feelings of self-sufficiency among the students.  
3.5       The Committee is of the view that there is a need to tap the vast potential of upcoming force of 
students who generally remain idle during holidays including summer vacation.  Millions of work days 
are just available at the asking with virtually no cost.   If they could be gainfully employed in projects of 
national importance or otherwise it will secure many purposes including out-station visits for students 
which are also a virtual education.   NCERT must give a serious thought to this aspect. 
IV   NATIONAL INSTITUTE OPEN SCHOOLING (NIOS) 
4.1       The National Institute Open Schooling (NIOS) has been pursuing its mission  of reaching the 
unreached by providing opportunities for continuing education to those who have missed opportunities 
to complete school education and developmental education through courses and programmes of general 
education, life enrichment and vocational education from primary to pre-degree level.  As an apex level 
resource organisation in school education through Distance and Open Learning Mode and as a National 
Board of School Education, the NIOS has been (i) developing curricula and self learning materials, (ii) 
organising Personal Contact Programme (PCP) at accredited study centres for enrolled students and (iii) 
examining them for its school level courses.   Steps are being taken to ensure that the NIOS curricula 
inter-alia take care of the children.    Keeping in view the educational needs of its clientele  groups, the 
NIOS has been providing flexibility in selecting academic,  pre-vocational and vocational courses as 
well as in examinations so that a candidate can learn and proceed according to his/her own pace. 
4.2       The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by NIOS in making  available  courses for 
physically, mentally and visually challenged children.   The Committee observes that NIOS must 
endeavour to reach more and more such children  and also try to make its system of education more 
responsive and need based.     
4.3       The Committee is also concerned about the recognition and acceptability of the Certificates and 
Diplomas for employment in both public and private sector.    While NIOS should endeavour to make its 
courses responsive and need based, Government must endeavour to ensure that the certificate and 
Diplomas awarded by NIOS are accepted  by the industry.

6.1       Navodaya Vidyalaya is an  effort on the part of the Government in the right direction to spread 
the light of education through the length and breadth of the country. Navodaya Vidyalayas aim to 
provide good quality education to the talented children particularly from the rural areas.  At present, 
there are 468 sanctioned and 432 functional JNVs covering as many districts in 34 States/UTs.  During 
Tenth Plan, the Samiti proposes to acquire built up accommodation or construct permanent office 
buildings for its Headquarters Office, ten Regional Offices and 10 training centres.  The Samiti also 
proposes to expand sports activities, computer education programme, vocational courses etc. during 
Tenth Plan.  It is also proposed to start ten schools for gifted children.

students to achieve the  target of 1,51,983 students fixed during the Ninth Plan.   The Committee has

Department intended to recoup the drop outs by enrolling more students in Class IX and XI in the 
functional Vidyalayas by the end of Ninth Five Year Plan. 
6.3       The Committee, feels concerned about students who have dropped out.   The Committee also 
notes with concern that the target of constructing 275 Vidyalayas buildings during the Ninth Plan could 
not be achieved.    The building constructed were less by 27 in number.    The Committee, recommends 
that the Department must examine the cases of drop outs as also the non-achievement  of the target of 
construction of buildings and take necessary remedial steps.

secondary education at 10+2 level since 1988 and in its revised format since 1992-93.     The scheme has 
not been a runaway success and acknowledging this, the working group under the chairmanship of 
Director, NCERT, recommended for the establishment of block-level vocational training institutes, 
treating vocational stream at par with other streams of education, appointment of full-time teachers, 
coordination and utilisation of resources with other implementing agencies/departments/ministries, 
development of national vocational qualification of development of  a short-term course and linkages 
with major industrial outfits. 
7.2       The Committee appreciates the proposed changes.   In fact, the system of education developed 
durin
g British period and still being largely  followed aims at producing white collar jobs which are

UNIVERSITY AND HIGHER EDUCATION 
X        UNIVERSITY GRANTS COMMISSION 
10.1     An amount of Rs.1630.55 crore has been proposed for UGC both under Plan and Non-Plan for 
the year 2003-2004. While the allocation under Non-Plan has been increased by Rs.13.80 crore as 
compared to the year 2002-2003, the allocation under Plan for 2003-04 in at the same level as  made 
during 2002-2003.  
10.2     Besides the role of giving grants to universities and colleges, UGC also advises Central and State 
Governments on the measures necessary for the development of higher education. It, thus, serves as a 
coordinating body between the Union and the State governments and the institutions of higher learning.   
10.3     In the reporting year 2002-03 (the first year of the Tenth Plan), the UGC had Plan budget 
estimates amounting to Rs. 516.75 crore for five sectors consisting of around 70 schemes/programmes. 
About 45 percent of the Ninth Plan schemes/ programmes have been dropped and 40 new schemes have 
been added for implementation during the Tenth Plan period. The five broad sectors of the Tenth Plan 
are general development of universities and colleges (219 crore Plan budget estimate), enhancing access 
and equity (29.50 crore), promotion of relevant education (70 crore), quality and excellence (99.25 
crore) and strengthening of research (99 crore). Out of the Plan budget estimate for the first year of the 
Tenth Plan, 10 percent of the allocation under each sector/scheme was to be allocated to North-Eastern 
universities and colleges. 
10.4     During the Tenth Plan period, the emphasis and focus would be on development of universities 
and colleges by making available infrastructural facilities, quality and excellence, access and equity with 
quality etc. During the reporting year, various UGC Visiting Committees were reviewing the 
implementation of various higher programmes during the Ninth Plan and assessing the financial 
requirements for the Tenth Plan period. The recommendation report of these Committees would be 
ready by the end of November 2002. Based on their recommendations Plan allocation would be made to 
the universities. 
10.5     It has been stated that the higher education system has seen a 13-fold increase in the number of 
universities and a 26-fold increase in the number of colleges since Independence. There are now 196 
universities, 76 Deemed Universities, five institutions established through state and central legislation, 
and 11 institutes of national importance established through Central legislation, and nearly 13,150 
colleges including around 1600 (12.7 percent) women colleges in the country in addition to the 
unrecognised institutions/foreign universities operating in the higher education sector.

education in universities and colleges has been 88.21lakh --- 11.66 lakh in university departments and

diploma/certificate levels. About 89.95 percent of all the undergraduate students and 66.02 percent of all 
the postgraduate students were enrolled in the affiliated colleges while remaining in university

10.16   The Committee appreciates the efforts of UGC in the field of university and higher education.

network and develop institutions engaged in programmes of  Gandhian Basic Education and Nai Talim.
