REPORT
 
I           INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The National Policy on Education-1986 envisaged establishment of a Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya (JNV) in each district
of the country. The Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVs) are fully residential, co-educational institutions covering classes VI to XII. The
Navodaya Vidyalaya Scheme started with two model schools in 1985-86 at present, covers 509 Districts in 34 States/UTs of the
country.
 
OBJECTIVES
 
            The main objectives of the JNVs as set forth are:
 
1.         To provide good quality modern education including a strong component of culture, inculcation of values, awareness of
the environment, adventure activities and physical education to the talented children predominantly from the rural areas
irrespective of their family’s socio economic condition;
2.          To serve the objectives of excellence coupled with equality and social justice.
3.          To ensure that all students of Navodaya Vidyalayas attain a reasonable level of competence in three languages as
envisaged in Three Language Formula;
4.          To promote national integration by providing opportunities to talented children, largely from rural areas of the country to
live and learn together and develop their full potential, and
5.         To serve, in each district, as focal points for improvement in the quality of school education in general, through sharing of
experiences and facilities.
 
           SALIENT FEATURES
 
The following features establish the separate identity of JNVs: -
           
(i)                  Good quality modern education for talented children predominantly from rural areas.
(ii)                Ratio/class of candidates  - 
Rural, atleast   75%, Urban at the most    25%
(iii)               Reservation of seats for students from SC/ST categories in proportion to their population in the district subject to the
national minimum.
(iv)              Reservation of seats for girls - 33%.
(v)                Co-educational and fully residential, upto Class-XII.
(vi)              Location- usually in rural areas on the basis of offer of cost free land and rent free temporary buildings by State/UT
Governments.
(vii)             Free education including boarding and lodging as well as expenses on uniforms, text books, and stationery etc.
(viii)           Affiliated to CBSE.
(ix)              Admission in only Class-VI through objective type test designed and conducted by CBSE.
(x)                Implementation of three-language formula.
(xi)              Regional language as medium of instruction for first three years and Hindi/English afterwards.
(xii)30% of students in Class IX from a Vidyalaya located in one linguistic area spend one academic year in a Vidyalaya in a
different linguistic region to promote national integration through understanding of the diversity and plurality of
country’s culture and people.
 
II    Organizational set-up
 
2.1       The Navodaya Vidyalayas are managed by Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti (NVS) which is an autonomous organization of

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Secondary and Higher Education.  The Samiti functions through an
Executive Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Minister of Human Resource Development. Union Minister of State
of Education is normally the Vice-Chairman of the Samiti.  Members of Parliament, representatives from industry, representatives
from State Governments and eminent educationists are nominated as Members of the Samiti. The Executive Committee is assisted
by Finance Committee and Academic Advisory Committee in its functions.
 
2.2       For each Vidyalaya, there is a Vidyalaya Advisory Committee and a Vidyalaya Management Committee for the general
supervision of the Vidyalaya. District Magistrate of the concerned district is the Chairman of these Committees with local
educationists, public representatives and officials from the district as members.
 
III        Norms for opening of Navodaya Vidyalayas 
3.1       As envisaged in the scheme, one Navodaya Vidyalaya each is to be established in all the districts, which were in existence
in the country at the commencement of Eighth Five Year Plan. However, due to reorganization/creation of new districts
subsequently during the Ninth Five Year Plan and thereafter, several new districts have been created in many States and proposals
have been received from the State Governments for opening more JNVs. Accordingly, it has been decided to cover 574 districts
existing in the country (excluding Tamil Nadu which has not yet accepted the Scheme). As on 31.8.04, JNVs have been
sanctioned in 509 districts of the country. Remaining 65 districts are proposed to be covered by the end of Tenth Plan Period.
 
3.2       The Committee was given to understand that out of 509 sanctioned JNVs, 485 JNVs are functional.  Out of the remaining
24 non-functional JNVs, 9 have been sanctioned only during the years 2003-04 and 2004-2005 and are likely to start functioning
from the next academic year.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that out of the remaining 15 non-functional JNVs,
three JNVs, one each in Bihar, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh were sanctioned in 2001-2002, ten JNVs, one each in Gujarat,
Haryana, Jharkhand, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Tripura, UP and Uttaranchal and two in Mizoram were sanctioned in 2002-2003.  In
all these cases, temporary accommodation has not been made available by the concerned State Governments so far.  The
Committee fails to understand the reasons behind the inability of the State Governments in fulfilling the minimum requirements
for proposals initiated by them. The Committee observes that majority of these districts are located in remote and tribal areas
where JNVs are primarily required to be opened. The Committee is particularly disturbed by the situation in Mizoram. The
Committee finds that out of the six JNVs sanctioned in Mizoram, two JNVs opened – one in 1987-1988 in Lungli District and the
other in Chimtupui District in 1992-93 had to be closed down due to less enrolment and administrative reasons. In respect of three
JNVs sanctioned in 2002-2003, temporary accommodation is yet to be made available.  At present, only one JNV is functional.
The remaining two districts of the State are yet to be covered. The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for the
Department for taking up such cases at the highest level.  The Committee feels that given the peculiar geographical location and
the overall backwardness of the North-East region, the Central Government should make special efforts on meeting all the
requirements to make JNVs functional at the earliest.
 
3.3.      The Committee recommends that concerted efforts should be made to expedite not only the sanctioning of all the 574
JNVs, but also to make them functional in a time bound manner. The Committee would like the Ministry to play the role of a
facilitator in clearing the proposals received as well as in encouraging other proposals to be put up for opening new schools in the
remaining districts.
 
3.4       As per the information made available to the Committee, out of the 485 functioning JNVs, only 368 JNVs are functioning
in permanent sites and 117 JNVs are functioning at temporary sites.  The Committee was given to understand that 35 JNVs are
likely to be completed by 31
st March 2005, 6 JNVs by 31st March 2006, 1 by 31st August, 2006, in respect of 13 JNVs, land is yet
to be transferred, and land allotted to 2 JNVs was under dispute.
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
3.5       The Committee is not aware about the latest position in all such cases.  The Committee, however, apprehends that no
significant progress would be there in most of the cases.  The Committee observes that different construction agencies both state
and national level are involved in the construction of school buildings.  The Committee, however, finds that civil construction in
the schools was generally running much behind the schedule, because of one reason or the other.  Apart from non-availability of
funds in time, the Committee found that long procedures and lack of proper coordination between different agencies involved in
the exercise were responsible for such delays resulting in time and cost over-run, which must be avoided.  The Committee
strongly feels that there should be a mechanism at central level working in co-ordination with all concerned state authorities which
would constantly monitor all such cases as per time bound action plan. The Committee would also like the Ministry to prepare a
consolidated estimate required for construction of pending buildings and plead strongly for that fund with the Ministry of Finance.
 
3.6       The Committee was informed that opening of JNVs depends upon receipt of the proposals from the concerned States/UT
Governments offering 30 acres of suitable land free of cost with sufficient temporary buildings and other infrastructure free of rent
or on permanent basis to accommodate 240 students and staff for three to four years or till the Samiti constructs its own buildings
at the permanent site. The Committee notes that the Samit is, however, not very rigid about the criteria of 30 acres of land which
can be relaxed to the extent of 10 acres of land in hilly areas or wherever there is extreme scarcity of land on case to case basis. 
 
 
3.7       The Committee was informed that 104 JNVs are located in less than 30 acres of land, { with the minimum area of land
(9.5 acres)  in JNV Bhadoi district, UP } out of which maximum number of 29 JNVs are located in Chandigarh region; as many as
26 JNVs do not have any play field; and most of the JNVs in J&K are not having even a permanent school building. The
Committee appreciates the compulsions to relax the condition of 30 acres of land in selective cases where land is scarce. 
However, the Committee recommends that the relaxation should be granted only after carefully examining the interests of the
students and their development.  For example, the paucity of land should not be a constraint for games & sports facilities and for
this the sports facilities available in nearby schools, institutions, clubs etc, could be shared so that the students are not deprived of
their educational and developments needs.  The Committee would also emphasise that all efforts should be made to provide
required facilities in JNVs   which can be made available in less than 30 acres of land area at the earliest.
 
IV        INFRASTRUCTURE
4.1       Every Navodaya Vidyalaya is stipulated to have a school building on 2000 sq. meters of space, having 30 classrooms, a
library, a computer room, a staff room, laboratory, six dormitories, boys and girls hostels, dining & kitchen facility, residence for
faculty & staff with ample open spaces for play and recreation.  A Smriti Van in the memory of late Sh. Rajiv Gandhi, former
Prime Minister of India, forms an integral part of all the Navodaya School campuses.  Besides, the provision for underground
water tank, one tubewell, a sub-station building, proper sewerage system, water supply and boundary wall for the entire building
also forms the components of the scheme.
 
4.2       The Committee during its visits observed general lack of or poor infrastructure in the Navodaya Vidyalayas. Same was the
report given by many witnesses with whom the Committee held discussions.  Upkeep of the buildings and facilities both in
schools and in hostels were found not upto the mark.  Less said is better about the infrastructure of Smriti Vans. 
 
4.3       The Committee was given to understand that out of 485 functional JNVs as on 31.8.2004, 368 JNVs are functioning in
permanent site.  The Committee, however, observes that out of these 368 JNVs, 104 are having land area less than the prescribed
areas of 30 acres.  And out of these JNVs, 11 JNVs are having less than 18 acres, 9 JNVs are having temporary buildings,
situation is really bad in J&K as out of 13 JNVs, 4 are running in S.P. sheds and 1 in temporary building.  The Committee is not

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
satisfied about the buildings and infrastructure available in the remaining JNVs in the state, as exact details have not been made
known to the Committee. Actual status of buildings and infrastructure of JNVs in Chandigarh, Hyderabad and Jaipur Region has
also not been made available to the Committee.  The Committee apprehends that these JNVs must be in a bad state, totally lacking
the minimum requirements.  The Committee is also not aware about the status of JNVs having 30 acres of land and functioning
from permanent sites.  The Committee feels that JNVs functioning from permanent site does not seem to make much difference. 
The Committee wonders about the factors delaying the provision of required infrastructure once land is made available.  The
Committee recommends that all JNVs having permanent site should be provided required buildings and infrastructure without any
delay.  The Committee strongly feels that an effective monitoring mechanism should be evolved for accomplishing this over
delayed task.  The Department/NVS should work out a time bound action plan in this regard in active coordination with Regional
Offices, State authorities and district administration.  Funds as and when required should be provided for this purpose but on the
condition that all works are implemented at the earliest.
 
4.4       The Committee further recommends that apart from providing the requisite basic infrastructure, provision for fire safety
should also be made on priority basis to make the buildings safer. Regular inspections should be made to see that buildings etc
were properly maintained.  The school authorities should also discuss the problem of maintenance of building in the Parents
Teachers Meetings, so that the local authorities could be pressurized to do the job.
 
V         STUDENT INTAKE
 
5.1       Prescribed student intake per Navodaya Vidyalaya is 600 students i.e. 400 boys and 200 girls.  The Committee is,
however, surprised to note that only 33 NVs have student intake ranging from 502 to 572.  Student strength as on 31.3.04 is much
below the prescribed limit in the remaining functional 452 NVs.  Position in some Regions is very disturbing.  Details as indicated
below are self-revealing: -
 
Region No. of JNVs Average student strength
Shillong 58 262
Pune 53 324
Chandigarh 42 328
Patna 50 343
Lucknow 66 350
Bhopal 75 351
Jaipur 47 379
 
           
Some of the state-wise figures are a cause for serious concern. The Committee apprehends that school-wise position would
be even more damaging. The Committee fails to understand the factors responsible for overall student intake in JNVs remaining
much below the prescribed limit.  Either JNVs have failed to attract students or adequate infrastructure for required student
capacity is not there.  Both the situations are very discouraging.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should take steps for conducting a survey for analyzing the reasons for low intake of student in JNVs with particular focus on the
JNVs having very low figures and based on the findings of the survey, take remedial action.  The Committee feels that except
under unavoidable circumstances, the seats must not be allowed to remain vacant.  The Committee opines that a merit list of all
the students aspiring for the admission may be prepared and the vacancies, if any, may be filled up from amongst the candidates in
the list after relaxing the qualifying forms.  The candidates belonging to weaker section of the society should be given preference
while filling up such vacancies.
 
VI        COMPUTER EDUCATION IN NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
6.1       JNVs being model pace-setting institutions in the district are equipped with required educational technology including
computers.  The Committee was given to understand that computers have been provided to 454 JNVs.  Under the Computer
Education Programme, each Vidyalaya is equipped to develop a Computer lab with minimum 7 P-III computers.  The main
objectives of Computer Education Programme of the Vidyalayas are to:
 
·                    Facilitate the students to learn computer literacy and hands on experience from class VI to XII.
·                    Create computer culture and consciousness among the young rural students.
·                    Familiarize the students with different range of computer applications and help them to understand the potential of
Information Technology in learning process.
·                    Integrate Information Technology with classroom transaction.
·                    Improving the capacities of the children in terms of their performance in scholastic and non-scholastic activities.
·                    Empower the teachers to use computers as one of their important teaching aid.
·                    Extending the facility of Computer Literacy to the students of neighborhood schools.
 
6.2       The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the Samiti in the field of Computer education.  It, however, notices that
a large number of schools were yet to have this facility. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the JNVs should be
covered under this scheme at the earliest. The Committee opines that the maintenance and connectivity with Internet should be
ensured to get optimum utilization of computers.  The Committee recommends that all the teachers should be encouraged and
suitably trained to work on computers.
 
VII      SMART SCHOOLS SCHEME
 
7.1       33 Vidyalayas have been identified as SMART Schools with one JNV from each State/UT.  Computer Equipment
comprising 34 computers (2 Server Computers, and 32 Node Computers), one Multimedia LCD Projector, one Laser Printer, one
Scanner, one CD Writer, one Modem, 6 UPSs (2 UPSs for Server Computers and 4 UPSs for Node Computers) are supplied to
each JNV selected as Smart School in addition to existing quota of computer equipment.  These Vidyalayas have developed
Computer Lab(s) with LAN facility.
7.2       The Committee recommends that more Vidyalayas may be covered under the scheme.  Local M.P. and MLA can be
associated for extending funds to such Vidyalayas for purchasing computers.
 
VIII     FUNDING

IX        CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDALAYAS
9.1       Admission to NVs is done on the basis of a Selection Test, for which a candidate has to fulfill the following eligibility
conditions: -
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
(a)    A candidate appearing for the Selection Test must be studying in Class V in a recognized school in that district where
he/she is seeking admission. Actual admission in Class VI is given subject to the condition of having passed Class V
before admission.
 
(b)   A candidate seeking admission must be between the age group 9-13 years on 1 st May of the year for which the Selection
Test is conducted.
 
(c)    A candidate must have studied and passed Class III, IV & V from recognized school/schools in the preceding three
continuous academic session for which the Selection Test is conducted spending one full academic session in each class
through the formal system of education, without any repetition of class, gap and/ or break in attendance.
 
(d)   A candidate who is not promoted to Class V before November of the preceding academic year, for which the test is
conducted, is not eligible to apply.
 
(e)    A candidate is not allowed second attempt to appear in the selection test under any circumstances.
 
(f)     A candidate seeking admission under the rural quota must have studied and passed III, IV & V from recognized school (s)
located in the rural areas.
 
            The above conditions are applicable to all the candidates irrespective to their caste or gender.  Efforts are made to ensure
that one-third of the total seats are filled up by girls.
 
9.2       The Samiti has given the following figures about the percentage of students belonging to SC/ST categories, girls and rural
areas in the Navodaya Vidayalayas, which is well above national norms (15% SC & 7.5% ST):
 
 SC
ST Girls Rural
2003-2004 23.90% 14.56% 34.01% 77.65%
 
 
9.3      The Committee appreciates the adequate representation of SCs, STs and girls in Navodaya Vidyalayas. It still feels that
there is scope for further increase in percentages of girls as well as students from rural areas. The Committee, however, expresses
its reservation about the eligibility condition requiring a rural candidate to pass class III, IV and V from recognized
school/schools, without any repetition of class, gap or break in attendance.  The Committee feels that it is not in consonance with
the ground realities and hardships faced in rural India. In villages, many times, parents are forced to take their children off the
school due to financial or personal reasons, resulting in break in studies. Consequently, many deserving children would stand
disqualified for the test.  The Committee feels that such restrictions for taking the test do not appear to be justified which might
deprive the poor children from getting quality education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this condition should be
reconsidered with a view to enabling those students who are talented, but are unable to afford continuous education. Such
students may be given remedial coaching, if need be.
 
9.4       During its study visits, the Committee was given to understand that admission process for NVs is a prolonged affair as the
admission tests are conducted in early May and the admission process is completed only by December.  However, the Samiti has
claimed that from the academic year 2001-2002 onwards, the system has been streamlined.  By and large, now the main admission
process is completed by July.  Only in case of new Vidyalayas, which are running in temporary accommodation, the admission
gets delayed mainly due to lack of necessary facilities.
 
9.5       The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to complete the admissions in time so that the studies of
children do not suffer.
 

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
9.6       During the course of discussions and also during visits, the Committee came to know about the problems being faced with
the State Governments in regard to the coordination of admission test as well issuing certificates of rural/urban, age, etc to the
children expeditiously by the District Administration.   The District Collector being the Chairman of the Vidyalaya Management
Committee is expected to overcome these difficulties.
 
9.7       The Committee recommends that the procedure as well as machinery for this purpose should be streamlined and sensitized
so that they could issue certificates to all the applicants after meticulously checking the details for rural/ urban areas, age etc.  The
Committee also recommends that the local MLA and President of concerned district Panchayat should also be included in the
Vidyalaya Management Committee.
 
X         PROBLEM OF DROPOUT
 
10.1     The Committee’s attention has been drawn towards the problem of drop-out in different classes of JNVs.  On a specific
query, various reasons were identified by the JNVs, which can be broadly classified as follows: -
-
                     medical ground, personal problem, family problem, transfer of parents to other station;
-                     non-eligibility of students for admission in science stream in class XI;
-                     Shifting to State Government Schools after passing class X for getting the benefit of State Quota in professional
courses.
-                     Unwillingness to move on migration in class IX.
 
10.2     The Committee was given to understand that the vacancies arising in classes upto VIII are not being filled up in view of
special identity of JNVs which are meant to provide quality education to children predominantly from rural areas.  Periodical
intake of students against the vacancies would create two types of children – those who have already adjusted to the system and
the newly admitted students not able to adapt themselves. Lateral entry is allowed only in class IX which is a stage when the
children are grown up, and special orientation programmes are conducted for them after their admission, with a view to bring
them on par with the regular students.
                  
10.3     The Committee is not inclined to accept this reasoning. The Committee is of the opinion that vacancies, if continued for a
long time, do result in wastage of scarce resources. It also results in denial of opportunity to students who badly need quality
education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts be made for filling the seats at first opportunity. Preference to girl
students of the area may be given in filling these vacant seats, as their adaptability to any situation is more than the boys. 
Regional offices of NVS may be empowered to fill up those vacancies under intimation to the headquarters.
 
10.4     The Committee notes with serious concern the tendency of most of the NV students, particularly in Maharashtra,
Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh leaving the school after class X to join schools run by State Governments with a view to get the
benefit of State quota in professional courses. The Committee finds that the percentage of students leaving the Vidyalayas after
class X in some of the states like Andhra Pradesh (43.75%) Karnataka (37.68%) and Maharashtra (45.91%) is very high.
           
10.5     The Committee was informed that the possibility of giving the option to the students to choose either CBSE or State Board
was explored by the Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti and the matter was taken up with the CBSE also. The CBSE, however, has not
agreed for the affiliation from both the Boards. The matter was also referred for further review to the Expert Committee
nominated by the Government for review of Management Structure and Operation Mechanism of JNVs which has given the
following recommendation:-
“The possibility of some or all Navodaya Vidyalayas offering affiliation both to the State Board and Central Board
simultaneously has been considered and has been found to be devoid of merit.  It is felt that such dual affiliation will
seriously undermine the concept of national identity and national uniformity in regard to teaching and learning in

Navodaya Vidyalayas.  Dual affiliation will also pose problem about the medium of instruction and it is likely to require
additional teachers”.
 
10.6     The Committee notes that while the students of Kendriya Vidyalayas in states like Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have
the options to choose between CBSE and State Boards, this facility of dual affiliation is not available in Navodaya Vidyalayas. 
The Committee also notes the concerns expressed by the Expert Committee nominated by the Government, which has been
quoted above.  The only concern of the Committee is that selective application of the principle of dual affiliation between KVS
and JNVs seems to be controversial.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this issue should be reviewed by the
Department at the earliest with a view to have uniform policy in this regard.
 
XI        FUTURE PROSPECTS OF NV STUDENTS
 
11.1     Every Navodaya Vidayalaya has a Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of Principal with Vice-Principal, four
teachers and three from Parent Teachers’ Council, to monitor the career guidance to the students. The Librarian of the Vidyalaya
collects all the data and information related to various career options. The Headquarters and Regional Offices also periodically
inform students about various courses and other career guidance information.
 
11.2     The Committee opines that outside agencies should also be roped in for specialized counselling on the career options
available, both inside as well as outside the country. There should also be counselling on various financial options available in the
form of study loans/assistanceships provided by the banks and other bodies. The students should also be taken out on study visits
to premier institutes of education like IIT, IIMs, and IISC etc. for an exposure to the academic/professional atmosphere so that
they also get motivated to set their respective goals and seriously endeavour to achieve such goals.
 
11.3     The Committee is also of the view that vocational education should be introduced in the JNVs.  Besides, Information
Technology, Computers, Engineering Drawing courses should also be introduced in NVs with a view to provide more
professional and career oriented options to the students.
 
11.4     The Committee was informed that a system has been developed by NVS to keep continuous rapport with the ex-students.

XIII     HOSTEL FACILITY
 
13.1     The Committee notes that out of 485 JNVs functioning as on 31.8.04, 368 JNVs are functioning in permanent site and 117
JNVs are functioning at temporary sites.  The Committee presumes that all 368 JNVs functioning in permanent site must be
having hostel facilities.  If that be so, the Committee is surprised to note that out of 339 posts of Matron sanctioned as on 30.6.04,
only 36 were in place.  In Bhopal, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow and Pune regions, not even one post of Matron has been filled up.
The Committee is unable to understand how the hostels can function properly without Matron.
 
13.2     The Committee was given to understand that teachers are also entrusted with the responsibility of supervising the hostels. 
The Vidyalayas being residential schools, a great deal of regular support in terms of care, counseling, guidance and emotional
attachment is to be developed among the students.  The parental care, which is otherwise not available, is to be provided by the
teachers.  In view of this, the hostel supervision is at time entrusted to the teachers.  The Committee is, not inclined to agree with
this approach. Engaging teachers for Matron’s job, the Committee is of the view, could be only a stopgap arrangement.  Teachers
are already over-burdened with their present assignment of teaching.  They can, at best, help the matron in smooth running of the
hostels.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that recruitment for the post of matron should be expedited within a stipulated
time frame.

XV TEACHERS
15.1     The Committee was informed that against sanctioned posts of 2972 PGT Teachers as on 30.6.04, 2550 posts were filled up
and 422 posts were vacant.  Similarly, out of 6681 sanctioned posts of TGT and Miscellaneous Category Teachers, 5876 posts
were filled up and there were 805 vacancies.
 
15.2     On a specific query about the efforts made by NVS for filling up the vacancies, the Committee was informed that the
Samiti had conducted a recruitment drive during June, 2004 on the basis of which offers of appointment were sent to 331
candidates for appointment as Post Graduate Teachers.  Offers could not be sent in 11 cases due to non-availability of suitable ST
candidates. Remaining 80 vacancies in the grade of PGT were to be filled by promotion by October, 2004. As regards 805
vacancies of TGTs, offers of appointment had been sent to 437 candidates selected during recent recruitment drive. 265 posts of
TGT posts were, however, still vacant.
 
15.3     Reasons for not filling up the vacancies as informed to the Committee were the following: -
1)
      New posts arise every year at the starting of new academic session due to upgradation of Vidyalayas from Secondary level
to Senior Secondary level.
2)      Vacancies arise due to retirement/resignation of existing teachers.
3)      Vacancies arise due to promotion from TGTs to PGTs, PGTs to Vice-Principals.
4)      Vacancies exist due to non-availability of suitable candidates in the reserved categories.
 
15.4     All Regional Offices/Principals have been empowered to fill-up the vacancies of teachers from time to time on contract
basis so that studies of children are not hampered. The Committee was informed that 483 Teachers - 205 PGT and 278 TGT
Teachers were working on contract basis.
 
15.5     The Committee observes that maximum numbers of vacancies of teachers are in Bhopal, Chandigarh, Pune and Shillong
Regions.  The Committee also notes that maximum number of teachers working on contract basis – 165 and 83 teachers
respectively are in Chandigarh and Shillong Regions.  Subject-wise, maximum vacancies were in Biology i.e. 89 PGT posts and 
in English  112 TGT posts lying vacant.
 
15.6     The Committee understands that quite a few incentives are being given to all categories of employees including teachers
opting for “Hard Stations”. However, the Committee is constrained to observe that these initiatives do not seem to be having the
desired results as maximum number of vacancies of both PGT and TGT Teachers are in Chandigarh and Shillong Regions
whereunder maximum number of hard stations fall.  Not only this, maximum number of teachers serving on contract basis are
posted in these two Regions only.
 
15.7     The Committee feels that the vacancies in the teaching staff adversely affects the overall performance of Navodaya
Vidyalayas. as the academic activities in schools get seriously hampered. The Committee is of the view that there is an urgent
need for reviewing the recruitment procedure of teaching staff. The Committee, also, recommends that the vacancies of teachers
in Navodaya Vidyalayas should be anticipated quite in advance and efforts should be made to complete the process of
appointments well before the start of next academic session.

XVII    POSTING IN HARD STATIONS
17.1     With a view to motivate employees for accepting posting in Navodaya Vidyalayas located in North East Region and other
hard and difficult stations, as identified by the Samiti provides the following incentives:
 
a)
                  On completion of mandatory tenure Category-I employees will be posted to station of their choice. Choices in respect of
three NVs and one State will be obtained from them at the time of posting to NE Region. All possible efforts are made to
post them to one of the three NVs of their choice. In case that is not feasible on account of unavoidable reasons, at least the
State of their choice is assured even if it amounts to displacement of someone.
 
b)
                  Orders for posting outside the NE Region in respect of category-I employees will be issued two months before the
completion of mandatory tenure. However, in case such orders are not received even after two months of completion of
mandatory tenure, they shall stand relieved automatically and report for duty to the Regional Office having the jurisdiction
of State of their choice.
 
c)
                  Category-I employees will further be assured of posting of their choice in the NE Region from within the available
vacancies.
 
In fact all such conditions will be incorporated in the transfer order itself.
 
17.2        This scheme has been introduced in the Samiti w.e.f. academic year 2003-04. The teachers who have willingly accepted
posting to NE Region under these instructions, would be due for transfer out of hard and difficult stations only in the year 2006-07
after completing mandatory tenure of three years at these places.
 
17.3     The Committee was informed that there has been very significant response to the incentives given by the Samiti for the
employees opting hard and difficult stations including North East Region. During the year 2003-04 and 2004-05, 260 teachers
have willingly opted for posting to these stations and are continuing at present.
 
17.4        The Committee recommends that the NVS should ensure a more transparent transfer policy for teachers.  The teachers
should be posted at hard stations only on rotational basis and should be transferred soon after completing their tenure. The
transfers/postings should be effected in the beginning of the academic year and the process of relieving/joining should be
streamlined. The Government may also consider extending additional facilities and allowances to motivate more teachers to join
and stay back particularly in the areas like North East and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
 
XVIII              PENSIONARY BENEFITS TO NVS EMPLOYEES
 
           
18.1     The Committee notes that the employees of NVs do not get pensionery benefits whereas employees of KVS, NCERT and
other similar autonomous organizations under the Department of Secondary and Higher Education enjoy the benefit of pension.
The Committee was informed thata proposal for introduction of pension scheme for the employees of the Samiti was referred to
the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure in July 1989 which did not support the proposal on the ground that the
pension provision would increase the expenditure of the Government as pension scheme is costlier than the Contributory
Provident Fund scheme.  Since then the proposal has been taken up with the Ministry of Finance at various levels on several
occasions but with no success.  The Ministry of Finance on different occasions advised the Samiti either to work out a suitable
annuity scheme through the Life Insurance Corporation based on voluntary contributions of the employees without any liability on
the Government or to consider opting for pension scheme notified by Ministry of Labour.  The Samiti had taken up this matter
with the Life Insurance Corporation but the schemes offered by LIC or the pension scheme notified by Ministry of Labour were

15th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/154threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
not accepted by the employees of the Samiti as they were not found comparable to the GPF/Pension Scheme in vogue in the
Government and other autonomous organizations.
 
18.2     Another initiativeat HRM level in 1998 was grounded down by the Ministry of Finance on the plea that there would be
similar demands from other autonomous organizations receiving grants-in-aid from the Government, which may be difficult to
resist. The Finance Ministry advanced the following reasons for rejecting the proposal: -
 
(a)    The cost of introduction of pension scheme is much higher than the CPF Scheme.  While CPF is an one-time
settlement, pension is a life-long commitment not only in respect of the pensioner but his family also.  The liability on
account of pension keeps on increasing with every increase/revision in pay/pensionary benefits on the basis of the
recommendations of the successive Pay Commissions, revision in the rates of dearness relief etc.  As most of the
autonomous organizations are fully funded through grants-in-aid received from the Government, Government’s
liability will increase to that extent if pension scheme is introduced.
 
(b)
   For servicing the pension scheme, a pension fund is required to be set up to be managed by a Trust.  Difficulties may
be experienced in judicious administration of the fund.
 
(c)    Under the Employees’ Provident Fund Act, the accretions to the Provident Fund are to be invested as per the pattern of
investment laid down by the Government.  With the formation of a Pension Fund, if accretions are invested elsewhere,
the Government will loose resources to that extent.
 
(d)
   In case the organization is wound up for one reason or the other, the Government may have to take over the entire
liability for pension.
 
 
18.3     The Committee takes note of the reservations of the Ministry of Finance in providing Pensionary benefit to employees of
NVS.   The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for having different approach of mind for employees working in two
organisations doing similar work under a similar set up and conditions.   The Committee would like to point out when employees
of Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan can enjoy the pensionary benefits on their retirement, what deters the Government in providing
similar facility for employees of Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti, many of them away from their families serving in residential
schools located in rural areas.  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that the position may be reviewed again and a decision
acceptable to employees of JNVs may be reached at the earliest.

to the Regional Offices, which are instrumental in managing the affairs of the JNVs in that particular region more effectively and
efficiently.  The Ministry of HRD should take the lead and pursue the State Government, if possible at the Minister’s level. 
 
21.3     Each Regional Office has been provided with one Deputy Director, 5 Assistant Directors, 1 Accounts Officer and 2
Section Officers along with supporting secretariat staff.  For monitoring and supervision of construction of Vidyalaya buildings,
one Executive Engineer and one Junior Engineer has been provided to each Regional Office by internal adjustment.  This staff
pattern was approved by the Government during 1988-89 and there has been no increase in the staff strength thereafter. On the
contrary 10% of secretarial posts have been reduced under economy instructions of the Government.  
 
21.4     The Committee notes that in spite of expansion of JNVs from 2 Vidyalayas started in 1985-86 to 509 at present, the staff
strength at Regional Offices has not increased proportionately.  These eight Regional Offices with the meagre sanctioned staff
strength, functional strength may be even less, are supposed to supervise the functioning of 509 sanctioned NVs (485 NVs being
functional), many of them located in remote and inaccessible areas.   The Committee can well imagine the state of affairs.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends to have an O&M study done urgently for the evaluation of the work & staff in ROs, so that the
requisite number of posts could be created for smooth functioning of NVs.

IX        CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDALAYAS
 
           The Committee appreciates the adequate representation of SCs, STs and girls in Navodaya Vidyalayas. It still feels that
there is scope for further increase in percentages of girls as well as students from rural areas. The Committee, however, expresses
its reservation about the eligibility condition requiring a rural candidate to pass class III, IV and V from recognized
school/schools, without any repetition of class, gap or break in attendance.  The Committee feels that it is not in consonance with
the ground realities and hardships faced in rural India. In villages, many times, parents are forced to take their children off the
school due to financial or personal reasons, resulting in break in studies. Consequently, many deserving children would stand
disqualified for the test.  The Committee feels that such restrictions for taking the test do not appear to be justified which might
deprive the poor children from getting quality education.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this condition should be
reconsidered with a view to enabling those students who are talented, but are unable to afford continuous education. Such
students may be given remedial coaching, if need be. (Para 9.3)

strength at Regional Offices has not increased proportionately.  These eight Regional Offices with the meagre sanctioned staff
strength, functional strength may be even less, are supposed to supervise the functioning of 509 sanctioned NVs (485 NVs being
functional), many of them located in remote and inaccessible areas.   The Committee can well imagine the state of affairs.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends to have an O&M study done urgently for the evaluation of the work & staff in ROs, so that the
requisite number of posts could be created for smooth functioning of NVs. (Para 21.4)
 
XXII    GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL
 
            The Committee is not satisfied with the functioning of the grievance redressal mechanism in NVs and feels that if teachers
grievances were not attended to in time, they will not be able to concentrate on teaching.  The Committee recommends that all the
Regional Offices should have a Grievance Cell so that the cases are attended to and disposed off quickly.  The principals should
also endeavour to get the matter sorted out early in consultation with the Regional Offices. The aggrieved person should also have
easy access to the officers. For this, a day in a week may be fixed enabling them to meet the officials.  The Teacher's Association
should also be encouraged to participate in the decision making process of the Samiti.  (Para 22.2)
 
XXIII    NON ACCEPTANCE OF THE SCHEME OF NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
 
 
23.3     The Committee is not convinced by the arguments of the State Government mainly because the JNVs are catering to the
educational needs of meritorious students from the poor and deprived sections of the society, with special emphasis on the girl
students.  The three language formula adopted by the JNVs needs to be encouraged by all the State Government as an element of
national integration.  The Government should, therefore convince and persuade the State Government on these broad objectives to
adopt the schemes of JNVs.  (Para 23.2)
           
XXIV  PROBLEMS BEING FACED IN RUNNING THE JNVS
24.2     The Committee feels that most of these problems can be solved with proper coordination and support from the State
Governments.  Since the Navodaya Vidyalayas do not have financial provision for laying connecting roads, electrical lines, and
levelling the lines, etc., the State Govt. should be requested to periodically monitor the support given to the Vidyalayas and ensure
that the minimum infrastructural facilities are extended uninterruptedly.  District Magistrate being actually associated in all such
issues  can take lead in  getting these problems redressed quickly. (Para 24.2)
 
XXV    SURVEY OF JNVs

(Chapter – IV) Total- 1
 
2.1     The final replies in respect of the recommendations/observations made in Chapter IV of the Report are still awaited
from the Department. The Committee may be apprised of the same as and when action is taken.
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.2       The Committee notes that increment in the allocations of the Department for the year 2004-05 is nominal with which
Department would hardly be able to carry out two of its main schemes (SSA & MDM) let alone other schemes.  These two
schemes would require Rs.10,919.00 crores for the year 2004-05, according to the Department.  The Committee notes that
the Government recognizing this need of the Department has provided for 2% education cess from this year. 
Department should put forth this aspect before the Ministry of Finance at appropriate stage.
 
2.3       Even if the entire Rs. 5000.00 crores expected to be generated from Education Cess is fully utilized to meet the
additional requirements, there will still be a shortfall of Rs.187.00 crores.  The Department should put forth this aspect
before the Ministry of Finance at appropriate stage.
 
Action Taken
 
2.2 & 2.3 Requirements for SSA and MDM for 2004-05 mentioned in para 2.2 was based on information furnished by the

155th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/155threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
Department to the Committee on 22.7.2004.
 
At that time, extension of MDM programme to Upper Primary stage was envisaged from this year itself.  Subsequently,
Government decided not to extend MDM programme to the Upper Primary stage for the present, resulting in reduction of
requirement for this programme from Rs.4499 crore to Rs.3261 crore, and of total requirement for SSA and MDM from
Rs.10,919 crore to Rs.9681 crore. As against this, additional provision of Rs.2000 crore and 1232 crore (total Rs.3232 crore)
have been made for SSA and MDM schemes respectively in 1
st    Supplementary Budget for 2004-05. With this, total
allocation for SSA and MDM has risen from Rs. 4732 crores to Rs. 7964 crores.
 
As suggested by the Committee, Department will continue to forcefully project its financial requirements before Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance at every opportunity.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.4       The Committee also notes considerable gap between the demand projected by the Working Group Report of the
Department before the Planning Commission both for the Elementary Education as well as Adult Education for the 10
th
Plan Period.  It feels that primary education has suffered from deprivation and degradation mainly due to inadequate
allocation of resources over several decades.  The Committee is happy that the education of children has received some
attention but is still not treated as priority area as far as resource allocation is concerned.  Some very good schemes have
been started with valuable components, which need to be strengthened and expanded.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that need for adequate funds for elementary education should be projected effectively by the Department
before the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission at the RE stage.  At the same time, the Committee has a word
of caution for the Department.  Although allocation of Rs.1951.25 crores for Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan in 2003-04 was
enhanced to Rs.2732.32 crores at the RE stage, the Department could utilize only Rs.2582.29 crores.  In the event of their
projected demand of Rs.6420.00 crores being met, the Department will have to take effective steps for optimum and
judicious utilization of enhanced allocation.
 
Action Taken
 
2.4       The issue of future requirements for the Department’s programmes will be projected to the Planning Commission as
part of its Mid-Term Appraisal exercise for the Tenth Five Year Plan.  
                                                        
BE for SSA in 2003-04 was Rs.1951.25 crore, which was raised to Rs.2732.32 crore at RE stage.  As against this, total
expenditure during 2003-04 was Rs.2710.64 crore (Rs.2582.29 crore under non-EAP and Rs.150 crore under EAP
components) which works out to be 99.2% of RE.   It appears that while quoting the expenditure figure of Rs.2582.29 crore
in para 2.4, the Committee omitted to include the expenditure of Rs.150 crore shown under EAP. 
 
However, Department has taken note of the Committee’s concern regarding effective steps for optimum and judicious
utilization of enhanced allocation, and will make all possible efforts in that behalf.
 
III SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN
 
 Recommendations/Observations
 
3.7       The Committee notes that there had been some underutilization of funds during the Ninth Plan.  Underutilization, in
Committee’s view, is a cause for serious concern.  It points out more towards the laxity on the part of the implementing
authorities than anything else.  Such a performance does not inspire confidence as to the success of this programme, hence it
should be avoided at every cost.
 
Action Taken
 
3.7       The concern of the Committee is noted for guidance and compliance.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.8       The Committee notes that assistance under the programme is on a 75:25 sharing arrangement between the Central
Govt. and State Governments.  The Committee is not aware about the acceptance level of this distribution by the States

155th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/155threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
already burdened by financial constraints.  The Committee apprehends that proposed 50:50 sharing between Central and
State Governments after Tenth Plan may not find favour with majority of the States.  The Department may need to have a
re-assessment of this funding pattern by having a Mid-Term appraisal of Tenth Plan during the current year, 2004-05.
 
Action Taken
 
3.8       A proposal for change in the sharing arrangement between the Centre and the States has been sent to the Planning
Commission for consideration during their Mid-Term Appraisal exercise for the 10
th Plan.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.10     The Committee is dismayed to note that of the 4,06,148 teachers sanctioned to be appointed, only 1,38,090 (i.e.
33%) could be appointed during the last two years.  Against the fixed target for recruitment of teachers, States like Bihar,
U.P. and West Bengal could achieve zero percent, 22 per cent and 21 per cent of the target respectively.  These States
constitute a large proportion of children between 6-14 years.  Such a dismal performance in the bigger States does not augur
well for the future of this programme.
 
Action Taken
 
3.10     As per latest available information, as against 5,35,203 posts of elementary teachers approved for Central assistance
during 2001-04, 310506 (58%) posts have been filled.  Of the three States mentioned in the Report Uttar Pradesh has since
made considerable progress by filling up 74% of the sanctioned posts of elementary teachers.  The matter is being pursued
with Bihar and West Bengal.
 
Recommendations/Observation
 
3.11     The Committee is concerned over the quality of education imparted under the Abhiyan.  The Committee is little
apprehensive about the feasibility of appointing education volunteer/para teachers for imparting quality education to the
children.  The Committee strongly feels that a child needs to be tended under well-trained hands to initiate him into the art
of learning.  The Committee is aware of the fact that there was problem in getting regular teachers in remote and
inaccessible habitations.  It, however, emphasizes the importance of trained teachers for child education.  The Committee is
happy to know that the Department had made a provision of pre-service induction/training as well as in service training of
Education Volunteers even at Block/Cluster levels.  But the Committee finds that due to shortage of teachers, not to speak of
trained teachers/qualified resource persons at block and cluster levels, aims of the Programme are not being achieved.
 
Action Taken
 
3.11     Para teachers are not necessarily under-qualified. On the contrary, data collected for 462 districts in 18 States for
2002-03 under District Information System for Education (DISE) has revealed that 97.6% have Secondary or higher
qualification, and 88.4% have Higher Secondary or higher qualification.
 
Under Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan there is provision of 20 days’ in-service training for all teachers annually, 60 days’ refresher
course for untrained teachers already employed as teachers, and 30 days orientation course for trained, new recruits. 
 
States are making use of the above provision under SSA to upgrade professional competence of their teachers.  Efforts are
being made by States for training of un-trained in-service teachers through Distance Mode, with the help of IGNOU and
recognition from NCTE.  These include a six month training programme for primary teachers especially designed for North-
Eastern States and Sikkim, and State specific elementary teacher training programmes for Orissa, Jharkhand, Madhya
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan and Gujarat.  In addition to this, NCTE has also approved, in principle, a one year training
programme in Distance mode for training of un-trained primary school teachers of Bihar.
 
 
IV  KASTURBA GANDHI SWATANTRA VIDYALAYA (KGSV)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.3       The Committee feels that KGSV is laudable scheme but is concerned about the snail’s pace at which it was being

155th Report of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/155threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:21:28]
implemented.  Changes and modifications from time to time, no doubt, were key to any Scheme being relevant, effective
and meaningful, the inordinate delay caused in restructuring the scheme does not appear to be quite justified to the
Committee.  The Committee is happy to learn that this scheme since has been revised.  It, therefore, expects that KGSV
would be implemented with full steam  and the Department would see that the allocation would not be reduced in the year
2004-05 as well.  About 700 residential schools are to be opened during the 10 th Plan Period, which would require
considerable planning, determination as well as adequate resources in the year 2004-05.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that adequate resources should be provided to spread this noble scheme for girls far and wide.
 
4.4       The Committee appreciates the idea of developing local specific curriculum suitable for girls from the SCs, STs,
minorities and OBCs communities.  The Committee desires to add that the curriculum should be such that it is not only
contextual and interesting to them but also empowers them economically in order to sustain themselves in the society.
 
Action Taken
 
4.3 & 4.4 The detailed guidelines for the Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV) scheme were disseminated to the 21
States eligible on 2
nd August, 2004.  The State Governments were requested to send in their detailed plans for opening of
KGBV Schools by 30th September, 2004.  The Hon’ble Human Resource Development Minister wrote to all the concerned
Chief Ministers on seeking the State Governments fullest cooperation in planning and effectively implementing the scheme. 
There were positive responses received from the States concerned.  A National Level Workshop was held on 2nd November,
2004 with the participant State Government representatives and experts with experience in running residential schools for
girls, in order for the States to develop a better understanding of the scheme’s implementation, learn from existing national
experiences and also to build capacity of implementation staff. The necessity for local specific curriculum along with the
elements of work experience has been emphasized at the Upper Primary level.
 
By 17
th December 2004 approvals for 525 KGBV Schools had been accorded to 17 States.
 
V National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education (Mid-Day Meal Scheme)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
5.6       The Committee finds that the Mid-Day Meal Scheme, no doubt, was a noble scheme, which not only motivates the
children to come to school and remain there but also takes care of the problem of malnutrition, particularly, in the rural
areas.  The Committee finds that the main problem is cooking and serving the food.  It would require huge funds, should the
Centre decide to support this as well.  Given the ground realities and financial constraints of some States, covering all the

Recommendations/Observations
 
5.3       It has been informed that as on January 2004, fourteen States and seven Union Territories were providing cooked

educationally backward also, Mid-Day Meal Scheme still remains to be implemented in the true sense and as per the
Supreme Court directive.

III.              INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13   The Committee notes that ICDS takes the major share of the budgetary allocation of the Department.  Success
of the scheme largely depends on the functioning of Anganwadi workers (AWWs).  The Committee is, however, not
satisfied with the plight of these workers.  The meagre pecuniary benefits and poor facilities do not attract people to
work as AWWs.  The Committee is surprised to see that their role still remains undefined; they are asked to do all
kind of odd works such as census operation, distribution of drugs etc.  This puts extra pressure on them and their
main role is diluted. 
 
Action Taken
 
            The role and responsibilities of the AWWs and AWHs are well defined in the ICDS Scheme.  However, over the
years, AWWs and AWHs have been increasingly called upon to discharge duties in relation to various other
schemes/programmes of Government of India, State Governments and local bodies, in addition to the task assigned to them
under ICDS Programme.  In view of this, a Core Committee comprising  of Secretary, D/WCD as Chairperson and
representatives from concerned Departments and State Governments has been set up to review the role and responsibilities
of AWWs and AWHs.  Three meetings of the Committee have already been held so far.

In so far as the laws to give equal rights to women in ownership of assets is concerned, the laws relating to intestate
succession among Hindus are codified under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The NCW has reviewed the said Act and one

Reasons for shortfall and remedial measures
 
            The scheme of Condensed Course stipulates that the objectives of the scheme is to provide educational opportunities
to the girls and women who are school  drop-outs or who could not join mainstream education system due to their adverse
circumstances.  The CSWB, during the initial years of 9th Five Year Plan i.e. the year 1997-98, 98-99 & 2000-01 took a
decision.
 
i)
                     Not to consider proposals of such voluntary organizations for above Primary level courses who did not have
educational experience.  Even proposals from the institutions with experience of literacy or non-formal education were not
considered for sanction, though the scheme makes it clear that the proposals of the institutions who were engaged in women
welfare activities can be considered.  By imposing such restrictions many institutions could not avail the grant under the
programme which led to non-utlization of funds.
 
ii)
                   The CSWB also took a decision not to sanction residential courses whereas there was persistent demand from the
voluntary organizations functioning in rural, tribal and backward areas for residential course.
 
iii)            Though, there is no provision in the scheme to stipulate the condition of 50% result in examination, the CSWB took
a decision that continuation courses (IInd & IIIrd batches) should not be considered for the institutions whose result of earlier
batch was less than 50% in spite of the fact that in many States results of even candidates from regular schools in
CBSE/Higher Secondary Examination was even less than 50%.
 
The above conditions restricted the scope of implementation of the scheme as per objective of the programme. 
However, the CSWB took remedial measures and the Executive Committee of the CSWB in its 136th Meeting held on
20.7.2000 had decided that 50% passed percentage for continuation courses shall not be insisted upon.  The average State
result of girl candidates shall be taken as a criterion for giving continuation grant.  The Executive Committee has also taken a
decision that educational experience for middle and matric/equivalent level courses should not be insisted upon as voluntary
institutions having experience in conducting women’s programme are also eligible for assistance as per the scheme.  It was
also decided that the applications of residential courses should also be considered particularly for the courses which are to be
conducted in tribal, rural and backward area.

III.
             INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS)
 
Recommendations/Observation
 
3.7       The fact that nearly 95 out of 1000 children under five die is nothing less than shocking.  The latest position of IMR
is not known as this figure is   for the year 1998.  Such a high IMR is certainly a very sad reflection on our efforts for child
development.  ICDS's main aim, in fact, is to lower the infant mortality because it focuses not only on child care but on
pregnant and lactating mothers as well.  If the IMR is taken as indicator, the performance/effectively of the ICDS tells a sad
story. The inability to operationalise ICDS projects, the Committee feels, is the main reason for this situation.  The
requirement must be much more as the sanctioned projects are as per the 1991 census. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should take up this issue with the States/implementing agencies at higher level to chalk out
an action plan to be taken up at emergency level and in time bound manner.  The Committee also emphasizes the need for
constant and effective monitoring of implementation of this scheme.  Having independent channel of getting feedback is
also of prime importance which needs to be put in place immediately.
 
Action Taken
 
There are various factors like low birth rate, pneumonia, birth asphyxia etc. which are attributable to death of
children.  One of the major findings of the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), which  conducted an
independent survey of ICDS projects in 1998, was that the infant mortality rate (IMR) was lower in ICDS areas than in non-
ICDS areas.
 
Regarding operationalisation of ICDS projects/AWCs, there has been continuous emphasis upon States to

letter from Secretary (WCD) to Chief Secretaries of the States.   In response to a Public Interest Litigation (PIL), the
Supreme Court has also, vide its order dated 29.4.2004, directed the States, inter-alia,  to operationalise all the sanctioned

Other options for improving supervision and monitoring at National level include establishment of a National
Programme Management Unit with consultants in the area of nutrition, community mobilization, health, pre-school

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee notes with concern that even after the directions of Supreme Court, the Department has shortfall of

The responsibility of providing Supplementary Nutrition, as per the Scheme, lies with the State Governments. 
However, it has been observed that many States do not make adequate provision for supplementary nutrition in their budget.
The State Governments have, therefore, been requested, from time to time, to ensure that Supplementary nutrition is
provided to all beneficiaries as per nutritional norms of the Scheme and to budget adequately.    To ensure that the States
make adequate provision for supplementary nutrition, Minister for HRD has taken up the matter with the Deputy Chairman,
Planning Commission to address this aspect during formulation and finalization of States’ Annual Plan.  The Government of
India has been supplementing the efforts of the States by providing food grains at BPL rates under the Wheat Based
Nutrition Programme (WBNP). Under PMGY Additional Central Assistance is provided to the States for providing
enhanced requisite nutrition requirement to children in 0-3 years. To provide free food grains to under– nourished
adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women, a Pilot Project has been launched in 51 identified nutritionally backward
districts across the country. Under this Project 6 kgs food grains (wheat/rice) per month are made available to the identified
beneficiaries, free of cost.  All these programmes are run through the Anganwadi Centres.

            The Committee notes that the Central Government has been supplementing the efforts of States in providing
supplementary Nutrition by providing food grains at BPL rates.  Besides that PMGY also takes care of nutrition requirement

3.10   While appreciating this development, the Committee would like to point out that the norm of one Anganwadi Centre
for 700 populations in tribal projects needs to be relooked into/revised in the case of Manipur.  Instead of one AWC for 700

Action Taken
The population of the country has increased over the years. The Supreme Court vide its order dated 28.11.2001 and
29.4.2004, has directed the Government of India, inter-alia, to increase the number of Anganwadi Centres so as to cover 14
lakh habitations.  The CMP states that attempts will be made to universalize the ICDS Scheme to provide a functional
Anganwadi in every settlement and ensure full coverage of all children. It may be noted that as on 31.3.2004, out of 7.5 lakh
sanctioned AWCs there are about 6.59 lakh functional Aganwadis in the country. These have been set up since the inception
of the scheme in the year 1975 i.e. in a period of 29 years. However, in the light of CMP and direction of the Supreme
Court, an Inter-ministerial Task Force has been setup to review the existing population norms for sanction of a Project and
Anganwadi Centre under the ICDS Scheme and suggest the revised population norms.  This will necessitate further
additional Projects and Centers and consequential increase in the Department’s Plan Outlay.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee finds the reply of the Department to be too technical and hence evasive.   The Committee's intention
was to evolve a more rationale approach in the norm of setting up Anganwadi Centres in case of Manipur and other States
having similar geographic location so that more Anganwadi Centres could be set up in these areas.  The Committee,
therefore, reiterates its recommendation.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.12    The Committee is surprised to know about so many schemes of child nutrition being implemented simultaneously by
different Department/Ministries.  Incidence of large scale malnutrition in children indicates that there is serious lacuna in the
existing system.  It is incomprehensible to the Committee as to why there is malnutrition in the children despite the number
of schemes operated through different Department as also by the State Governments.  The Committee feels that multiplicity
of schemes as well as Departments is also creating confusion leading to wastage and duplication of resources and efforts. 
The Committee recommends that a coordinated approach amongst all the concerned Department/Ministries is the need of
the hour.  The Department of Women and Child Development should be a nodal agency for all such scheme to achieve
optimum results.  Inter-departmental meetings should be held regularly to review the progress on nutritional level of the
children. 
 
Action Taken
 
Different programmes of the Government in the area of health and welfare are indirect nutrition interventions for
promoting nutrition of the people, including vulnerable groups like children and pregnant and lactating women. The existing
nutrition interventions namely the ICDS, anaemia control and vitamin A prophylaxis programmes, iodisation of salt,
targeted public distribution system touch only the outer edge of the complex problem of malnutrition which requires a multi-
pronged action at different levels with substantial resources.  The problem of malnutrition is so huge and complex that inter-
sectoral efforts in the area of food security, health and education are necessary.
 
The Department of Women and Child Development is the nodal agency for institutionalizing the multi-sectoral
strategy of National Nutrition Policy.  Interdepartmental meetings are held from time to time to set the nutrition goals and to

frame the strategy for achieving the same.  Existing inter-sectoral coordination mechanism has been upgraded to the highest
level by notifying the constitution of National Nutrition Mission under the Hon’ble Prime Minister in July 2003.  The
Executive Committee of National Nutrition Mission recently met on 3rd September 2004 and the meeting of the National
Nutrition Mission is likely to be held shortly so that directions to concerned sectors for promoting nutrition of the people is
provided through this forum besides assigning high priority and resources for programmes required to address the complex
problem of malnutrition.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee is aware that the problem of malnutrition is so huge and complex that inter-sectoral efforts in the
areas of food security, health and education are necessary.  The Committee reiterates that different schemes of child
nutrition being implemented by various Ministries/Departments and also at State level need to be brought under one nodal
agency with special focus on tribal and remote areas of the country.  Interdepartmental meetings for setting nutrition goals
and framing the strategy for achieving the same do not seem to have led to any visible improvement.  The Committee,
therefore, reiterates that the Department mandated to look after the welfare of children and women has to play a more pro-
active role.

18. 1     The Committee was informed that some of the schemes of the Department were being implemented through NGOs.

yeoman service.  Department gave a list of NGOs blacklisted by it.  The Committee feels that simply blacklisting such
NGOs would not deter the delinquent ones and they might come back with change names/address.  Government needs to
streamline the procedure of their selection as well as regular monitoring of their work.  We should have penal provisions for
recovering the grants given to defaulting NGOs.  The NGOs doing good job needs to be suitably rewarded so as to motivate
others.   
 
Action Taken
 
            A State Level Empowered Committee (SLEC), under the Chairpersonship of Secretary, WCD/Social Welfare of the
concerned State, comprising  representatives of Finance/Planning/Technical Department etc. has been set up in all the States
for scrutiny of proposals  under various schemes of the Departments.    The proposals received from NGOs/
Corporations/Undertakings are scrutinized by the SLEC before these are passed on to GOI for consideration.  The idea is
that the SLEC would be in a better position to know about the credibility, reputation, genuineness and past performance of
the Organisations/ NGOs.
 
            As regards monitoring of implementation of projects, the same is being undertaken by the State WDCs/Central
Social Welfare Board(CSWB).  Besides, the University Women Development Centres are also engaged by the Department
for monitoring the implementation.  A performance report (i.e.Mid-Term Evaluation Report) from the State Government is
insisted upon at the time of release of second instalment to the NGOs/organisations.

NGOs/organisations.  The  NGOs/ organisations found wanting in certain respects or defaulting in the implementation of the
projects are black-listed/penalised accordingly.

COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
         
The reasons advanced by the Department for continuous underutilization of allocated funds for various welfare
schemes confirms Committee’s apprehensions about major drawbacks in the formulation and implementation thereof.  While
unsatisfactory performance of implementing agencies, i.e. NGOs has been cited as the factor responsible in the case of
scheme of Short Stay Homes, it is the inherent shortcomings noticed in the salient features of the scheme of “Condensed
Courses on Education for Women.”  The Committee is surprised to observe that it has taken years to make the Department

situation confirms Committee’s doubts that programmes continue to be announced without any assessment preceding the
same.
 
            The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the inefficiency and lack of direction and to some extent lack of
leadership at the Central and State level which have culminated in the poor and dismal utilization of budget allocation for
many socio-economic programmes.  These Programmes, if implemented in right earnest, would have benefited thousands of
needy and distressed children and women.  The reply of the Department appears to be shifting the responsibility to other
agencies for various reasons.  The lackadaisical approach of CSWB, which is directly under its control, has miserably failed
in achieving its targets.  The Committee desires that the Department should take up with various agencies/State

of NGOs in a district (subject to area) should be indicated.  The Committee feels that mere noting of Committee’s
recommendations for compliance will not serve the purpose.   The Committee reiterates that there is an urgent need for
having such guidelines otherwise instances of excess number of NGOs operating from a limited area will continue to occur.
(Para 18.2)
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee is dismayed to note that the Department has failed to share its apprehension for strengthening the
monitoring mechanism by making sanctioning/approving authority accountable for the non-performing/under performing
NGOs.  It seems the Department has confined its responsibility only to sanctioning the loans. (Para 18.4)

2.2       The Committee notes that initially, Rs. 9.32 crores was earmarked for the Afro-Asian Games in BE 2003-04 on the
plan side and subsequently Rs. 55.00 crore was obtained as supplementary grant for this purpose, but on non-plan side.  The
Committee also notes that Rs. 8.00 crore was re-appropriated from plan side to non-plan side for a newly created head.  In
view of this, the Committee feels that assessment about Afro-Asian Games requirements was highly unrealistic, because
ultimately, a total Rs. 64.32 crores had to be given (Rs. 9.32 crores + Rs. 55.00 crore) for this purpose, instead of Rs. 9.32
crore originally provided for.  Secondly, the re-appropriation of funds from plan to non-plan, according to the Committee, is
not a healthy practice, which leaves less money for the schemes, which are already cash-starved.
 
Action Taken
 
The Games were earlier scheduled to be held at New Delhi from 3
rd to 11 th November, 2001.  The details of
expenditure and financial arrangements for the Games were to be settled between Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Youth
Affairs.  However, on 14th September 2001 Government after reviewing the overall security scenario that emerged as a result
of the terrorist attacks in USA decided to postpone the Games.  Subsequently on the proposal of Indian Olympic Association,
on 1st September, 2003 Government had approved the holding of the Games from 24 th October to 1 st November, 2003 at
Hyderabad instead of New Delhi.
 
As such at BE 2003-04 a nominal provision of Rs.9.32 crores was kept at the time of preparing the estimates. 
However, as per the financial arrangements settled between Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports,
this Ministry was to provide Rs.8.00 crores and Ministry of Finance was to provide Rs.55.00 crores as additionality for
First Afro Asian Games.
 
Since the funds were to be transferred to State Government, a new budget head under Non-Plan was opened.  In
view of this, the plan allocation of Rs.8.00 crores (as a Central Government Share) was re-appropriated from Plan to Non-
Plan.  The additionality of Rs.55.00 crores (Non-Plan) provided by Ministry of Finance was also kept under this head.
 
In view of the above there has been no financial impact on any plan scheme of this Ministry.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
2.3
              The Committee notes that the allocation of the Ministry for the year 2004-05, has been marginally increased and
believes that it would hardly suffice to implement the ongoing projects, leave alone new initiatives proposed by the
Ministry.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should place its requirements for this year, before the
Ministry of Finance/Planning Commission justifying its need for higher allocation at the RE Stage.
 
Action Taken
 
Ministry has already projected its requirement of additional funds for expansion of National Service Scheme (NSS)

3.3       The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to take interest in the development of sports among the
Indian women who have brought laurels to the country in the past and have shown good potential for sports like athletics,
