together for finding out ways to enable such students for participating in NSS activities.
 
6.10     The Committee also feels that regular monitoring mechanism for NSS activities at different levels is not there. 
The Ministry depends on reports and review from the Regional Directors of NSS who get reports from State Liaison
Officers - employees of the States.  Such a channel, the Committee feels, may not be  free from biases etc. in reporting
the feedback about impact and outreach of the programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a more
independent/dependable mechanism should be provided for this purpose.
 
6.11     The 15 training and 4 research centres fully supported by the Union Ministry are there to provide training to all
the NSS functionaries.  When the Committee expressed its own doubt about the impact of training, the Ministry replied: 
"they have been in existence for a long time but they have not been effective".  The Committee feels that number of
training and research centres are inadequate for the entire country. Even the existing training and research centers are not
functioning properly.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training aspect of this scheme must be
strengthened and their number also must be increased and to ensure that there is no gap in providing training to NSS
functionaries.
 
6.12     Evaluation of this scheme was got done by the Ministry with the help of the IIPA.  The Committee would like to
know the steps proposed to be initiated in the light of the findings of the IIPA report.
 
6.13     To a query about the major constraints faced while implementing the NSS scheme, the Committee was informed
that (i) some States/UTs delay the settlement of account resulting in holding of further releases of grants and (ii) State
Liaison Cells which are fully funded by the Ministry are not functioning in some of the States/UTs.  The Committee is,
no doubt, aware of this perennial problem of undue delay in settlement of accounts by the States in implementing Central
sector schemes.  It is the main bottleneck in implementing them.  It further feels that this problem is projected more often
than not as insurmountable.  Similarly, the problem of State Liaison Cell not functioning in some States and UTs also
falls in the same category.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry should take up these two problems with the
concerned States at the highest level with a view to sort out the same and report the action taken in this regard to the
Committee.
 
VII.     NATIONAL DISCIPLINE SCHEME (NDS)
7.1       The National Discipline Scheme was decentralised in 1972 and the employees under the NDS were transferred
and absorbed in the services of the State Governments on the condition that the Central Government would reimburse
their pay and allowances so long as they remained in the service.   Accordingly, about 6145 NDS Instructors were
transferred / absorbed to/ under  various State Governments. The Committee observes that due to inadequate budgetary
provisions, the Central Government has never been able to bear the liability to full extent which, over the years, has
continued to grow upto about Rs.300 crores.  On a specific query about any assessment about the period till when this

provision is required to be made, the Committee was informed that a   reference was made to all concerned State
Governments to furnish requisite information.  However, except Rajasthan, Gujarat, M.P. and Punjab, requisite
documents from other States are awaited.  The case of Rajasthan has also been referred back for revised documents. The
Committee was given to understand that only on receipt of these documents from the State Governments, it will be
possible for the Ministry to make an assessment of the total amount, which is to be paid by the Government of India to
the various State Governments.
 
7.2       The Committee notes that against a non-plan  allocation of Rs. 5 crores in  2004-05, expenditure incurred upto
28
th Feb., 2005 is Rs.3.90 crores.  During 2002-03 and 2003-04, an expenditure of Rs. 3.50 crore and Rs. 3.00 crores has
been made respectively.  A budget provision of only Rs.1 crore has been made for 2005-06.  Obviously, the Ministry
would not be in a position to meet even the annual liability under the Scheme, not to speak of the accumulated liability.
 
7.3       The Committee observes that more than 30 years have passed since the transfer of the Scheme to the States in
1972.   Central Govt. has been simply releasing funds to various State Govts. without having any idea about the annual
as well as the accumulated liability to be paid to States.   This is indeed a very strange situation.  The Committee
wonders about the status of 6145 NDS Instructors whose services were transferred in 1972.   At that point of time also,
many of them must have already rendered some service.   After passage of more than 30 years, quite a few of them must
have crossed the retirement age by now and some of them might have joined some other profession. 
 
7.4       It appears very surprising to the Committee that the Ministry has not made a serious attempt even to assess the
exact amount of liability (State-wise) so far. The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for ascertaining
the number of such Instructors, State-wise.  The Committee is of the considered view that a complete assessment about

VIII.    RASHTRIYA SADBHAVNA YOJNA
8.1       The new Scheme named Rashtriya Sadbhavna Yojna was approved in February, 2005 to provide a platform for
youth to develop a spirit of voluntarism, leadership and sensitivity towards community needs and development. Under
the scheme, 10-20 volunteers in each of 500 districts would be enrolled as volunteers and a period of one year at a
monthly honorarium of Rs.1000/-. Each of the best selected registered Youth Club /Rural Sports Club /Mahila Mandal in
a block and the Youth development Centre and Rural Information Technology Youth Development Centre (RITYDC) in
a district will select from amongst its members (with minimum matriculate educational qualification) volunteer to
represent it.
 
8.2       The Committee was informed that the volunteers named as 'Nehru Yuva Sathee' will act as a link between the
youth, community and government and non-government programmes for development and empowerment of youth. The
Committee notes that this Scheme has been designed to inspire competitiveness among Youth Clubs for participative
selection of leaders and is aimed at empowering youth and developing leadership qualities in them as a sustainable
solution. A format for conducting competitions among the participating registered youth Clubs and Youth Development
Centre has been finalised and circulated.
 
8.3   The Committee finds the idea behind the scheme laudable.  The Nehru Yuva Sathees, the Committee hopes, would
act as catalysts of change and would help in empowering Youth across the country. The Committee underlines the need
for proper training to mobilize youth and in motivating them to participate in programmes for youth and community
development. A proper monitoring mechanism, the Committee feels, would be required to be put in place to ensure
effective implementation of the scheme.  Transparency in selection of the Yuva Sathees must also be ensured.  The main
criteria for selection may be the social commitment of the candidates.  The Committee expresses its doubt about the
efficacy of 10-20 Sathees in a district as well as adequacy of Rs. 1000/- per month honorarium for them. 
 
8.4   The Committee notes that this scheme has taken the place of erstwhile National Reconstruction Corps Scheme,
which continued upto March, 2003.   It has taken two years in formulation of the revised scheme.   The Committee hopes
that this scheme would not suffer from the shortcomings experienced in the implementation of the earlier scheme.

finds that during the Ninth Plan, a token provision of 4 lakh was kept for this Council. This token provision has been

IV.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS
 
The Committee feels that the Ministry's projection for the annual plan, 2005-06 was quite justified because it
constituted only 10% increase over the previous year’s allocations and also because the Ministry has to fulfill its
obligation for the preparations of the Commonwealth Games, 2010 and expansion of NSS upto the school level.  There
appears to be no justification in applying cut to its allocations, particularly when the Ministry was
able to spend more than 66.72% of its allocation upto December, 2004, as per the existing norms in
this regard.  (Para 4.1)
 
The Committee considers it disappointingly low in view of the mandate of the Ministry being to develop the
personality of our youth as also involving them in nation-building activities.  This group, which constitutes nearly 40 per
cent of total population of India, is the most vibrant and potent segment of our society.  Allocation below one per cent to
youth development and sports reflects a low preference.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that there is a
strong case for adequate allocation for the Ministry in the coming years.  Department's demand for a share in the funds
collected through education cess must be considered favourably, particularly for expansion of NSS upto 9 th class and
also in all the remaining schools. (Para 4.2)
 
Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the disturbing trend of under-utilisation of funds meant for NE
States both under the Youth and Sports Programmes during the Tenth Plan period so far.   The Committee is also
disturbed by the status of scheme of ‘Promotion of Sports Among Disabled.’   Not even single rupee could be spent
under this scheme against the Ninth Plan allocation of  Rs. 15 lakhs .  Position remains unchanged during the Tenth Plan
also so far.   This Scheme has been continuing on paper only.  Performance Budget of the Department for 2005-06
indicates that the Scheme is now being merged with the Scheme relating to Events.   The Committee does not appreciate
the way scheme  ‘Promotion of Sports among Disabled’, which is meant to serve the under-privileged class of society, is
being handled.  It needs to be strengthened. (Para 4.3)
 
            Even during the Ninth Plan, funds remained underutilised in different categories.  For example, of the total Ninth
Plan outlay of Rs. 352.24 crores for Youth Welfare, only Rs. 336.94 crores could be spent.  The schemes suffering most
were:  National Reconstruction Corps, Youth Hostels and Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Youth Development.  Similarly,
spending Rs. 558.50 crores in Ninth Plan period against an outlay of Rs. 472.61 under Sports and Physical Education
also indicates towards fiscal (mal)practices such as unspent balances or re-appropriation etc.  The Committee is of the
view that these situations - under-utilization as well as unspent balances - indicate that both our delivery mechanism as
well as system of flow of funds are not foolproof and need to be streamlined further.  It reflects a poor physical
performance because it is directly related to the financial performance. (Para 4.4)
 
            While appreciating the formulation of quarterly Action Plans during Tenth Plan by the Ministry, the Committee
feels that it has not been able to achieve the desired results. The Committee would like to emphasize the need for the
judicious and optimum utilisation of funds by the Ministry allocated for various schemes by the Ministry. (Para 4.5)
 
            The Committee is of the view that a detailed review of the schemes showing poor performance should be
undertaken so as to identify the shortcomings and initiate remedial measures. The Ministry should involve the Planning
Commission, the State Governments and other implementing agencies in this exercise. (Para 4.6)
 
            The Committee is aware of the structural problems inherent in our system from Union level down to the
Panchayats in implementing the central sector as well as centrally-sponsored schemes.  Ours being basically a
cooperative federation, States have got to play a more pro-active and coordinated role in this exercise for obtaining the
desired impact of the schemes at the ground level. (Para 4.7)

            The Committee is happy to note that the physical and financial performance of the NSS during 2002-03, 2003-04

universities/colleges /schools are yet to be covered by NSS. (Para 6.4)
 
            The Committee notes that there is a large gap between the existing universities, colleges, etc. and those in which
NSS units have been provided.  For example, 79 universities, 9683 colleges, 33,210 schools and 2031 technical
institutions are yet to be provided with NSS units.  In States like Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand, scheme seems to
have been implemented half-heartedly.       The Committee further notes that States like Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura
were also not performing well, whereas other States like Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra  and Kerala are doing exceedingly
well. The Committee would like to describe the implementation of this scheme as lop-sided.  In such a scenario, the
Committee feels that  it would be difficult to achieve the goal of providing NSS to all the universities, colleges and other
educational institutions in the country, let alone expanding it to all the secondary schools as well.  (Para 6.5)
 
            The NSS has played a good role in the field of mass literacy, environment protection, health education,
community development, drive against social evils, etc.  The Committee wishes to place on record its appreciation for
the NSS volunteers who have always come into the forefront to extend voluntary services particularly in natural
calamities like drought, flood, cyclone, earthquake and Tsunami tragedy.  It is heartening to note that more than 6,000
NSS volunteers of 110 institutions from 10 universities were deployed in 16 districts and 2 UTs of Andaman and
Nicobar Islands affected by Tsunami for carrying out relief and rehabilitation activities. (Para 6.6)
 
The Committee would also like the Ministry to review system of release of funds for implementing the NSS
scheme. It would be appropriate if the institutions get the 1
st instalment of the amount by the month of May for the
implementation of the scheme without delay. (Para 6.7)
 
In view of the significance and popularity of the NSS, which is basically meant for preparing our students for
self-development as well as community development, the Committee strongly recommends to provide adequate funds at
appropriate stage for expanding/strengthening this scheme so that it covers the remaining educational institutions as well
as expanding it upto 9th class. (Para 6.8)
 
The Committee believes that a large number of students at senior secondary level do not join NSS in view of the
huge curricular load including that of competitive exams that they are forced to take up at 10+2 stage.  This trend is
increasing day-by-day, as a result, a large number of such students are not able to join NSS.  The Committee, therefore,
feels that Ministry, CBSE, NCERT and the Department of Secondary and Higher Education should put their head
together for finding out ways to enable such students for participating in NSS activities. (Para 6.9)
 
            The Committee also feels that regular monitoring mechanism for NSS activities at different levels is not there. 
The Ministry depends on reports and review from the Regional Directors of NSS who get reports from State Liaison
Officers - employees of the States.  Such a channel, the Committee feels, may not be  free from biases etc. in reporting
the feedback about impact and outreach of the programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a more
independent/dependable mechanism should be provided for this purpose. (Para 6.10)

             Evaluation of this scheme was got done by the Ministry with the help of the IIPA.  The Committee would like to
know the steps proposed to be initiated in the light of the findings of the IIPA report. (Para 6.12)
 
The Committee is, no doubt, aware of this perennial problem of undue delay in settlement of accounts by the
States in implementing Central sector schemes.  It is the main bottleneck in implementing them.  It further feels that this
problem is projected more often than not as insurmountable.  Similarly, the problem of State Liaison Cell not functioning
in some States and UTs also falls in the same category.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry should take up
these two problems with the concerned States at the highest level with a view to sort out the same and report the action
taken in this regard to the Committee. (Para 6.13)
 
VII.     NATIONAL DISCIPLINE SCHEME (NDS)
The Committee observes that due to inadequate budgetary provisions, the Central Government has never been
able to bear the liability to full extent which, over the years, has continued to grow upto about Rs.300 crores.   (Para 7.1)
 
Obviously, the Ministry would not be in a position to meet even the annual liability under the Scheme, not to
speak of the accumulated liability. (Para 7.2)
 
            The Committee observes that more than 30 years have passed since the transfer of the Scheme to the States in
1972.   Central Govt. has been simply releasing funds to various State Govts. without having any idea about the annual
as well as the accumulated liability to be paid to States.   This is indeed a very strange situation.  The Committee
wonders about the status of 6145 NDS Instructors whose services were transferred in 1972.   At that point of time also,
many of them must have already rendered some service.   After passage of more than 30 years, quite a few of them must
have crossed the retirement age by now and some of them might have joined some other profession.  (Para 7.3)
 
            It appears very surprising to the Committee that the Ministry has not made a serious attempt even to assess the
exact amount of liability (State-wise) so far. The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for ascertaining
the number of such Instructors, State-wise.  The Committee is of the considered view that a complete assessment about
the status of NDS Instructors may be made without any further delay to settle their cases.   The Committee would like to
be apprised about the same. (Para 7.4)
 
VIII.    RASHTRIYA SADBHAVNA YOJNA
 
The Committee finds the idea behind the scheme laudable.  The Nehru Yuva Sathees, the Committee hopes,
would act as catalysts of change and would help in empowering Youth across the country. The Committee underlines the
need for proper training to mobilize youth and in motivating them to participate in programmes for youth and
community development. A proper monitoring mechanism, the Committee feels, would be required to be put in place to
ensure effective implementation of the scheme.  Transparency in selection of the Yuva Sathees must also be ensured. 
The main criteria for selection may be the social commitment of the candidates.  The Committee expresses its doubt
about the efficacy of 10-20 Sathees in a district as well as adequacy of Rs. 1000/- per month honorarium for them.  (Para
8.3)
 
The Committee notes that this scheme has taken the place of erstwhile National Reconstruction Corps Scheme,
which continued upto March, 2003.   It has taken two years in formulation of the revised scheme.   The Committee hopes
that this scheme would not suffer from the shortcomings experienced in the implementation of the earlier scheme. (Para
8.4)
 
IX.       
SCHEME OF PROMOTION OF NATIONAL INTEGRATION

targets must be fixed every year for holding camps and exchange programme etc. (Para 9.4)
 
The Committee recommends that the institutions assigned the job of the assessment should be asked to adhere to
a time frame in submitting their reports.  The Committee would also like to be apprised of the outcome of the assessment

X.        YOUTH HOSTELS
 
            The Committee was informed that there are 65 hostels and 25 others were under different stages of construction. 
The Committee is dismayed that approval for construction of most of these Youth Hostels dates back to 1986 to 1994. 
These are still not complete even after two decades.  Against an approved outlay of Rs. 22.99 crores for their
construction, Rs. 8.41 crores has been released so far to various State Governments. In most of the cases, just one to two
instalments have been released to State Governments. There are also cases where land is yet to be allotted.  The reason
given for this state of affairs were: (i) non handing-over of the fully developed piece of land by the State Government to
the construction agencies; and (ii) non-submission of preliminary estimates and drawings by the State Governments for
approval. (Para 10.4)
 
            The Committee is astonished to see the fate of this scheme.  Delays of twenty to twenty five years in getting the
Hostels constructed is simply unbelievable.   The Committee is not satisfied by the explanation given by the Ministry
that in case the required details in respect of hostels are not received within the specified period, the approval of yet to be
started hostels will be cancelled and the grant already released will be recovered.  The Committee feels that this
proposed line of action is too late.   It appears to the Committee that Ministry has left everything to the States.  It shows
lack of regular monitoring of this scheme resulting in such a huge backlog.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
this matter be taken up at the level of Minister/Chief Secretaries for expediting the construction of Hostels.  The
Committee would like to be apprised of the actions taken in this regard within three months. (Para 10.5)
 
XI.       FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO RURAL YOUTH CLUBS / SPORTS CLUBS
 
The Committee notes that allocation for this scheme has been nearly doubled in 2005-06 and hopes that entire
amount would be utilised for achieving targets of setting up 500 each YDCs  and RITYDCs. The Committee
recommends that the proposed RITYCDS and YDCs should be proportionately distributed so as to cover all the regions
of the country. (Para 11.3)
 
XII.     PROMOTION OF YOUTH ACTIVITIES AND TRAINING
 
            The Committee notes that vocational training is one of the components of the scheme.  In view of the number of
youth being unemployed due to diminishing job opportunities, it is advisable that more and more vocational training
programmes aimed towards gainful employment be designed.   These training programmes would go a long way in
channelising the hidden potential and energies of the youth towards constructive work.  And at the same time, it would
also prevent migration of rural youth to cities where they are forced to live a sub-human life apart from falling victims of
anti-social elements. (Para 12.3)
 
            The Committee observes that against an allocation of Rs. 17.84 crores under the Scheme during the Ninth Plan,
utilisation figures amounted to Rs. 21.68 crores.   During the first three years of Tenth Plan also, there has been optimum
utilisation of allocated funds which has already reached the utilisation level of Ninth Plan.   The Committee also notes

XIII.    NEW INITIATIVES FOR ADOLESCENT YOUTH
 
            The Committee appreciates the move of the Ministry for setting up a Special Cell for Adolescent Youth and the
project titled support to Adolescent Health and Development (2004-07) as part of UNFPA's Sixth Country Programme.
The Committee notes that 82 District Counselling and career guidance centres have been sanctioned under the scheme,
which is targeted towards adolescents. A number of projects amounting to Rs. 7.00 crores have been sanctioned during
the year 2004-05. The list provided by the Ministry indicates that all the States are not covered under the scheme and the
distribution is also not even region-wise. The Committee understands that the responsibility for monitoring has to be
shouldered again by District Collectors. The Committee opines that the DC would not be able to spare much time to
oversee the working of the agencies as he is already overburdened with tremendous responsibilities.  The Committee,
therefore, recommends that some other officer like District Education Officer or District Youth Officer may monitor this

The Committee is apprehensive whether all precautions had been taken while sanctioning a large number of
projects in such a short period.  The poor utilization of funds in previous years reflects the lack of priority for this
scheme. (Para 13.3)
 
XIV     ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL AND STATE YOUTH CENTRES
 
The Committee observes that during 2005-06, which is the fourth year of the Tenth Plan, a token provision of Rs.
1 lakh has been made.   This clearly indicates that this scheme will continue to be in the formulation stage by the end of
Tenth Plan period.  The committee reiterates that prior to launching of any new scheme, all procedural formalities should
be completed. (Para 14.1)
 
XV     OVERLAPPING OF SCHEMES
            The Committee observes that the Scheme of Financial Assistance for  Promotion of Youth Activities and
Training has three components-Vocational Training, Entrepreneurship Development  and Exhibition.   Under the
Vocational Training component, vocational training is provided to rural youth to prevent their migration to cities.   The
Committee finds that one of the regular programmes run by NYKS is also Vocational Training.   Rs. 30,000 per Kendra
is earmarked every year for this activity.   Similarly, under the scheme of Financial Assistance to Rural Youth
Clubs/Sports Clubs, financial assistance is provided to Youth Clubs, @ Rs. 10,000/- per Youth Club for normal areas
and Rs. 15000/- per Youth Club for tribal areas.   NYKS also provides assistance of Rs. 7810/- per Youth Club

Scheme of Establishment of National/State Youth Centres provides a platform to the youth for organizing

            The Committee observes that there is a need for review of components of all the Youth related schemes to ensure
that element of overlapping between two schemes  is eliminated.   A composite scheme administered by designated
authorities will lead  to better results.    The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may initiate this
exercise at the earliest. (Para 15.2)
 
XVI     NON GOVERNMENT ORGANISATIONS
 
            The Committee finds the amounts given to the NGOs under different schemes mind-boggling, for which
utilization certificates are pending from 2001-02 onwards.  The Committee is more concerned about the fact that the

submit necessary papers and report is received from the office of the District Collector.  The Ministry should ensure that
good NGOs should not be harassed and money should come to them smoothly so that work does not suffer. (Para 16.4)
            The procedure of applying to get grants by the NGOs appears to be quite complicated.  As a result, lot of persons
work as facilitators who do all the procedure for some money.  In the process some of the NGOs coming from rural and
remote areas get fleeced by middlemen.   This problem, the Committee feels, may be overcome by making the entire

an element of accountability at every level – Centre/State/district to ensure proper and effective implementation of
various schemes. The Committee, therefore, recommends to devise a fool-proof mechanism for selection as well as
monitoring of activities of the NGOs. Efforts should also be made to avoid concentration of many NGOs in one
particular district in view of an equitable distribution of benefits of this scheme. (Para 16.6)

XVIII   COMMONWEALTH GAMES, 2010
 
            The Committee hopes that the report of Task Force would be submitted in time so that the action in this regard is
initiated timely. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should be provided adequate fund at RE stage so that the
works pertaining to Commonwealth Games, 2010 were not delayed. A plan should be chalked for phase-wise
development of the infrastructure and the money be spent judiciously. The Committee feels that efforts should be made
to build proper infrastructure in time-bound manner with a view to avoiding last minute pressure of work.
While creating infrastructure for the Commonwealth Games, we should not ignore preparation/training of our
sportspersons. This should be treated as an opportunity to enhance our nation's prestige by winning more and more
medals. Selection and training of prospective participants must take place now so that they get enough time to prepare
themselves. (Para 18.3)
 
            The Committee feels that hosting 2010 Commonwealth Games is a privilege accompanied with a lot of
responsibility.  It is understood that more than 600 crores of rupees would be required to set up Commonwealth
Games Village.  Funding would, therefore, be totally based on a well-planned need based approach. An amount as
big as Rs. 600 crores of rupees approximately can leave huge deficit after the Games are over.  The Committee
feels that the Government should have a way out for utilizing the facilities and infrastructure after the Games are
over, so that the project would not block Government money from other pressing matters.  We have, therefore, to
remain highly alert in the use of infrastructure after the games.  The Committee hopes that the planners would
seriously study the funding pattern in the light of the experiences gained from other countries who have hosted
such games in the past. (Para 18.4)
 
            The Committee notes that India’s performance in international sports is not at all commensurate with the size of
our country as well as the population. The Committee wants to cite the example of People's Republic of China in this
regard.  If China can do, there is no reason why India cannot.  (Para 18.5)
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that unless all those responsible for promoting sports, particularly, the Ministry,
the SAI, the State Governments, Sports Federations/Associations take it up as a challenge and work in tandem with each
other, a visible impact cannot be made.  The present tendency of shifting responsibility on one another has to be
stopped.  We should have to work in a time-bound manner with the dynamic categorization of sports disciplines,
transparent selection procedure, country-wide talent hunting, modern training facilities, etc.  The Committee in this
regard would like to mention about “Operation Gold” Scheme launched by the Kerala Sports Council in which district
panchayats have been involved in talent search from the local level.  The Committee feels that this scheme can be
applied at the national level also.  (Para 18.6)

            The Committee observes that during the Ninth Plan these five schemes were operating independently.  During
the first two years of Tenth Plan also these schemes continued their independent status.  Performance of two schemes,
Sports Scholarship Scheme and Pension to Meritorious Sportspersons seemed to be satisfactory as there was optimum
utilization of funds allocated therefor.  However, position was different in respect of the other three schemes, namely
Rural Sports Programme, National Sports Development Fund and Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools.  Funds
provided for these Schemes remained unutilized/under utilized. The Committee is constrained to note that convergences

scheme is one of the main schemes of the Ministry encompassing important components in it such as Promoting Rural
Sports, Sports and Games in schools as well as providing Sports Scholarships, Pension for Meritorious Sportspersons
and Sports Development Fund.  The performance of this scheme as a whole does not inspire enough confidence.  The

SPORTS AMONG DISABLED
The Committee expresses its displeasure at the manner in which the scheme meant for disabled persons was
being handled.  It reflects our insensitivity towards them who need special support and motivation to enable them to join
the mainstream.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that this scheme should be finalised for implementation from

XXI.    INFRASTRUCTURE SCHEMES
 
            The Committee notes that four schemes relating to creation of sports infrastructure have been transferred to the
State/UTs governments since 1
st  April, 2005.  This, according to the Committee, amounts to virtually abandoning all
these schemes.  Due to financial constraints, currently the States/UTs governments are not in a position to provide their
share towards the cost of projects already approved. As a result, 508 projects were lying pending for completion
involving financial liability of around Rs. 160 crores on the Central Government.  Keeping in mind the financial
constraints of the States, the Committee is of the firm opinion that it will not be possible for the States to fully fund the
sports infrastructure projects.  The Committee fails to understand how this financial liability will be taken care of.  (Para
21.3)
 
            Our country suffers from massive lack of infrastructure facilities for sports, which needs to be taken up
seriously.  This activity being highly cost intensive, the Committee is sure, it will be difficult for the States to undertake
this work. Adequate infrastructure at the ground level is a must for broad-basing the sports as well as achieving
excellence.  The scheme of providing infrastructure in rural schools, which is a part of NCMP of the Government, would
also remain on papers only.  The Committee was informed that the Department has also taken up the issue with the
Ministry of Finance as well as Planning Commission but with no avail.  In view of above, the Committee calls upon the
Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance to review the decision of transferring infrastructure schemes to the
States and allow these to be retained with the Ministry only. (Para 21.4)

REPORT
           
The Manipur University Bill 2005 seeks to convert the existing Manipur University into a Central University with
a view to ensure its accelerated development and minimize the imbalance in educational facilities in the North Eastern
Region.
 
2.         The Manipur University was established at Imphal in June 1980, under the Manipur University Act, 1980 enacted
by the Manipur Legislative Assembly.  Prior to the establishment of this University, the Centre of Post Graduate Studies
of the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), established at Imphal in the year 1972, was catering to the educational needs
of the students of Manipur at the postgraduate level and the undergraduate colleges, including some professional
colleges, in the State were affiliated to Guwahati University.
 
3.         The Committee was informed that with the coming into force of the Manipur University Act, 1980, Guwahati
University ceased to exercise jurisdiction in the State of Manipur and the erstwhile Centre of Post Graduate Studies of
JNU was merged with the newly established Manipur University.
 
4.         The Committee was further informed that the Manipur University has at present 23 post-graduate teaching
departments under three Schools of Studies.  It also has 73 affiliated colleges including a medical college, three law
colleges, six teacher-training colleges, three technical/engineering colleges and a college of physical education and
sports.  The number of students presently enrolled in the teaching departments and affiliated colleges of the University is
about 2,000 and 30,000 respectively.
 
5.         According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, as the Manipur University started without any
foundation grant and could not get adequate plan assistance from the Government in the succeeding years, it has not been
in a position to create the required infrastructure and to diversify its courses  to the  extent required  so far.  It is
surrounded by central universities of the North-Eastern Region at Kohima, Silchar, Tezpur, Aizawl and Shillong.  This
has caused a huge imbalance in educational facilities within the region, and a consequent migration of teachers, students
and researchers in search of better infrastructural and academic facilities in other states.  Not only this, many years of
insurgency in different parts of the State resulted in the exodus of a large number of students from the State to places like
Delhi.

164threport of committee on HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/164threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:36]
 
6.         Against this backdrop and the fact that the State Government, with its limited resources, was not in a position to
provide adequate funding for the development of the Manipur University, there had been a persistent demand for making
it as a central university.  Besides repeated requests from the State Government, the Manipur Legislative Assembly had
also passed unanimous resolutions to this effect on the 9th July, 1999 and more recently on the 13th March, 2003.
 
7.         Accordingly, the Manipur University Bill 2005, has been introduced in the Rajya Sabha for the establishment and
incorporation of Manipur University as a central university and for repealing of the existing Manipur University Act,
1980, enacted by the Manipur Legislative Assembly.  The Bill is broadly based on the pattern of the University of
Mizoram, the most recent of the North-Eastern Universities.
 
8.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:
(i)                  The Bill seeks to establish and incorporate the existing Manipur University, a state university of
Manipur, under the proposed Central Act by the same name of 'Manipur University' with perpetual
succession and common seal, and to provide for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
 
(ii)                The University would be a teaching and affiliating university with its Headquarters at Imphal and
territorial jurisdiction extending to the whole of the State of Manipur.
(iii)               It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities, particularly of those of
the North-Eastern region.
(iv)              All colleges, Institutions, Schools and Departments affiliated to, or admitted to the privileges of, or
maintained by, the existing Manipur University shall stand affiliated to, or admitted to the privilege of, or
maintained by, the University.
(v)                The existing Institute of Technology, Imphal shall also be maintained by the University.
(vi)              The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of
India and shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament along with the audit report and the annual report
of the University.
(vii)             During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers and the constitution of the first
Authorities of the University would be made by the Visitor for specified terms.
 
9.         The Committee, heard the Secretary, Department of Secondary and Higher Education and took up clause-by-
clause consideration of the Bill.   It suggested the following amendments additions to various clauses of the Bill.
 
Clause 2 (m)
 
10.       The Committee notes that the definitions for `college' and `institution' provided in 2(e) and 2(m) leave some
scope for confusion, particularly in view of different categories of colleges existing/likely to exist under the Manipur
University.   For example, `constituent colleges' and 'affiliated colleges' have not been defined.   The Bill, Committee
finds, does not provide explicitly for converting an affiliated college into a constituent college. Such a demand in future,
in fact, cannot be ruled out, if a college or an institution feels that it has required standards/facilities for the purpose. 
The Committee, therefore, is of the view that there is need to amplify the definitions of the terms `constituent college',
``affiliated college' and 'institution' with a view to removing possible ambiguities in these regards.   The Committee,
therefore, recommends that necessary amendments should be brought in the relevant provision of the Bill for this
purpose. 
 
Clause 9(3)
 
11.1     Clause 9(3), page 5, provided that the Visitor shall have the right to cause an inspection to be made, by such
person or persons as he may direct, of the University, its buildings, laboratories and equipment, and of any college or
institution maintained by the University or admitted to its privileges; and also of the examinations, teaching and other
work conducted or done by the University and to cause an inquiry to be made in like manner in respect of any matter
connected with the administration or finances of the University, and the said Colleges and Institutions.

11.2     The Committee feels that libraries are important and integral constituents of the University system and need to
be included in the above provision for inspection.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause 9(3) in line 33
after the word "buildings," the word 'libraries' should also be added.
 
New clause for providing Chief Rector
 
12.1     The Committee is of the view that Governors should have a role in those Central Universities which are located in
border States like Manipur. The Governor being an important link between the Centre and the State, may also be made a
part of the University, even though it is mere ceremonial.
 
12.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the following clause be added in the Bill after clause 9 and the entire
clauses from 10 to 46 may be renumbered accordingly:-
 
            "10.  The Governor of the State of Manipur shall be the Chief Rector of the University".
 
12.3     All the consequential changes may also be carried out in the Bill.
 
Clause 10
 
13.1     Clause 10, page 6, provides that the following shall be the officers of the University:-
(1)               the Chancellor;
(2)               the Vice-Chancellor;
(3)               the Pro-Vice Chancellor;
(4)               the Deans of Schools;
(5)               the Registrar;
(6)               the Finance Officer;
(7)               the Librarian and
(8)               such other officers as may be declared by the Statutes to be officers of the University.
 
13.2     The Committee feels that holding of examinations and awarding degrees is one of the most important functions of
a university.  If Librarian can be made as an officer, the Controller of Examinations, being an equally important
functionary of any university, should also be included as one of the officers of the university in the Act itself.  Moreover,
the post of 'Controller of Examinations' has already been provided in the existing Manipur University Act 1980, passed
by the State Legislature.
 
13.3     The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Controller of Examinations may be added as an Officer of the
University in Clause 10 of the Bill at Page 6.
 
Clause 12(3)
 
14.1     Clause 12(3), page 7, provides that the Vice-Chancellor may, if he is of the opinion that immediate action is
necessary on any matter, exercise any power conferred on any authority of the University by or under this Act and shall
report to such authority the action taken by him on such matter.
 
14.2     The Committee while accepting the rationale behind providing emergency powers to the Vice-Chancellor to deal
with urgent matters, feels that the Vice-Chancellor should be required to report such actions taken by him to the
appropriate authorities at the earliest available opportunity.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in Clause 12(3),
in line 8, the words 'at its next meeting' should be added after the word 'authority'.
 
14.3     The second proviso to clause 2(3) provides for making an 'appeal' by a person aggrieved by the emergent actions
of the VC to the EC.   The Committee feels the word 'appeal' may have different legal connotations leading sometimes to
avoidable situations.   The Committee, therefore, recommends substituting the word 'appeal' with 'representation' in line
12 of the second proviso to clause 12(3).

Clause 20 (1)
 
15.1     Clause 20 (1) provides that the constitution of the Court and the term of office of its members shall be prescribed
by the Statutes.      The Committee, however, notes that the Statutes appended to the Bill do not provide for the
constitution of the Court as well as the term of office of its members.
 
15.2     The Committee feels that the Court being the apex body of the university, provision for its constitution and term
of office of its members be provided in the first statutes itself.
           
Clauses 21(2), 22(2) and 23(2)
 
16.1     Clause 21(2) provides that the constitution of the Executive Council, the term of office of its members and its
powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
 
16.2     Clause 22(2) provides that the constitution of the Academic Council, the term of office of its members and its
powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
 
16.3     Clause 23(2) provides that the constitution of the College Development Council, the term of office of its members
and its powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
 
16.4     The Committee notes that the Executive Council, Academic Council and College Development Council are the
important decision-making bodies of the University.  The Statutes appended to the Bill contain provisions only about the
powers and functions of these bodies but are silent about their constitution and term of office.
 
16.5     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the provisions for the constitution and term of office of the
Executive Council, Academic Council and the College Development Council, also be included within corpus of the first
Statutes itself

SCHEDULE
 
Clause 5(1) & (2) of the Statutes
 
17.1     Clause 5(1) of the Statutes provides for the appointment of Dean of a School by the Vice-Chancellor from
amongst the professors of the school for a period of three years, who shall be eligible for re-appointment.  The
Committee finds that the Statutes is silent about any criteria for selecting the professors for appointment as Dean.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the seniority as well as rotation should be included as criteria for this purpose.
           
17.2     The first proviso to clause 5 (1) of the Statutes provides that a Dean would cease to hold office at the age of 60.  
The Committee notes that the retirement age of Professors is sixty-two.  It feels that the Deans being professors, should
also retire at the age of sixty-two.
 
17.3     Clause 5(2) of the Statutes authorises the Vice-Chancellor to appoint "any person" as the Dean when the office of
the Dean is vacant or is unable to perform duties.  The Committee notes that this is a blanket power given to the Vice-
Chancellor and it should be limited only to the senior most Professors.
 
17.4     In view of the above, the Committee recommends that clause 5(1) of the statutes, its two provisos and clause 5(2)
may be deleted and the following may be substituted.
 
5(1) Every Dean of school shall be appointed by the Vice-Chancellor from amongst the Professors in the School
by rotation in the order of seniority for a period of three years;
 
Provided that in case there is only one Professor or no Professor in a School, the Dean shall be appointed, for the
time being, from amongst the Professors, if any, and the Readers in the School by rotation in the order of seniority;

Provided that a Dean on attaining the age of sixty-two years shall cease to hold office as such;
 
5(2) When the office of the Dean is vacant or when the Dean is, by reason of illness, absence or any other cause,
unable to perform duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by the senior-most Professor or Reader,
as the case may be in the School.
 
Clause 6(3) of the Statutes
 
18.1     First Proviso to Clause 6(3) at page 17, of the Statutes provides that the Registrar shall retire on attaining the age
of sixty years.
           
18.2     The Committee learnt that retirement age of Registrar in other Central Universities was 62 years.  Sometimes, a
senior Professor might also be appointed as Registrar of the University, who would retire at the age of 62 years.  It might,
the Committee feels, put them at disadvantage.  The Committee, therefore, is of the view that the retirement age of the
Registrar should be made sixty-two.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that in Proviso to clause 6(3) line 44 of
the Statutes, the words 'sixty years' should be substituted by 'sixty-two years'.  Consequently, the 'sixty years' in the
succeeding proviso should also be made as sixty-two years.
 
Clause 6(6) of the Statutes
 
19.       Clause 6(6) provides that the Registrar shall be ex officio  Secretary to the Executive Council, the Academic
Council and the College Development Council, but shall not be deemed to be a member of any of these authorities.  The
Committee has learnt that in the existing administrative set up of the Manipur University under the State Act, there is a
Director of the College Development Council. The Committee, feels that it would be convenient as well as appropriate if
he functions as the ex-officio Secretary to the College Development Council and not the Registrar as proposed by the new
Bill.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words "and the College Development Council" at page 18, line 20
may be deleted from clause (6)(6).
 
Clause 9(5) of the Statutes
 
20.1     Clause 9(5) of the Statute prescribes that twelve members would constitute quorum for a meeting of the Court.
 
20.2     The Committee notes that generally the quorums are in odd number, otherwise it might lead to deadlock in
decision-making by the Court.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in line 12 of page 20 (statute 9(5)), the word 
'twelve' may be substituted by 'eleven' or thirteen as the case may be.
 
Clause 16(1) of the Statutes
 
21.1     Clause 16(1) of the Statutes prescribes that the College  of Technology , Imphal shall be maintained by the
University.
 
21.2     The Committee has learnt that the name of the College of Technology, Imphal has been changed to the Manipur
Institute of Technology.  The Committee, recommends that the name of the Institution should accordingly be corrected in
the clause.
           
Clause 19(1) of the Statutes
 
22.1     Clause 19(1) of the statutes at page 24, provides that notwithstanding anything contained in Statute 18, the
Executive Council may invite a person of high academic distinction and professional attainments to accept a post of
Professor or Reader or any other academic post in the University, as the case may be, on such terms and conditions as it
deems fit and on the person agreeing to do so, appoint him to the post.
 
22.2     The Committee notes that this sub clause empowers the university to appoint persons of eminence in the

be restricted only to the level of professors or equivalent posts.  The Committee, accordingly,  recommends  that  in  line 
43 of  Clause 19(1) of the statutes, the
words 'or Reader' may be deleted and the word 'equivalent' may be added after the word 'other'.  Also the words 'as the

Clause 35(1) (ii) of the Statutes
 
23.       In Clause 35(1)(ii) of the statutes the word 'undercharged' is a typing mistake and it should be substituted by the
word 'undischarged'.
 
Miscellaneous
Students Council
 
24.       The Committee notes that the Mizoram University Act provides for constitution of a Students Council, whereas
Manipur University Bill is silent about it.  The Committee is of the view that to accommodate the views of the student
community in academic as well as welfare matters, Students Council can be formed with suitable powers of
consultation.  The selection of students to the Council may be purely on the basis of merit. It, therefore, recommends that
the following may be added as Statutes at an appropriate place:
(1) There shall be constituted in the University, a Students' Council for every academic year, consisting of -
(i)                  the Dean of Students' Welfare who shall be the Chairman of the Students' Council:
(ii)                all students who have won prizes in the previous  academic year in the filed of studies, fine arts,
sports and extension work;
(iii)               twenty students to be nominated by the Academic council on the basis of merit in studies, sports,
activities and all-round development of personality;
 
Provided that any student of the University shall have the right to bring up any matter concerning the University
before the Students' Council if so permitted by the Chairman, and he shall have the right to participate in the discussions
at any meeting when the matter is taken up for consideration.
 
(2) The functions of the Students' Council shall be to make suggestions to the appropriate authorities of the
University in regard to the programmes of studies, students' welfare and other matters of importance, in regard to the
working of the University in general and such suggestions shall be made on the basis of consensus of opinion.
(3)        The Students' Council shall meet at least once in an academic year preferably in the beginning of that
year.
 
Alumni Association
 
25.       The alumni of a university represent its proud achievements.  A regular interaction with them will help in the over
all growth of the university. The experiences and the feed back received from the past students can be an asset to the
university.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the necessary provision for an "Alumni Association" may be
incorporated in the Bill itself as has been done in the case of Mizoram  University.  The Committee recommends that the
following may be added in the statute:-
 
            (1) There shall be an Alumni Association for the University.
(2) The subscription for membership of the Alumni Association shall be prescribed by the Ordinances.
            (3) No member of the Alumni Association shall be entitled to vote or stand for election unless he has been a
member of the Association for at least one year prior to the date of the election and is a degree holder of the University of
at least five years standing:
            Provided that the condition relating to the completion on one year's membership shall not apply in the case of the
first election.

                  At its meeting held on the 2 nd June 2005, the Committee decided that given the wider ramifications of the Bill,

NEW DELHI            
August 17, 2005
Sravana 26, 1927, (Saka)
VAYALAR RAVI
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development
                                                                                                      
REPORT
 
The Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Bill, 2005 seeks to provide for the constitution of a National
Commission and State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights and Children’s Courts for providing speedy trial of
offences against children or of violation of child rights and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The
Committee was informed that India had the largest child population in the world.  Constitution of India guarantees several
rights to the children including equality before law, free and compulsory primary education to all children between six to
fourteen years, prohibition of trafficking and forced labour by children and employment of children below the age of
fourteen years in factories, mines or hazardous occupations. The Constitution requires the State to make special
provisions for children and directs that the policy of the State shall be such that their tender age was not abused. Inspite of
Government's commitment to give children opportunities, healthy environment and facilities to develop, they continue to

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
remain vulnerable to various forms of abuse, exploitation, maltreatment, etc. 
2.         Various child-related indicators present a very dismal scenario, despite a number of child-related laws and
schemes being administered by different Departments.  The Committee was given to understand that currently child
protection, welfare and their development is being taken care of by several agencies.  As a result, many gap areas are
noticed in this regard.  The Secretary emphasised that there was a need for an authority which could take a holistic view
of the matters pertaining to children and oversee the existing programmes, policies, laws etc. for them with a view to
getting these implemented and recommend corrective measures, if required.
3.         The Government of India is a party to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) which requires
signatory States to realign their child laws with a view to make their legal, judicial and administrative systems child-
friendly as well as sensitive to interests of the child.  Thus, in view of the national as well as international developments,
the need for a National Commission for Protection of Child Rights was being felt by all those working for the
development and welfare of the children including the Government.  The Committee was informed that the draft National
Commission for Protection of Child Rights Bill, 2005 is the outcome of a prolonged and extensive interaction with all the
States/UTs, Ministries, Departments, institutions, voluntary organisations, experts, social workers, etc.
4.         The Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development apprised the Committee at its meeting held on the
16
th June, 2005 about the background for bringing the proposed legislation on protection of child rights before
Parliament.  The Secretary then touched upon the basic features of the Bill giving an idea about the composition and
appointment of the Commission, its functions, special powers, constitution of State Commissions, Children's Courts,
procedure for enquiry, presentation of its reports and other miscellaneous provisions.
5.         The Committee had invited views/suggestions from the general public through a notice published in newspapers
on various provisions of the Bill.  The Committee also had the opportunity to hear the views of a number of Voluntary
Organizations, social workers and legal persons working in areas like child welfare, protection of child rights, their
education and health, juvenile justice, child labour, etc.  These extensive deliberations and also the voluminous written
material received from all concerned, has greatly helped the Committee in formulating its views on various provisions of
this special piece of legislation, very much required for the development and protection of our future generations. 
6.         The Committee likes to place on record its appreciation for the Department for bringing out this Bill for setting up
a Commission to protect and promote interests of Children. Keeping in view vast population of children in the country,
mostly being under-privileged, setting up of such a Commission is the need of the hour. Protecting and promoting their
interest is laudable and challenging as well. The Committee after detailed discussion came to the conclusion that certain
provisions, particularly those relating to appointment and removal of the Chairperson and members of the proposed
Commission, its functions, procedure  for transaction of its business, powers relating to inquiries and children's courts
needed some amendments.  Need for adding more provisions was felt necessary to provide required autonomy as well as
powers to the proposed Commission so that it can carry out its mandate in a more credible and effective manner and it
does not appear to be a body controlled by the Government of the day.            
7.         The Committee at its meeting held on the 4
th August, 2005 took up the Bill for Clause-by-clause consideration.
The Clauses where amendments were suggested by the Committee have been discussed in the succeeding
paragraphs.        
Clause 3
8.         Sub-clause (2) (b) of clause 3 provides that six members of the Commission will be appointed by the Central
Government from amongst persons of eminence, ability, integrity, standing and experience from different fields
mentioned therein. Although, this particular Clause, Committee notes, does not prohibit the appointment of women as

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
members of the Commission, almost everybody who appeared before it, impressed upon the need for having an explicit
provision that at least two of its members have to be women.  It is a well-known fact that women have better
understanding of problems as well as needs of the children.  By ensuring women representation in the Commission, cause
of children would be served better.  The Committee also concurs with this line of thinking.  It, therefore, recommends that
out of the six members appointed to the Commission, at least two should be women.  A provision to this effect should be
inserted in the Bill.
Clause – 4
9.         The Committee notes that as per the Clause 4 of the Bill, the Chairperson and members of the Commission shall
be appointed by the Central Government.  However, appointment of the Chairperson shall be based on the
recommendation of a three member Selection Committee headed by the Minister of Human Resource Development.  The
Committee feels that this selection procedure might impinge upon the autonomy and independence required for
functioning of such a Commission.  It, therefore, is of the view that a National Commission of such a great significance
should be appointed by a higher/independent authority and certainly not by the government alone. The Committee notes
that the President of India is the appointing authority for the Chairman of the National Human Rights Commission and an
independent body having representation of high dignitaries as the Selection Committee for its members.  The Committee
strongly feels that similar provision be provided for the appointment of the Chairman and the members of the
Commission being set up for promotion of child welfare. The Committee therefore recommends that the existing Clause 4
of the Bill should be substituted by the following:-
(1)
               The Chairperson and other Members shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
 
Provided that every appointment under this sub-section shall be made after obtaining the recommendations of a
Committee consisting of:-
(a)    The Prime Minister – Chairperson
(b)   Speaker of the House of the People – Member
(c)    Minister in-charge of the Ministry of Human Resource Development in the Government of India –
Member
(d)   Minister in-charge of the Ministry of Social  Justice and Empowerment of the Government of India -
Member
(e)    Leader of the Opposition in the House of the People – Member
(f)     Leader of the opposition in the Council of States – Member
(g)    Deputy Chairman of the Council of States – Member
Clause – 5
10.       Clause 5(1) provides for the term of office of the Chairman and Members of the Commission.  The Committee
notes that there is no restriction on the number of terms the Chairman or the Member of the Commission can serve.  It
feels that a specific provision in this regard is required to be made.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Chairman
and Members should not be allowed to function for more than two terms.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to
insert a provision to this effect in Clause 5(1) of the Bill.
Clause 5(2)
11.1     Clause 5(2) provides that the Chairperson and Member may by writing under his hand addressed to Central
Government, resign his office at any time.  In view of the Committee's recommendations to make President of India their
appointing authority, consequential changes in clause 5(2) should also be made.
11.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that in sub clause (2) of Clause (5) the words “Central Government” may
be replaced by “President of India”.
Clause-7(1)
12.1     Clause 7 provides for the removal of Chairperson or any other Member from his office by an order of the Central

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
Government on the ground of proved misbehavior or incapacity.
12.2     The Committee feels that the Chairperson and Members of the Commission may be removed only after a proper
enquiry.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the sub-clause (1) of clause 7 may be substituted by the following:-
Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the Chairperson or any other Member of the Commission shall
only be removed from his office by an order of the President on the ground of proved misbehaviour or
incapacity after an inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf, reported that the
Chairperson or such other Member, as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removed.
Clause 7(2)
13.       In clause 7(2) in line 23 of page 3 the words “Central Government” may be replaced by “President of India”.
Clause-8
14.1     The Committee notes that clause 8(2) of the Bill sets the procedure about the vacation of office by the Chairperson
or its members.  No specific time-limit has been prescribed for filling up of vacancies, if any.  This may create a situation
wherein the vacancies might remain unfilled for a long time which may affect the functioning of the Commission
adversely.
14.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that if a casual vacancy occurs in the office of the Chairperson or a
Member, whether by reason of his death, resignation or otherwise, such vacancy shall be filled within 90 days in
accordance with the provisions of Clause 4.
Sub-clause (1) of Clause 10
15.1     Sub-clause (1) of clause 10 provides that the Commission shall meet at its office at least once in every six months.
15.2
          The Committee notes that in view of the heavy responsibilities and work-load of the Commission and the fact that
it has whole-time, regular and paid Chairperson/Members (barred from taking any other paid employment), it
would be required to meet at shorter intervals.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that sub clause (1) of
clause-10 may be substituted as follows:-
            “The Commission shall meet regularly at its office at such time as may be fixed by the Chairperson but in any case
at least once in three months”.
Sub-clause (4) of Clause 10
16.1     Sub-clause (4) of clause 10 provides that the Commission shall observe such rules of procedure for the transaction
of its business at a meeting including the quorum at such meeting, as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
16.2     On being asked about the specific reasons for not empowering the Commission to lay down its own procedure, the
Committee was informed that where a Statutory Commission was headed by a person who is/has been a Supreme
Court/High Court Judge, the regulation of the procedure is left with the Commission.  This was primarily because they
would be aware of all such rules.  In contrast, where persons from other fields are appointed as Chairpersons, rules of the
procedure are framed by the administrative Ministry in consultation with Ministry of Law.  The Committee is not
convinced by the clarifications given by the Department.  It would like to point out that this is not so in the case of the
National Commission for Women.  Its Chairperson is of similar status as envisaged for the proposed Commission, yet it
has the power to regulate its own procedure.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that sub-clause (4) of clause 10
should also provide that the Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure.
COMMITTEES OF THE COMMISSION
Clause 10A
 
17.       The Committee observes that inspite of a huge mandate given to this six member body, it does not have the power
to appoint any Committee or any authority so as to facilitate its functioning as and when required.  The Committee's

165th Report of HRD Committee
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/165threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:24:37]
attention was drawn towards by such a power given to the National Commission for Women.  On being asked about this
provision, the Committee was given to understand that the proposed Commission was empowered to take any action as it
might consider necessary for the promotion of child rights and any other matter incidental to the functions proposed for it
as per Clause 13 (i).  It was further informed that provision for Committees etc. can be provided in the Rules.  The
Committee, however, feels that such a provision needs to be enshrined in the Act itself.  The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that a new clause, a clause 10A may be added as follows:-
            "The Commission may appoint such committees, rapporteurs, amicus curie, as may be necessary for dealing with
such special issues as may be taken up by the Commission from time to time".
 
Clause 13
 
18.1     The Committee notices that a very crucial aspect - violation of child rights, does not occur anywhere in Clause 13
listing out functions of the Commission.  In other words, the Commission would have no power to inquire into child right
violations.  If it is so, the Committee feels, the Commission's powers shall remain highly truncated.  Besides, the Clause
15 (i) empowers the Commission to recommend initiation of proceedings in cases of violations of child rights.  The
Committee is at a loss to understand that if the Commission does not have an explicit power to go into violations of child
rights, how can it recommend such cases for action?  The Committee, therefore, strongly feels that going into violations
of child right should be expressly provided in Clause 13. 
18.2
          For this, the Committee recommends that the Clause 13 (c) and 13 (d) to be restructured as follows to make these
more harmonious and exhaustive.
(c)                examine all factors that violate and inhibit the enjoyment of rights of children and recommends appropriate
remedial measures.
(d)               look into the matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,
marginalised and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family,
children of prisoners and also children affected by terrorism, communal violence, riots, natural disasters,
domestic violence, HIV/AIDS, trafficking, mal-treatment, torture and exploitation, pornography and
prostitution and recommends appropriate remedial measures.
18.3     The Committee also recommends to add “violation and” after “deprivation” in clause 13(i) (i)
Clause 14
 
19.1     In Clause 14, the Committee notices that there is no provision to deal with tendering of false or fabricated
evidence during inquiries under clauses 13 (i) and 14 (2), empowering the Commission to refer cases to the Magistrate of
jurisdiction under section of 346 of Criminal Procedure Code, covers only cases of contempt by way of intentional refusal
to produce a document, or to take oath, or to answer questions, or to sign the statement, or intentionally insulting or
obstructing proceedings by a public servant (punishable under sections 175, 178, 179, 180 and 228 respectively of the
Indian Penal Code).  It does not, the Committee feels, empower the Commission to refer cases of "giving or fabricating
false evidence" (punishable under Section 193 of the Indian Penal Code), which can be referred to a Magistrate of
jurisdiction under section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code.  Even the term "all the powers of a civil court" used in
Clause 14 (1) does not empower the Commission to refer cases under section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code as
under sub-section (3) of this section, a public servant/Tribunal has to be specifically "declared by the relevant Act to be a
Court for the purposes of this Section".  
 
19.2     The Committee is of the considered view that without these powers, as given in Section 13 of the National Human

Rights Act, the Child Rights Protection Commission would be greatly hampered in effective performance of its functions
relating to inquiries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Clause 14 of the Bill should be substituted by Section
13 of the Protection of Human Rights Act with suitable modifications, to include all the powers given to the National
Human Rights Commission under that Section as child rights are of same importance, if not more, as human rights.

20.       In view of the Committee's recommendation about taking cognizance of violation of child rights and its inclusion
in Clause 13 of the Bill, the Committee feels the power of investigation would have to be necessarily given to the
Commission.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the following should be added as new Clauses 14A, 14B and
14C.

STATE COMMISSIONS
 
25.1     The Committee, in view of its recommendations to amend provision of the Bill relating to constitution,
appointment, removal, etc. of the National Commission recommends that the corresponding provisions pertaining to the
State Commissions should also be amended accordingly.
25.2     Chapter IV deals with the constitution of State Commissions.  The Committee observes that as per Clause 17(i), it
is not mandatory for a State Government to set up State Commission.  The Committee is somewhat worried by the
experience with quite a few State Governments not fulfilling the provision of setting up of State Human Rights
Commissions and State Commissions for Women inspite of a provision being there in the respective Acts.  The
Committee, accordingly, recommends that it should be made mandatory for every State Government/UT Administration
to set up Child Rights Commission.
 
25.3     Provisions regarding State Commissions indicate that the State Commissions will be functioning independently. 
The Committee feels that there is a need for some kind of interface and co-ordination between State Commissions and
National Commission specially in view of the experience so far with regard to State Commissions of NHRC and NWC. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that such a provision could be made in the Rules.
 
25.4     The Committee observes that there are a number of Commissions/Boards such as National Commission for
Women, National Human Rights Commission, Juvenile Justice Boards, Child Welfare Boards and Central Social Welfare
Board, all of which are directly or indirectly involved in child welfare and also in the exercise of protecting their rights. 
With the enactment of the proposed Bill and State Commissions for child rights being set up, need for effective
coordination among these bodies so as to avoid any confusion/over-lapping will be increasingly felt.   The Committee has
been informed that a National Co-ordination Group having representatives from all concerned Ministries on children
issues has been set up.  The Committee hopes that this will prove to be an effective mechanism.
 
25.5     The Committee recommends that the Bill should have a provision at appropriate place to expressly prohibit State
Commissions to take up an issue, which is under consideration of the National Commission.
Clause 25
 
26.1     The omnibus provision under Clause 25 for trial of all "offences against children" or "violation of child rights" by

165th Report of HRD Committee

'Children's Courts' in Committee's view, would be difficult to implement and could lead to complications/conflicts in view
of the following factors:
(i)                  While offences committed against children or crimes in which children are the victims are considered as
'offences against children', there is no separate classification of such offences under the IPC and Criminal
procedure Code, which could be earmarked for trial by such courts. 
 
(ii)                In cases where the victims comprise both children as well as adults, there cannot be separate trials in two
different courts of the same offender(s) for the same offence.
 
(iii)   Offences in which the offenders are also juveniles are triable by Juvenile Justice Board under the Juvenile Justice
(Care and Protection) Act, 2000, and cannot be tried by Children's Courts under this Bill.
 
(iv)              All 'violations of child rights' may not amount to punishable offences triable by such courts.
 
26.2     In the light of the above observations the Committee feels that suitable amendments/additions should be made in
the Clause 25 with a view to ensure speedy trial of cases relating to Children.
 
Miscellaneous
 
27.       The Committee observes that human rights and child rights are integrated and inter related.  It would only be
appropriate if the two Commissions have some interface in their working at the higher levels.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Chairperson of the National Commission may be deemed to a Member of the National Human
Rights Commission.  The Department may take this up with the Ministry concerned for bringing an amendment to this
effect in the NHRC Act.
28.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill without any amendments.
 
29.       The enacting formula and the title are adopted with consequential changes.
 
30.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendment additions suggested
by it. 
 
32.

made by the Committee, which could not be incorporated in the Bill.

NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENTS’ REPLY
 
V         ISSUES FOR GENDER BUDGETING
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS
 
4.1       The Committee is of the opinion that in view of integration of gender equality with sustainable development,
need and importance of gender budgeting can hardly be over emphasized.  The aim of gender budgeting is to
generate/capture the gender-based data/information, which will be relevant  input for assessing the gender specific
impact of budgetary allocations.  The Committee found that currently gender segregated macro-economic data were not
available in India.  In the absence of such data from different sectors of our economy, the Committee feels it will be
difficult to analyse the budgetary allocations on the basis of gender.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
process of gender budgeting should necessarily contain not only the segregation of gender based data but also aspects
like quantification of contribution of women in the economy; impact of Government budget on women; and policy
alternatives for evolving a gender sensitive social order.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
4.1       Recognizing the need to widen the ambit of gender budgeting, the Department held a consultation on 8
December 2004, with experts and representatives of various Government organizations and para-statal bodies to arrive
at a consensus on the framework of gender budgeting.  The meeting was chaired by Secretary (WCD) and was attended
by Advisor, Planning Commission, Joint Secretary (Budget), Member, NCW, representatives of UNIFEM and UNDP
and a few social experts.  The Department has adopted the following slogan as a mission statement for gender budgeting
–
 
            ‘Budgeting for Gender Equity’
 
The broad-framework recommended for gender budget analysis is as follows
 
Broad framework of activities
Quantification of allocation of resources for women in the Union, States and Local Administration budgets
and expenditure thereof.
q       Refining and standardizing methodology and development of tools.
