The Committee recommends that RMK should develop a pool of projects/ schemes/activities which are locally viable and implementable and which can generate income. The RMK can advise the beneficiaries to opt for any of these schemes which will be beneficial for them. The Committee feels
that if such an option is available, the disbursement level will increase and the objectives of the scheme can be achieved.                                  (Para 14.5)
 
                        The Committee was given to understand that a Sub Committee has been setup to examine different aspects of micro credit programmes, economic viability and sustainability of Kosh under RMK.   In this connection, the Committee would like to recall its earlier recommendation with regard to lowering of interest rate on loans to be given by RMK.    The Committee is surprised to note that Governing Body of RMK in its meeting held on 21.12.2005 decided that constitution of a Sub Committee for examination of various operational issues including lowering of interest rate be left to the discretion of MOS, Ministry of
Women and Child Development and  Chairperson, RMK.    The Committee expresses its serious reservation on the handling of such a sensitive issue.    The Committee strongly feels that the existing system under which RMK charges interest@ 8 % on reducing balance from borrowing agency which in turn charges any rate on or above 8% on reducing balance from the ultimate beneficiaries subject to maximum upto 18% needs to be reviewed at the earliest.  One should not forget that the main objective of RMK is to provide micro credit support to poor women.          (Para 14.6)
 
XV.                  NEW  SCHEMES
 
SCHEME FOR RESCUE OF VICTIMS OF TRAFFICKING
 
                        The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 3.00 crore for this scheme was made in 2004-05 which was reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06.   Allocation in 2006-07 stands at Rs.45 lakhs.  The Committee is not happy with the undue delay in launching of this scheme. The scheme needs more publicity and proper implementation. Since the scheme is to be implemented through NGOs, the Ministry has to be very careful while releasing funds. Monitoring of the scheme is to be strictly followed. The publicity should focus on protection and awareness-raising among parents and guardians.  (Para 15.3)
 
RELIEF AND REHABILITATION OF VICTIMS OF RAPE
 
                        The Committee feels that the victims of rape undergo the conditions of psychological stress and trauma notwithstanding the physical assault. The rehabilitation process of such victim involves psychological support as well as economic assistance. The Committee would like the Ministry to create a separate rehabilitation fund for victims of rape to ensure that they get all sort of psychological and economic assistance in time.                                                                                                   (Para 15.5)
 
XVI.                PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT AT WORKPLACE
 
                        The Government of India constituted a Central Committee under the Chairpersonship of the Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development to monitor the implementation of the Supreme Court’s Guidelines for prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace. The Committee in its Meeting held on 29.10.2002 recommended that Awareness needs to be given on this issue and this task had been assigned to National Commission for Women (NCW) and Central Social Welfare Board alongwith Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Commission for Women has taken up sexual harassment
of women at work place as one of the focal issues in the realm of promotion of gender equality and women's empowerment.  The Commission had widely circulated the Visakha Judgement for compliance along with a code of conduct for workplace formulated by the NCW. The Committee is not aware of the activities/initiatives undertaken by the CSWB and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to create awareness on the SC Guidelines. This has become all the more important in view of increasing incidents of sexual harassment in BPOs and other private institutions.(Para 16.1)
                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                        The Committee is constrained to observe that that the Supreme Court Guidelines had not been properly followed both by the Government Departments.  In a number of cases, Complaint Committees had not been formed.  Where these committees existed, they did not have 50 per cent reservation for women.  Also in many cases the Committees were headed by men instead of women and without the involvement of a third party (NGO).  Lack of awareness among the Members of the complaint Committee was also noticed. The Committee is of the firm view that Supreme Court directive needs to be implemented in letter
and spirit.   The Committee would like to have full details about the 799 organisations covered so far by the NCW alongwith theorganizations where complaint Committees are yet to be set up.    The Committee would also like to have an idea about the additional organizations covered by NCW. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should come forward with a comprehensive legislation for prevention of sexual harassment in work places. The private institutions may also be brought under the purview of the legislations related to prevention of sexual harassment.   (Para 16.5)
 
XVII.               NUTRITION
 
                        The Committee notes that the FNB provides training to the Anganwadi functionaries. However the Committee notices huge gap between the target and achievement especially in case of training of grassroot level functionaries. The Committee wonders how the Ministry can take a casual approach to the gap reflected and let on increase in the number of malnourished children.                                                                        (Para 17.5)
 
                        The Committee’s attention is drawn by the media reports appearing on regular basis about large number of deaths of children due to malnourishment in the tribal belts of different parts of the country. Such incidents shows the non existence of Government machinery in those areas which can effectively cater to the nutrition requirement of the poor and deprived sections of the Society. The Committee recommends that it is the bounden duty of the Government to ensure that not a single child is dying due to malnourishment especially in view of the facilities being provided through AWCs  under ICDS. The Committee
strongly feels that the FNB needs to train maximum number of functionaries of AWCs so as to sensitize them about the preventive measures to be taken in malnutrition cases of children and mothers. The Committee would appreciate if FNB makes an effective beginning by targetting the functionaries of AWCs located in tribal belts.          (Para 17.6)
 
NATIONAL NUTRITION MISSION (NNM)
 
                        The Committee notes that not much progress has been achieved in the implementation of the scheme. The Committee notes that the objectives of the mission are realistic in nature and if implemented in its totality a healthy child population will be the result. The Committee emphasize that the Ministry should make the scheme functional so as to achieve the desired result of nutrition in a time bound manner.                                      (Para 17.10)
 
XVIII.             GENDER BUDGETING
 
                        The Committee recommends that being the nodal Ministry, the Ministry of WCD should ensure that Gender Budget Cells which are set up in the Ministries have become operational and also pursue this issue with the remaining Ministries.                                                                                                                                             (Para 18.4)
 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the implementation status of the aforesaid initiatives taken by the Ministry.                                      (Para 18.5)
 
                        Committee’s attention has been drawn by the details regarding scheme-wise provisions and physical targets benefiting women in the Budget of Ministry of Women and Child Development as given in the Performance Budget (2006-07). The Committee finds that all the schemes whether targeting children or women have been shown to be providing 100% benefit to women alone. The Committee does not dispute the fact that welfare ofthe child is ultimately the welfare of its mother.However, in view of the emerging concept of child budgeting, it cannot be claimed that flagship schemes like ICDS are benefiting cent
percent women.The Committee recommends that the allocation on programmes and schemes benefiting women may be delineated specifically. The Committee also recommends that the components of gender budgeting may be made more clear and included in the guidelines for gender budgeting.            (Para 18.6)

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports was set up as the Department of Sports in 1982 at the time of
organisation of the IX Asian Games in New Delhi.   Thereafter, during the celebration of the International Youth Year
in 1985, it was converted into the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports. It became a full-fledged Ministry on the 27 th
May, 2000.
1.2       The Youth i.e. those falling within the age group of 15-35 years constitutes nearly 40% of the total population of

176th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/176threport%20.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
the country.   To optimally tap the constructive and creative energies of this most valuable human resource, the Ministry
of Youth affairs and Sports has taken a number of new initiatives since its inception.    The Ministry organises a large
number of programmes in the field of youth development, sports and physical education.
1.3       The Joint Secretary (Sports), while deposing before the Committee, highlighted the various activities undertaken
by the Ministry during the year 2005-2006. He informed the Committee that Nehru Yuva Kendra played a major role in
providing relief materials, organizations of camps, counselling and career guidance to Tsunami victims.  SAI hostel,
Port Blair acted as both the center for housing inmates and for giving relief to Tsunami victims.  Contribution made by
NYK in providing relief to the earthquake victims in Kashmir was also worth-mentioning. Another initiative taken by
the Ministry was identification of Sports Federations performing well for giving them additional Funds.
1.4       A mention was also made about the new initiatives planned for 2006-07. A new Scheme ‘Yuva Shakti Abhiyan’
was going to be launched in Panchayats in all the States. Similarly all the Youth organizations like NYKS, NSS, NCC,
Bharat Scouts and Guides are being involved in the campaign on HIV/AIDS. States are going to be involved more and
more in the monitoring of different schemes.  He also drew the attention of the Committee towards the commendable
performance of Indian players who won a total of 50 medals and retained 4
th position in Commonwealth Games held at
Melbourne, 2006. These achievements were made possible to a large extent by the financial assistance made available to
the Sports Federations by the Ministry and also providing the necessary facilities to the participating players.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The total outlay, both Plan and Non-Plan taken together provided to the Ministry for the year 2005-2006 was Rs.
506.99 crores which was reduced to Rs. 478.01 crores at RE stage.  The expenditure booked upto 20
th March 2006 was
approximately Rs. 413 crores which means the Ministry was supposed to spend  Rs. 93 crores in remaining 11 days of
last financial year. The allocation for 2006-2007 is Rs. 669.00 crores (Plan Rs. 600.00 crores and Non Plan Rs. 69.00
crores). The Ministry informed thatagainst a projected demand of Rs. 929.29 crores under Plan for the year 2006-2007 a
provision of only Rs 600.00 crores has been made.   The projections were made, taking into consideration, higher
requirements for a number of ongoing and proposed schemes to be implemented by the Ministry during 2006-2007.
2.2       The Ministry informed that the cut made in the actual allocation from the proposed allocation would definitely
hamper proper implementation and ultimately have a negative impact on performance of the following schemes:
(Rs. in crores)
 Proposed Actual Allocation
SAI 173 150
Creation of Sports infrastructure 90 27
Commonwealth Games 200 150
Training of Indian Athletes 75                      --
            Not only this, proposed expansion of NYKS to 123 uncovered districts and promotion of Rural Sports Club
movement in the Villages would also be adversely affected due to the cut in the proposed demand of the Ministry.
Activities proposed to be initiated under the Action Plan for Youth to combat HIV/AIDS epidemic in the country were
also going to be restricted. The Committee notes that no allocation has been made for Training of Indian Athletes
against its proposed allocation for Rs. 75 crores. Such sweeping cut may have some concrete reason. The Committee
presumes that the Ministry have some contingency plans to arrange the finance for the Training of Indian Athletes for
the forthcoming Asian, Commonwealth Games and other International events. The Committee would like to be apprised
of such plans/scheme.
2.3       The Committee is aware that under the Constitution, Sports being a State subject, State
Governments/autonomous organisations/NGOs have to play a very active role in the implementation of the different
Youth and Sports related schemes.  The Committee observes that Tenth Plan Outlay of Rs. 1825.00 crore is more than
double of the Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 826.09 crore for the Ministry.   Whereas there has been optimum utilisation of
allocated funds during the Ninth Plan, position is somewhat different during the Tenth Plan.  Plan allocation of Rs. 600
crore for 2006-07, last year of the Tenth Plan, is at a very enhanced level when compared with the previous  years of the
Tenth Plan.  The Committee notes that the allocations remained underutilised inspite of reduced projections at the RE
stage as indicated below –

The Committee fails to understand the constraints being faced by the Department in the optimum utilisation of
allocated funds for Youth and Sports related schemes. It remains a guess work for the Committee whether the under-
utilisation is due to the inability of implementing agencies (both Govt. & private sector) to take the full benefit of these
schemes or inherent flaws in the scheme itself are attributed to the same. The Committee observes that funds remained
underutilised under the schemes of Promotion of Adventure Activities, Promotion of Scouting and Guiding, National
Service Volunteer Scheme, Promotion of Youth Activities and Training, Rashtriya Sadhbhavna Yojana, Assistance to
Rural Youth and Sports Clubs, Scheme for welfare and development of Adolescents, Grants to Sports Federations. What
is more worrisome is that under Schemes like National Sports Championship for Women, National Welfare Fund for
Sportspersons, Promotion of Sports among Disabled, Scheme relating to Talent Search and Training, Scheme for Dope
Test, All India Council for Physical Education, and States Sports Academy expenditure remained nil. The Committee
also finds that provision made both under Youth and Sports Scheme for NE States remained underutilized.
 2.4      The  Committee can  afford to conclude that even the formulation  of   a  quarterly  annual   action  plan for 2005
- 2006 by the  Ministry  has  not  been  able  to  achieve  the desired results. It’s the case of failure in planning.  It
appears to the Committee that the Ministry remained engaged in projecting higher requirements and launching   new  
schemes without any considerations of the judicious and  optimum  utilisation  of  funds  allocated  for the existing
schemes. It is quite contradictory that on one hand the Ministry talk of resource crunch and on other hand the allocated
resources are not fully utilized.  Huge unspent balances are lying with the Ministry under various schemes.  This fiscal
disorder in the Ministry has done more harm. The case for higher allocations has weakened to a great extent.  The
Committee is of the view that a detailed review of all the ongoing schemes should be undertaken so as to assess the
shortcomings being noticed and take remedial steps for removal of the same.   Active involvement of the State
Governments and other implementing agencies in this exercise is called for. The Committee would like the Ministry to
adopt better fiscal management practices to avoid the last minute spending for achieving the targets.
III        NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR YOUTH
3.1       Report of the National Commission for Youth was laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament on
23.12.2004.  Fourteen recommendations made by the Commission have been accepted by the Ministry in principle
which include:-
-
                     Setting up of Rashtriya Yuva Kosh on the pattern of the Rashtriya Mahila Kosh;
-                      Expansion of National Service Schemes in all universities and colleges and scheme to be introduced at
class IX level and amalgamation of NSS & NCC Comments of the Ministry of Defence to be asked for
and to make serving either NSS or NCC mandatory for every student to become eligible for award of
degree.            
3.2       The Committee finds the recommendations made by the Commission very useful in empowering the youth. 
Unfortunately not much progress has been made in the implementation of these recommendations.  No follow-up action
appears to have been taken after the meeting with the officials of the Rashtriya Mahila Kosh on the feasibility of
formulation of Rashtriya Yuva Kosh.  Similarly the proposal with regard to amalgamation of NSS and NCC sent to the
Planning Commission simply remained a referral. The Committee would like the Ministry to expedite the action on all
recommendations particularly with regard to setting up of Rashtriya Yuva Kosh. The Committee feels that either the
NCC or NSS should be made compulsory from class IXth.
IV.       NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN
4.1       Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS),  an autonomous body of the Ministry which functions in Districts all
over India is engaged in conducting various youth programmes. Being the largest grass root level organization in the
world it is presently catering to the needs of more than 8 million non-student rural youth enrolled through about 2.30
lakh village based youth clubs.  The vast network of the youth clubs is the real strength of NYKS.
4.2       NYKS accomplishes its task through three categories of programmes i.e. Regular Programmes such as, Youth
Club Development, Vocational Training, Work Camp, Awareness Generation, Cultural Programme, Sports Promotion,
Adventure Promotion, Seminars and Workshops and Celebration of National and International Days/Weeks; second
category of schemes include National Service Volunteers, Financial Assistance to Youth Clubs, Awards to Outstanding
Youth Clubs at District, State and National levels, Rural Information Technology and Youth Development Centres
assigned to it by the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports for implementation.  The third category being the special
programmes undertaken in collaboration with other Ministries and Organizations.
4.3       An allocation of Rs. 34.00 crores was made at BE and RE stage during 2005-06. The actual expenditure was Rs.
33.21 crores.  The allocation for 2006-07 is Rs. 45 crores against proposed outlay of Rs. 61.18 crores.  The Committee

VI.       NATIONAL DISCIPLINE SCHEME
6.1       The National Discipline Scheme was originally started in 1954 by the Ministry of Rehabilitation, which was
later transferred to Ministry of Education and Social Welfare in 1958. Consequent upon the recommendations of Dr.
Kunzru Committee in 1963, introducing discipline programme at school stage, the integrated scheme called “National
Fitness Corps” (NFC) was evolved.  The Scheme was transferred to the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports (Now
Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports) in eighties when a separate Department was formed.
6.2       On the basis of the recommendations of Dr. Kunzru Committee, the decision to transfer NDS Instructors to
various State Governments was taken in consultation with the State Education Secretaries.  In the year 1969, the Central
Cabinet took a decision that the employees under the NFC would be transferred to the services of the State Governments
on the condition that the Central Government would reimburse their pay and allowances so long as they remained on the
strength of the State Governments. The Committee was informed that 6145 NDS Instructors were transferred to various
State Governments after decentralization of NDS scheme.
6.3       Though physically the NDS Instructors were absorbed in the services of the State Governments, the Central
Government was committed to bear the liability of their pay and allowances and this system has been continuing since
seventies. Due to inadequate budgetary provisions, the Central Government has never been able to bear its liability to
the fullest extent and thereby the accumulated liability continued to grow to unmanageable level. The Committee was
informed that the total liability towards pays and allowances for States of M.P., Punjab, Haryana, H.P., Rajasthan,
Kerala and Maharashtra from which information has been received is to the tune of Rs. 184.21 crores. Information from
remaining ten States is yet to be received. The total projected liability in respect of all the States is to the tune of Rs. 300
crore. A budget support would be required on that account.          
6.4       The Committee regrets that repeated reminders from the Department to some States have not evinced any
response and the issue of committed liabilities remains un-resolved for years together. The Committee feels that this
situation of uncertainty should come to a halt. A time has come when the Ministry should fix a final deadline for such
States to avoid this never-ending chaotic scenario. The Ministry should settle the issue once for all after paying the
liabilities to those States who have furnished the information. The States who do not respond may have to forgo their
claims. The Committee hopes that the Ministry would plan the whole process to ensure settlement of committed
liabilities within this financial year itself. The Committee would also like the Ministry to appeal to the States to avail
this opportunity and expedite their claims without further loss of time.

XVI.    SCHEME RELATING TO ‘HIV/AIDS’
16.1     The Committee notes that a new scheme relating to HIV/AIDS has been introduced and is under formulation.
The scheme is aimed at controlling the spread of HIV/AIDS in India. An Action Plan has been made in a comprehensive
way for 2006-2011 and one year for implementation during 2006-07. The total budget projected for one year (2006-07)
is Rs. 82. 34 crores in which the Ministry will dovetail its own programme fund of Rs. 55.50 crores relating to NSS,
NYKS and SAI. The budgetary provision has been kept at Rs. 10.00 crores, which will be utilized after its in-principle
approval by the Planning Commission and the balance 16.84 crores will be outsourced from other development partners
and international organizations.
 
16.2     The Action Plan aims to mainstream HIV/AIDS in the existing activities and programmes of the MYAS. It has
been suggested that the proposed activity of generating awareness among the youth of the country would be best
implemented under the Ministry’s umbrella. The Action Plan is to be implemented through the Nehru Yuva Kendra
Sangathan (NYKS), the National Social Service Scheme (NSS), Rajiv Gandhi National Institute for Youth Development
(RGNIYD), and Voluntary agencies, such as, Bharat Scouts and Guides (BSG) and National Cadet Corps (NCC), Indian
Red Cross-and Sports Councils at State level. The objective of the proposed new scheme is that every adolescent and
youth has access to information, education, counseling and services to protect themselves against the deadly disease and
to help others to do so.
16.3     The Committee is happy to note the introduction of the scheme aimed at achieving victory over AIDS in India. 
The Committee feels that proper strategy should be developed to achieve the objectives of the scheme. 
Adolescent/youth clubs and youth information centers  require proper back up of counseling and resource materials. 
The Committee underlines the need for establishment of linkages amongst all the field organizations with health
facilities and VCTCs for service access. The Committee would like the Ministry to pursue the Planning Commission to
seek in principle approval in respect of the scheme.

REPORT
 
1.         The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages University Bill, 2006 was introduced on the 20th March,
2006, in the Rajya Sabha and was referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human
Resource Development on 27th March, 2006 for examination and report. 
 
2.         The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages is currently functioning at Hyderabad offering courses
for the teaching/ study of English and major foreign languages.  It is a society registered under the Hyderabad Societies
Registration Act, 1950. In July 1973, it was conferred deemed university status under section 3 of the University Gants
Commission Act, 1956.
 
3.         This Bill seeks to accord the Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages at Hyderabad a Central
University status and dissolve the Institute as a society. 
 
4.         Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill justifies the need for converting this institute into a
Central University in the following manner: “With the advent of globalization and opening of world economies, the
mobility of people of all walks of life, across international boundaries, had phenomenally increased during the recent
years, resulting into added pressure on the institutions offering foreign language courses world over.   The
responsibilities of the Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages, Hyderabad have also increased manifold on
this count and it would require greater autonomy for discharging its added responsibilities.   At the same time, it needs to
be made more accountable and transparent in its functioning.  Both these requirements, may be met by conferring on it
the status of a full-fledged Central University”.
 
5.         During the course of deliberations on the Bill, apprehensions were voiced by some members of the Committee
that there appeared to be unjustified haste in according the central university status to this Institute. It was pointed our
that there may be any number of more reputed and better performing educational institutions in the country, more
deserving to get central status than this Institute.  These members felt that the objective could be better achieved by
strengthening/empowering the Departments of Foreign Languages in the existing institutions/universities.   Doubts were
raised that the proposed university might also go the same way as the Mahatma Gandhi Hindi Vishvavidyalaya has gone,
where even after a decade of its creation, it remains virtually a non-starter.
 
6.         The Committee is surprised to note that instead of there being any demand from any quarter/stakeholder for
making the Institute a Central University, this idea was mooted by the Central Government.  Not only this, no formal
inspection of the Institute- its academic and other infrastructural facilities has been carried out so far.
 
7.         The Committee sought clarifications on a number of issues connected with the functioning of the Institute and its
present status from the Department of Secondary and Higher Education.  Representatives of the Department also
appeared before the Committee and replied to various queries raised by the members. With the advent of globalization,
manifold increase in the responsibilities of the Institute, resultant need for expansion and diversification of its activities
and greater autonomy emerged as the main factors on which Committee held extensive discussions.  
 
8.         As regards the increased responsibility, the facts made available to the Committee indicated otherwise.  The
Committee found that there were only 300 regular students pursuing M.A., M. Phil & Ph.d from five Schools of studies
and 700 students were enrolled for different courses through distance education mode.  Besides that, the Institute was

177th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/177threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
also offering Part time 
Certificate/diploma/advanced diploma courses to about 650 students.  The Committee was given to understand that the
two regional Campuses of the Institute at Shillong and Lucknow were fully functional.  However, the Committee found
that although both the Campuses were set up in 1970s, they did not have their own buildings for academic,
administrative and hostel purposes.  The Committee also noted that large number of faculty positions were lying vacant-
44 at the main campus and 4 at the Lucknow campus. 
 
9.         The Committee was informed that over the years, the Institute had “grown in stature and had earned recognition
as a centre of excellence” in the study of English and major foreign languages.  The Department could, however, not
provide specific data/information, which could support this claim and provide an idea about the past performance of the
Institute.  Specific information indicating placement of the students passing out of the Institute also could not be made
available to the Committee by the Department, reason being that no formal study in this regard has been conducted so
far.   
10.       As regards the autonomy of the Institute, the Department argued that the CIEFL presently being a registered
society and an institution declared to be a deemed university under Section 3 of the UGC Act, was “susceptible to
erosion by the various authorities like Registrar of Societies, UGC and the Ministry of HRD.  Presently, the Institute had
to have prior approval of the UGC for starting any course, etc.  The Department contended that the Institute was
constrained tremendously by the procedures and guidelines laid down by the UGC.  The Bill, therefore, sought to
remove representation of the UGC from any authority of the proposed university and the VC will be appointed by the
President of India in his capacity as its Visitor.  The Department contended that the granting of central university status
would bring in systemic structural changes in the Institute with larger administrative and academic autonomy and
complete freedom from governmental control.
 
11.       The Committee then inquired about any specific case where the Institute could not take decision based on the
principles of autonomy.  The Committee further sought to know the structural bottlenecks that might have prevented
proper development of the Institute.  To this, the Department replied that any proceeding of the Institute may be annulled
by the Central Government, if it is not deemed to be in conformity with the rules and bye-laws of the Society.  It was,
however, argued that once the Institute was accorded the status of a central university, its autonomy would be
safeguarded in terms of the statutory provisions of the Act, where the Central Government or the UGC will not have any
say. 
 
12.       The Committee found these arguments/justifications given by the Department quite unconvincing. The
contention of the Department clearly implies that within UGC framework, there is no scope for autonomy and that UGC
works as road-block to development of educational institutions.  It further implies that the real autonomy and
development of an educational institution is possible only if it were a Central university.  The question arises: are the
State universities like Bombay University, Kolkata University and others are functioning without autonomy and
therefore, are not progressing?  The Committee finds this argument not only bizarre but also fraught with grave
implications.  It also raises question about the existing framework as well as functioning of the UGC.  It also underlines
the need for revisiting the whole concept/system of ‘deemed university’ because CIEFL is said to be ailing mainly due to
the UGC and the deemed university status and therefore, it needed no less than Central university status.          
 
13.       The Committee, despite all the questions and reservations on the aspects mentioned in preceding paragraphs,
would like to emphasize that it is not against empowering and strengthening an educational institution financially and
otherwise.  The Committee is aware of the importance of English and other foreign languages in the emerging scenario
at the global level.  India, today has become a force to reckon with in areas like science, information and communication
technology, medicine, space, nuclear energy, etc.  Apart from their/talent this can be upto a large extent attributed to the
compatibility of our young boys and girls with English and other languages.   In principle, therefore, the Committee
agrees with the strengthening of any institution promoting teaching and learning of English and foreign languages. 
Therefore, the Committee after expressing these sentiments suggests following amendments in the Bill:-
 
 Clause 1 (1)
14.       The Committee notes that the Act is named “The Central Institute of English and Foreign Languages University
Act, 2006”.  The Committee, however, feels that the use of words ‘institute’ and ‘university’ together should be
avoided.  Instead it would be more appropriate to call the proposed Act in Clause 1(1) as “The English and Foreign

177th Report of Committee on Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/177threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:47]
Languages University Act, 2006”.
 
Clause 3(1)
15.       In view of its recommendations for clause 1(1), the Committee proposes that the name of the proposed University
be named “English and Foreign Languages University”.
 
Clause 6(viii)
16.       Clause 6 relates to Powers of the University.  As per clause 6 (viii) the University shall have the power to appoint
persons working in any other University or organization as teachers of the University for a specified period.
 
17.       The Committee is of the considered opinion that the word “organization” in this clause leaves enough scope for
including extraneous agencies/bodies as well. The Department clarified that the word ‘organization’ generally meant “a
teaching or a research institution, other than a university”.  The Committee feels that it needs to specified.  It therefore,
recommends that the word ‘organisation’ may be substituted by the words ‘educational institution’ so as to remove any
ambiguity about the nature of the organization.
 
Clause 30(1)(i) 
18.       Clause 30 deals with power to make Ordinances. The Committee finds that this sub-clause provides for making
special arrangements “for residence, discipline and teaching of women students.”  The Committee is of the considered
opinion that while this is valid in terms of  residence and specific courses for women students, the word “discipline”  in
this clause appears to be unnecessary and discriminatory.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the words
‘discipline and’ be deleted from line 12 of clause 30 (1) (i) of the Bill.
 
Clause 30(1)(j)
19.       This Clause provides for cooperation and collaboration by the proposed University apart from other universities
with “other agencies”. The Committee feels that there is a possibility of considering agencies, which are private and
might be for profit.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words ‘not for profit’ may be added before the word
‘agencies’ in page 10, line 15 of Clause 30 (1) (j).
 
 Clause 35(3)  
20.       Clause 35 pertains to conditions of service of employees. According to sub-clause (3) of this Clause, the decision
of the Tribunal of Arbitration shall be final and no suit shall lie in any civil court in respect of the matters decided by it. 
This sub-clause gives an impression that the employees were debarred from all other judicial remedies against the
decision of the Tribunal.  The Committee is aware that no Act can debar the remedies available under Articles 226 and
32 of the Constitution.  The Bill also doesn’t intend to do this.  The Committee, however, recommends that the following
Explanation may be added in the said sub-clause for removing the erroneous impression in this regard.
             “This does not preclude the employees from availing the remedies provided for under Articles 226 & 32 of the
Constitution.”
 
Clause 39
21.       This Clause provides for the final authority in respect of any question regarding election or appointment of a
member of any authority or other body of the University.  The Committee notes that the Bill nowhere mentions about an
elected membership of an authority of the University.  The Committee is of considered opinion that ideally the
composition/membership of these bodies should have been provided in the Statute itself as was done in the case of
Allahabad University. In view of the fact that the composition of authorities of the university would be subsequently
decided by the university bodies, the Committee wishes to emphasise the need for having elected elements in all the
bodies/authority of the university.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable mention for the purpose be
made in the Bill at appropriate places.  The Committee further recommends that an enabling provision must be provided
in the Act itself to ensure democratization in true spirit.
Clause 46
22.       Clause 46 pertains to Transitional Provisions. The Committee is of the considered opinion that since the first
officers and authorities of the university is to be appointed or nominated by the Central Government, their term of offices
as provided in transitional provisions should not be long enough. The Committee notes that in some cases it is five years
and in others it is three years.  It, therefore, recommends that the term of office of the first Chancellor, the first Vice-

Chancellor as well as other officers and bodies provided in various sub-clauses of Clause 46 on page 13 should be
reduced from five and three years to three and two years respectively.     
 
THE SCHEDULE
 
Clause 6 and 7 (b), (c) and (d) of the Statutes
23.       The Committee notes that these provision of the Statute provided in the Schedule mention about College
Development Council but this body is not amongst the authorities of the university.  The Department clarified that it was
mentioned ‘erroneously’.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that name of this body be deleted from the above
clauses.
 
Clause 17 of the Statutes
24.       The Committee notes that in case of the ‘Finance Committee’, while its composition has been given, there is no
representation from the University Court.  The Committee opines that University Court being the largest body should
have representation in the Finance Committee. The Committee, therefore, recommends that  a new sub-clause “atleast
one person to be nominated by the Court” may be added immediately after line 11 of Clause 17 of the Statutes on page
22 of the Bill.
 
Clause 37 of Statutes
25.       The Committee is of considered opinion that the Act must provide for elected representation of students, teachers
and non-teaching staff in all authoritative bodies of the University and ensure their right to form associations.  However,
the Committee found no such provision for students.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words ‘two
elected representatives of students” should find place in the constitution of the Student Council and Clause 37 be
redrafted accordingly.
 
26.       The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of the Bill without any amendments.
27.       The enacting formula and the title are adopted with consequential changes.
28.       The Committee recommends that the Bill may be passed after incorporating the amendment additions suggested
by it. 
29.       The Committee would like the Department to submit a note with reasons on the recommendations/suggestions,
which could not be incorporated in the Bill.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present this Hundred Seventy-Eighth Report of the Committee on
the National Institutes of Technology Bill, 2006 of the Department of Secondary & Higher Education, Ministry of
Human Resource Development.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee, The Chairman,
Rajya Sabha had referred the National Institutes of Technology Bill, 2006, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 22nd
May, 2006 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.         The Committee considered various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Secondary &
Higher Education, and also heard the Secretary and other officials of that Department on the said Bill in its meeting held
on 13
th June, 19th July and 8th September, 2006.

REPORT
 
1.         Eight Regional Engineering Colleges (RECs), two in each regions-east, west, north and south, were set up in
early sixties as joint and co-operative ventures of the Central and State Governments concerned with a view to providing
the required technical manpower for the industrial projects being contemplated during the 2nd Five-Year Plan (1956-61).
These institutes were registered as autonomous bodies under the Society Registration Act 1860 and affiliated to the State
Universities in their respective regions. Gradually, 17 RECs were set up in the country.
2.         Main aim of setting up the RECs was to create the required technical manpower by providing undergraduate
education and training in different branches of engineering & technology. Further the RECs were also envisaged to

178th Report of Human Resourse Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/178threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:48]
function as pace setters and to provide academic leadership to the technical institutions in their respective regions.
3.         The Programme of Action (POA), 1992 of the National Policy on Education, 1986, had recommended that "in
order to enable the RECs to effectively act as pace setting institutes and to provide leadership to the technical education
institutes in respective regions, steps will be taken to give maximum autonomy and detailed review will be conducted for
deciding the future thought and orientation so as to broaden their horizon by improving the existing management
structure." The Union Government accordingly, set up a High Powered Review Committee (HPRC) under the
Chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar, Director-General, Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR) in 1996.
4.         The High Powered Review Committee submitted its report entitled "Strategic Road Map for Academic
Excellence of Future RECs" in 1998. The main recommendations of HPRC were as follows:-
 
(a)        The Institutes be empowered to award degrees through an Act of Parliament.
(b)        The Chairman of the Board should be a non-official of eminence and that he/she must not hold any
statutory powers of execution in the RECs.
(c)        The Head of the Institute should be a person of distinction in Engineering and Technology who, apart
from leading the Institute, will provide its public face.
(d)        The demand for new RECs may be examined on a case to case basis.
(e)        RECs should be encouraged to admit foreign and NRI students, both in undergraduate and postgraduate
programmes. These students be admitted against seats in addition to the seats meant for Indian Students.
 
5.         After due consultation with the State Governments, the Government of India decided to convert these RECs into
National Institutes of Technology (NITs) with the status of a Deemed to be University and structural changes in
governance. The Union Cabinet accorded its approval on February 19, 2003 for taking over the 17 RECs as NITs and
make them fully funded Institutes of the Central Government. The Cabinet in its meeting held on November 6, 2003
decided to upgrade the Bihar College of Engineering, Patna to the status of an NIT with full Central funding.
Subsequently, the Cabinet also cleared two proposals for converting Government Engineering College, Raipur and
Tripura Engineering College, Agartala to that of NITs in its meetings held on November 10, 2005 and February 23, 2006
respectively, thereby enhancing total number of NITs to 20 in the country.
6.         The philosophy behind making NITs as fully funded institutes of the Central Government was to upgrade them as
National Centres of Excellence for developing technical manpower, create conducive work atmosphere and provide
academic autonomy. The annual intake in all NITs since the take over has gone up substantially both at Undergraduate
and Postgraduate level of engineering & technology. The annual intake at UG level has increased from 5800 to 7200
while in PG it has gone up from about 1500 to 2500. Besides, the increase in intake, NITs have also started introducing
many new courses in emerging areas of science & technology such as bio-technology. Nationwide, NITs are a preferred
destination of students after IITs. These Institutes therefore need to be strengthened further.
 
7.         The proposed National Institutes of Technology Bill, 2006 brings all the NITs under its ambit. The Committee
was informed that this Bill was being proposed in the light of the following reasons:-
 
(a)        The High Power Review Committee (HPRC) had recommended that these institutes be developed as
autonomous and flexible academic institutions of excellence to enable them to function most effectively
through responsive and relevant academic programmes in the light of sweeping changes taking place in
the industrial environment in post liberalized India and rapidly changing scene of technical education
globally. Additionally, the new national perspective on technology, as a key instrument of development
and growth, needed to be embodied in the very character and functions of NITs.
 
(b)        There are seven IITs in the country and all of them are functioning under an umbrella Act viz; the
Institutes of Technology Act, 1961. On a similar pattern, it is proposed to bring all the NITs under an
umbrella legislation. Therefore, the proposed Bill would provide necessary legal framework in designing
a robust structure for governance and development.
(c)        The proposed Bill will also help and encourage the NITs to become "centres of excellence".
(d)        The proposed Bill would enhance the status of NITs and give a boost to Post Graduate technical
education and research.
(e)        The proposed Bill will provide academic, administrative and financial autonomy to these Institutes.

8.         The Committee asked if all the NITs could be brought under the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961, because
having two sets of similar Acts might not be that fruitful an exercise. The Committee, was informed by the
representatives of the Department that since the IITs had gained an international repute whereas, the NITs are still to
attain this status, it would be not proper to place the NITs also under the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961. The
Committee was informed that there were substantial differences between the two categories of technical Institutes. IITs
have a specialized high level entrance examination and are funded on a very different scale. Apprehensions were voiced
that brand equity of IITs may be adversely affected, given the differences in their evolution, extent of funding
methodology and composition of student intake.
9.         The Committee observes that NITs also have a Region/State specific focus as they cater to the needs of the local
industry. In the governance structure that is envisaged in the Bill, NITs would have enough autonomy to maintain their
individuality.   Taking note of the fact that NITs have their own admission policies as far as giving specific preference to
local students is concerned, the Committee enquired about the impact of the Bill on the interests of local students. The
Committee is happy to note that the existing admission policy would continue under the proposed Act and there would
be no change in the composition of the student intake. It believes that the NITs will develop and grow faster separately
than with the IITs. In this backdrop the Committee suggests following amendments in the Bill:-
Clause 5 (d)
 
10.       The Committee is of the considered opinion that the Clause 5 (d) allows a status quo and takes away any
possibility of improvement in service conditions of the employees of NITs as regards pension, leave, gratuity, Provident
fund and other. The Committee recommends that the service conditions of the employees should have uniform
application in all the NITs.  Accordingly, the Department should bring necessary change in the clause with a view to
ensuring uniformity in service conditions, pensions etc. in all the Institutes.
11.       The Committee is also wary of the words “duly altered by the statutes” in page 2, line 45 of Clause 5 (d).  The
Committee feels that this provides scope to alter to the disadvantage of the tenure employees in terms of their
remuneration and conditions of service.  The Committee recommends that it must be ensured that alteration in service
conditions should not be to the disadvantage of the employees.  Accordingly, clause 5 (d) may be redrafted.
12.       Committee has been informed that at present employees of 17 NITs are enjoying the facility of Pension Scheme
and GPF Scheme. Employees of the three remaining NITs i.e.,  Kurukshetra, Jalandhar and Silchar are not getting this
facility. A representation was also received by the Committee from the Chairman, Board of Governors, NIT,
Kurukshetra requesting for bringing parity in the NITs so far as Pension/GPF was concerned. On a specific query in this
regard, the Committee was informed that as per the Fourth Pay Commission recommendations Pension Scheme on the
pattern of Central Government Rules was extended to Central autonomous organizations by the Central Government,
State Governments were responsible to take decision on introduction of Pension Scheme in the RECs. All the State
Governments except Punjab, Haryana and Assam have introduced Pension Scheme in the RECs. The Committee has
been given to understand that the reason for non-introduction of Pension Scheme the three RECs might be huge financial
implications on the part of respective State Governments.
13.       The Committee notes that all the 17 RECs were converted into NITs by granting them Deemed to be University
Status with 100% central funding from the financial year 2003-04. On the request of the three NITs, the issue of
introduction of Pension Scheme was referred to the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) on 8
th March,
2004. The proposal was, however, not found acceptable. Reason given was that with the introduction of new pension
scheme from 1
st January, 2004, permission to any autonomous body to introduce Pension Scheme on Government of
India pattern would not be appropriate.
 
14.       The Committee is not fully convinced by the justification given by the Ministry of Finance. From the papers
submitted to the Committee, it is evident that the respective Board of Governors of all the three RECs of Jalandhar,
Kurukshetra and Silchar had approved introduction of Pension/GPF Scheme for their employees at the right time, which
could not materialize due to financial constraints of the State Governments. The Committee strongly feels that the
Pension Scheme should be made applicable to all the NITs only exception being those employees who joined service on
or after 01.01.2004. All the RECs after getting the status of NITs have the same mandate and enjoy the same status and
perform the same functions. This uniformity should be extended to the service conditions of employees also. One time
exception can be made and the Department should pursue this issue if need be, at the highest level so that rightful
demands of employees of NITs of Kurukshetra, Jalandhar and Silchar are accepted.
Clause 6 
15.       The Committee recommends that a new sub clause enabling the Institutes to undertake consultancy in the areas/

disciplines relevant to the Institutes may be added.
Clause 6 (1) (n)  
16.       Clause 6 relates to powers of Institutes.  As per Clause 6 (1) (n), the Institute shall have the power "to do all such
things as may be necessary, incidental or conducive to the attainment of all or any of the objects of the Institute".  The
Committee finds that objects of the NITs have not been given in the Bill. The Committee is of the considered opinion
that objects of the Institute be clearly defined in the Bill itself at appropriate place.
Clause 9 (3)
17.       As per clause 9(3), the Institute shall be bound to comply with the directions issued by the Visitor. However, no
time-frame has been indicated. The Committee therefore, recommends that the words “within reasonable time” may be
added in page 4, line 9 of Clause 9 (3) after the words “.... with such directions”.
Clause 11
18.       The Committee is of the considered opinion that state’s say in representation in BOG appears to be negligible in
the Bill.  The Committee recommends that suitable addition be made for consultation with State Governments in Clause
11.
Clause 11 (a)
19.       Clause 11 specifies the composition of the Board of Governors.The Committee is of the view that the
Chairperson of the Board of Governor should be an eminent person in the technical field.  The Committee recommends
that this fact must be mentioned appropriately in clause 11 (a) itself.
Clause 11 (f)
20.       As per clause 11 (f), two professors of the Institute to be nominated by the Senate will be members of the Board
of Governors. The Committee recommends that instead of two professors, one Professor and one Reader/Lecturer may
be nominated to the Board of Governors. Clause 11 (f) may be modified accordingly.
Clause 12 (c)
21.       The Committee notes that the term of office of a member nominated under clause (f) of Section 11 shall be two
years from the 1st day of January of the year in which he is nominated.  The logic behind giving a retrospective effect to
terms of office of such members nominated under clause (f) of Section 11 is not clear.  The Committee recommends that
the term of office of a member nominated under clause (f) of Section 11 shall be made two years from the date of his/her
nomination.
Clause 12 (f)
22.       The Committee notes that Clause 12 (f) allows an outgoing member to continue in office until another person is
nominated as a member in his place.  The Committee is of considered view that this provision leaves possibility of
making delay in the nomination of a new member for extraneous considerations.  The Committee recommends that the
Bill should clearly specify maximum period in which such nomination has to be done.  The Committee recommends that
insertion to this effect be made in the Bill at appropriate places.
Clause 13 (2) (f)
23.       Clause 13 (2) (f) requires the Board to submit the annual report, the annual accounts and the budget estimates of
the Institute for the next financial year together with a statement of its development plans to the Council.  The
Committee feels that it would be better if this power of the Council were a little moderated. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the words “and the Council shall ordinarily accept the statement made to it” be added after the words
“…development plans” in page 5, line 15 of Clause 13 (2) (f).
Clause 14 (d)
24.       Clause 14 provides for the constitution of the Senate. As per sub-clause (d), three persons, not being employees
of the Institute are to be nominated by the Chairperson in consultation with the Director. The Committee strongly feels
that under this category, one member should be a woman.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the words
“one of whom to be woman” may be added after the words “three persons” in page 5, line 25 of clause 14 (d).
Clause 14 (e)
25.       The Committee recommends that the Statutes must provide for the representation of students in the Senate.  The
Committee accordingly, recommends that the words “and students” be added after the words “…of the Staff” in page 5,
line 28 of clause 14 (e).
26.       The Committee further recommends that the Statutes in this regard must also provide for election of staff and
students on the Senate. The staff and students should be elected rather than being nominated on the Senate. 
Clause 17
27.       Clause 17 pertains to Director and Deputy Director of Institute.  The Committee finds no mention of the term of
office of the Director and Deputy Director.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a term of five years may be

178th Report of Human Resourse Development

specified for the Director and Deputy Director in Clause 17 of the Bill.
Clause 18
28.       The Committee also finds no mention of the term of office of the Registrar.  The Committee is of the considered
opinion that the Registrar should be taken on deputation for a period of three years.  The Committee, accordingly,
recommends the Department to redraft Clause 18 suitably.
Clause 25
29.       Clause 25 provides for the items on which the Statutes may be made by an Institute.  The Committee has the
impression that through this Bill, the Institutes are being provided with uniform management/administrative structure,
service conditions, rules and regulations and procedure for appointment of employee, pensions, etc.  However, the
Committee is of the opinion that Clause 25(g) leaves the possibility of difference in service conditions of the employees
in different Institutes.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Clause 25 (g) be suitably amended in the Bill so that
there is uniformity on the subject contained in Clause 25 (g) across the board.
 
30.       The Committee also takes note of Clause 25 (n) whereunder matters regarding the meetings of the Board, the
Senate, or any Committee, the quorum at such meetings and the procedure to be followed in the conduct of their business
is to be laid down in the Statutes. The Committee is of the view that the subject matter contained in Clause 25 (n) be
placed in the Bill itself and laid out clearly. Necessary amendments may, accordingly, be made in the Bill.
Clause 26(1)
 
31.       Clause 26 deals with the procedure regarding the making of statutes.  Clause 26 (1) entails that the first statutes
of each Institute shall be framed by the Central Government with the prior approval of the Visitor. The Committee notes
that under the IIT Act, 1961, the first Statutes of each Institute shall be framed by the Council with the previous approval
of the Visitor. The Committee is of the view that same provision should be there the NIT Act also.  The Committee
accordingly, recommends that the words “Central Government” be substituted by the word ‘Council’ in page 7, line 33
of clause 26 (1).
Clause 29
32.       Clause 29 relates to Tribunal of Arbitration.  The Committee considers the redressal of grievances of employees
paramount to the principles of justice and equity.  The Committee finds that as per clause 29 (1) any dispute out of a
contract between an Institute and any of its employees shall, at the request of the employee concerned or at the instance
of the Institute be referred to a Tribunal of Arbitration.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that the option
granted to the Institute to refer the dispute for arbitration can be exploited against the wishes of the aggrieved employee
who might be inclined to approach the court.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words “or at the instance
of the Institute” may be deleted from page 8, line 26 of clause 29 (1).
33.       The Committee also notes that according to sub-clause (2) of this Clause, the decision of the Tribunal of
Arbitration shall be final and shall not be questioned in any court.  This sub-clause gives an impression that the
employees were debarred from all other judicial remedies against the decision of the Tribunal.  The Committee is aware
that no Act can debar the remedies available under Articles 226 and 32 of the Constitution.  The Bill also doesn’t intend
to do this.  The Committee, however, recommends that the following Explanation may be added in the said sub-clause
for removing the erroneous impression in this regard.
            “This does not preclude the employees from availing the remedies provided for under Articles 226 & 32 of the
Constitution.”
 
Chapter III - The Council
Clause 30
34.       Clauses 30 to 34 under chapter III deal with the establishment of the Council, its terms of office, vacancies
among, and allowances payable to members, its functions, rule making power. However, there is no stipulation regarding
the minimum number of times the council shall meet every year.  The Committee recommends that the Department may
suitably redraft the Bill to ensure that the Council meets at least once every year.
Clause 35 (a)
35.       The Committee notes that Clause 35 (a) saves acts and proceedings of the Council, or any Institute or Board or
Senate on the ground of any vacancy in, or defect in the constitution there of.  The Committee is of the considered
opinion that saving any act or proceeding of a body despite a defect in its constitution is likely to be misused. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that this provision may be redrafted suitably so that no act or proceeding gets
validated despite a defect in the constitution of any decision-making bodies or any defect in the election, nomination or

JANARDAN DWIVEDI
Chairman,

REPORT
 
The Sikkim University Bill, 2006 seeks to establish and incorporate a teaching and affiliating University in the state of
Sikkim by the name ‘Sikkim University’ with a view to cater to the needs and aspirations of the people of the State and
to minimize the imbalance in educational facilities in the North Eastern Region.
2.         According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, there is no university in Sikkim and the
colleges of the state are affiliated to the North Bengal University of West Bengal.  These are mostly degree colleges and
are following the courses and syllabi designed by the North Bengal University, which do not meet the specific
requirements of the state of Sikkim.  Due to lack of post-graduate courses in Sikkim, majority of the students do not get
opportunity to pursue higher studies.  But the Sikkim government, with its limited resources, is not in a position to
provide adequate funding for the establishment and running a university of its own.  Besides, existence of a good
number of central universities in other States of the region, viz., at Kohima, Silchar, Tezpur, Aizawl, Imphal and
Shillong has caused a huge imbalance in educational facilities within the region, and a consequent migration of teachers,
students and researchers in search of better infrastructural and academic facilities to other States.
3.         The Committee was informed that the University Grants Commission (UGC) had commissioned the Educational
Consultants India Limited (Ed.CIL) to assess the existing facilities for higher education in Sikkim and also to determine
the likely growth in the student strength/enrolment in the next 2-3 years and the requirement for creation of necessary
structure to cater to those needs, either by extending the jurisdiction of the North Eastern Hill University, Shillong or by
establishing a state university or a central university in the state.  According to the report of Ed.CIL/UGC, establishment
of a central university would be the most viable option to cater to the higher education needs of the state.
4.         Accordingly, the Sikkim University Bill 2006 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha for the establishment and
incorporation of the Sikkim University, Gangtok as a central university. The Bill is broadly based on the pattern of the
University of Manipur, the most recent of the North-Eastern Universities.
5.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:-
The Bill seeks to establish and incorporate a teaching and affiliating university in the state of Sikkim under the proposed
Central Act by the name of 'Sikkim University' with perpetual succession and common seal and to provide for the
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
The University would be a teaching and affiliating university with its Headquarters at Gangtok and territorial
jurisdiction extending to the whole of the State of Sikkim.
It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities, particularly of those of the North-Eastern
region.
The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall be
laid before both Houses of Parliament along with the audit report and the annual report of the University.
During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers and the constitution of the first Authorities of the
University would be made by the Visitor for specified terms.
 
6.         The Committee after going through all the papers and documents and hearing the Secretary, Department of
Secondary and Higher Education took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.   It suggested the following
amendments/additions to various clauses of the Bill.
Clause 5(ix)
7.1       Clause 5(ix), page 3, provides that the University shall have the power ‘to appoint persons working in any other
University or organization as teachers of the University for a specified period.’
7.2       The Committee is of the considered opinion that the word ‘organization’ in this clause leaves some scope for
different interpretations. The Department clarified that the word ‘organization’ generally meant ‘a teaching or a research
institution, other than a university.’  The Committee feels that this needs to be specified in the Bill with a view to
remove any ambiguity about the nature of the organization.
Clause 5(xix)
8.1       Clause 5(xix), page 4, provides that the University shall have the powers ‘to confer autonomous status on a

179th Report of Human Resourse Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/179thReport.htm[01-07-2016 15:28:48]
College or an Institution or a Department, as the case may be, in accordance with the Statutes.’
8.2       The Committee feels that the provision of the clause amounts to giving unbridled powers to the University for
conferring autonomous status on a College, an Institution or a Department.  The Committee is of the opinion that some
kind of requirements and conditions necessary for making an institution autonomous may be specified. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that Clause 5(xix) may be suitably amended.
Clause 21 (1)
9.1       Clause 21(1), page 7, provides that the constitution of the Court and the term of office of its members shall be
prescribed by the Statutes.  The Committee however, notes that the Statutes appended to the Bill do not provide for the
constitution of the Court as well as the term of office of its members.
9.2       The Committee feels that the Court being the apex body of the university, provision for its constitution and term
of office of its members be provided in the first statutes itself.
Clauses 22(2), 23(2), 24(2), 25 and 26
10.1     Clause 22(2), page 8, provides that the constitution of the Executive Council, the term of office of its members
and its powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
10.2     Clause 23(2), page 8, provides that the constitution of the Academic Council, the term of office of its members
and its powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
10.3     Clause 24(2), page 8, provides that the constitution of the College Development Council, the term of office of its
members and its powers and functions shall be prescribed by the Statutes.
10.4     Clause 25, page 8, provides that the constitution, powers and functions of the Board of Studies shall be
prescribed by the Statutes.
10.5     Clause 26, page 8, provides that the constitution, powers and functions of the Finance Committee shall be
prescribed by the Statutes.
10.6     The Committee notes that the Executive Council, Academic Council, College Development Council, Board of
Studies and Finance Committee are the important decision-making bodies of the University.  The Statutes appended to
the Bill contain provisions only about the powers and functions of these bodies but are silent about their constitution and
term of office.
 
10.7     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the provisions for the constitution and term of office of the
Executive Council, Academic Council,  College Development Council, Board of Studies and Finance Committee, also
be included within corpus of the first Statutes itself.
 
Clause 30(1)(i)
11.       Clause 30, page 10, deals with power to make Ordinances. The Committee finds that this sub-clause provides for
making special arrangements ‘for the residence, discipline and teaching of women students.’  The Committee is of the
considered opinion that while this is valid in terms of residence and specific courses for women students, the word

profit’ may be appropriately added in page 10, line 25 of Clause 30 (1) (k).

13.1     Clause 35(3), page 11, provides that the decision of the Tribunal, in respect of any dispute arising out of the

impression in this regard.

REPORT
            The Tripura University Bill, 2006 seeks to convert the existing Tripura University, Agartala, into a Central
University with a view to cater to the needs and aspirations of the people of the State and to minimize the imbalance in
educational facilities in the North Eastern Region.
2.         The Tripura University was established at Agartala in 1987, under the Tripura University Act, 1987 enacted by
the Tripura Legislative Assembly. 
3.         According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, the Arunachal Pradesh government, with its
limited resources, is not in a position to provide adequate funding for development of the Tripura University.  Besides,
existence of a good number of central universities in other States of the region, viz., at Kohima, Silchar, Tezpur, Aizawl,
Imphal and Shillong has caused a huge imbalance in educational facilities within the region, and a consequent migration
of teachers, students and researchers in search of better infrastructural and academic facilities to other States.  There has,
therefore, been persistent demand for conversion of the Tripura University into a central university.   
4.         The Committee was informed that the University Grants Commission (UGC) had constituted a Committee to
consider the issue of conversion of Tripura University into a central university and to estimate the quantum of funds
required for up-gradation of its existing facilities and staff.  The UGC Committee visited the University and had
discussions with the authorities/officers of the State government, the Vice-Chancellor, teaching and non-teaching
employees as well as the students of the University. The Committee after taking stock of the existing infrastructure,
recommended conversion of the Tripura University into a             full-fledged central university through an Act of
Parliament. 
5.         Accordingly, the Tripura University Bill 2006 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha for the establishment and
incorporation of Tripura University as a central university and for repealing of the existing Tripura University Act,
1987, enacted by the Tripura Legislative Assembly. 
6.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:-
The Bill seeks to establish and incorporate the existing Tripura University, a state university of Tripura, under the
proposed Central Act by the same name of 'Tripura University' with perpetual succession and common seal and to
provide for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
The University would be a teaching and affiliating university with its Headquarters at Agartala and territorial
jurisdiction extending to the whole of the State of Tripura.
It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities, particularly of those of the North-Eastern
region.
All colleges, Institutions, Faculties and Departments affiliated to, or admitted to the privileges of, or maintained by, the
existing Tripura University shall stand affiliated to, or admitted to the privilege of, or maintained by the University.
The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall be
laid before both Houses of Parliament along with the audit report and the annual report of the University.
During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers and the constitution of the first Authorities of the
University would be made by the Visitor for specified terms.
7.         The Committee after going through all the papers and documents and hearing the Secretary, Department of
Secondary and Higher Education took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.   It suggested the following
amendments/additions to various clauses of the Bill.

different interpretations. The Department clarified that the word ‘organization’ generally meant ‘a teaching or a research
institution, other than a university.’  The Committee feels that this needs to be specified in the Bill with a view to
remove any ambiguity about the nature of the organization.
Clause 6(xix)
9.1       Clause 6(xix), page 5, provides that the University shall have the powers ‘to confer autonomous status on a
College or an Institution or a Department, as the case may be, in accordance with the Statutes.’

REPORT
The Rajiv Gandhi University Bill, 2006 seeks to convert the existing Rajiv Gandhi University, Itanagar, into a Central
University with a view to cater to the needs and aspirations of the people of the State and to minimize the imbalance in
educational facilities in the North Eastern Region.
2.         The Rajiv Gandhi University was established at Itanagar in 1984, under the Rajiv Gandhi University Act, 1984
enacted by the Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly. 
3.According to the Department of Secondary and Higher Education, the Arunachal Pradesh government, with its limited
resources, is not in a position to provide adequate funding for development of the Rajiv Gandhi University.  Besides,
existence of a good number of central universities in other States of the region, viz., at Kohima, Silchar, Tezpur, Aizawl,
Imphal and Shillong has caused a huge imbalance in educational facilities within the region, and a consequent migration
of teachers, students and researchers in search of better infrastructural and academic facilities to other States.  There has,
therefore, been persistent demand for conversion of the Rajiv Gandhi University into a central university.   
4.         The Committee was informed that the University Grants Commission (UGC) had constituted a Committee to
consider the issue of conversion of Rajiv Gandhi University into a central university and to estimate the quantum of
funds required for up-gradation of its existing facilities and staff.  The UGC Committee visited the University and had
detailed discussions with the authorities/officers of the State government, the Vice-Chancellor, teaching and non-
teaching employees as well as the students of the University.  The Committee after taking stock of the existing
infrastructure, recommended conversion of the Rajiv Gandhi University into a full-fledged central university through an
Act of Parliament. 
5.         Accordingly, the Rajiv Gandhi University Bill 2006, was introduced in the Rajya Sabha for the establishment
and incorporation of Rajiv Gandhi University as a central university and for repealing of the existing Rajiv Gandhi
University Act, 1984, enacted by the Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly. 
6.         The salient features of the aforesaid Bill are as under:-
The Bill seeks to establish and incorporate the existing Rajiv Gandhi University, a state university of Arunachal
Pradesh, under the proposed Central Act by the same name of 'Rajiv Gandhi University' with perpetual succession and
common seal and to provide for the matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
 
The University would be a teaching and affiliating university with its Headquarters at Itanagar and territorial jurisdiction
extending to the whole of the State of Arunachal Pradesh.
 
It would function broadly on the pattern of the existing central universities, particularly of those of the North-Eastern
region.
All Colleges, Institutions, Faculties and Departments affiliated to, or admitted to the privileges of, or maintained by the
existing Rajiv Gandhi University shall stand affiliated to, or admitted to the privilege of, or maintained by the
University.
The annual accounts of the University shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall be
laid before both Houses of Parliament along with the audit report and the annual report of the University.
During the transitional period, the appointment of the first Officers and the constitution of the first Authorities of the
University would be made by the Visitor for specified terms.
7.         The Committee after going through all the papers and documents and hearing the Secretary, Department of
